Recommended, mostly out of respect: this is the game the entire genre has been trying to be for 25 years.

review:
4AM. Insomnia. What to do? What to play?

Team Fortress Classic for the first time ever apparently.

I booted into a populated server. People and bots harmoniously obliterated each other until a vote was held and all the bots vanished. Only humans remained, "hawing" as they jumped and "gah-ing" as they died.

I used to play the ♥♥♥♥ out of Team Fortress 2. I still pop in occasionally but avoid 2fort because I HATE it with a bloody passion. It always felt like you're fighting tooth and nail to make any sort of progress against and with people who are TOO into it for it to be fun. My friends LOVED it so I would grit my teeth and mostly Engineer camp in quieter areas because I just hated the whole loop of the map that much.

This is relevant because, cosmic joke of jokes, the first map I encountered was 2fort. *sigh*  But I ended up appreciating the experience of the foundation. Maybe I would have hated it too back in this game's heyday like, maybe it suffered from the same stalemate and bottlenecking commotion. But with a handful of people where no one was blasting ♥♥♥♥♥♥ music or shouting racial slurs into their over-cranked mic, dare I say it was... pleasant? It was a little odd seeing the framework skinned 'primitively' as I was used to the sort of rustic set dressings and plentiful details modern 2fort has but I think the sparseness helped me understand why the loop is satisfying. The map has good bones. Modern 2fort is visually a lot and coupled with the fact it's always a full map, it definitely could use some room to breathe. Especially from cheaters who shoot you through the spawn room's door. 

As for feel of play, DOOM, Quake, Wolfenstein come to mind. Maybe not as sluggish as my memory says they were but I also wasn't super big into gaming yet, or shooters for that matter. My friends would drag me into gaming cafes for Counterstrike and such and I grew to appreciate the quickness versus the killness. Killness is a word now. :p

Anyway, I think it was on Well I noticed a sort of swinging jazzy footfall pattern on some of the metal scaffolding. Like your dude was dancing through life, (or death) and it made me wonder if anyone has taken it and made a track. That discovery was more exciting to me than figuring out how to lining up Demo's bombs just right or mowing down a flag taker. It's probably odd to be appreciating ambiance and texture over kill counts and such but that's who I am when I'm not being coerced into competitive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. :p

Speaking of classes, the Medic (my preferred class) was really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bizarre. He felt like a different class though I think he still has his needle gun of doom but the projectiles are triangular which like... That's fine. 1999 graphics, what are you going to do? But what really threw me was healing. No healing visual, no charge, no uber, just a box that you have to be close enough to your target that their readout pops up in the lower left corner of the screen so you can initiate healing. Maybe it's because this was my first time playing but it was finicky as ♥♥♥♥. People jumping all around and you have to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ glue one eye to the corner to know you're close enough to activate and the other is watching madmen be mad. Chameleons would love this class if they could play video games. I'm sure of it!

Anyway, I really enjoyed comparing the two in my mind's eye. TF2 provided a refreshed update on a lot of fronts but I can appreciate a right click for a whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ drop down menu. You need to build a sentry? Right click. Call for Medic? Right click. Change your character? Right. Click. However, pressing Y and not being able to see what you're typing until after you hit Enter, is criminal but perhaps that was just the quirk of the server I landed on.

2 hours to run around and give the whole roster a test drive, enjoy some levels in a new olde scope, and even capture a flag or two with a chill and ancient vibe. It may not have cured my sleeping troubles but the distraction it provided woke me up to some fun.

Edit: Cleaned up a few typos. We'll blame soup brain for those. :p

review:
Probably a better game than the original Half-Life.

Opposing Force lets you take on a new role as a soldier, fighting for the other side and understanding their motives and mission. It follows the same story from a different set of eyes, allowing you to experience it differently, but the greatest moments occur when situations you previously played as Morgan Freeman intersect. 

Level design is still excellent, although finding the right path sometimes proved difficult, leading to some frustration and time wasted. New, most of the time annoying to face but interesting enemies. Great atmosphere. More weapons to cycle through with cool concepts and overall funnier to play with. Night vision. Tactical combat where you fight alongside a squad with specific roles but mostly unreliable and poor AI.

Short but fulfilling.

review:
Opposing Force is a great expansion to Half-Life 1, this time putting you in the shoes of a military corporal. While you technically play as one of Gordon’s enemies, without spoiling too much, you are mostly focused on surviving rather than carrying out some morally dubious mission.

The game is about half the length of Half-Life and keeps the same core gameplay while adding quite a few new weapons, enemies, and other mechanics. This helps it feel like a proper expansion rather than just more of the exact same Half-Life.

It is a bit of a shame that the game was not made by Valve and was never confirmed to be canon, so it feels more like a possible scenario than a real piece of Half-Life lore. Still, I really liked what they did with the story and how naturally they integrated it into the events and world of the original game.

If you enjoyed Half-Life 1, this is an easy recommendation and almost a must-play.

review:
Just for context, I've had this game in my library for as long as I can remember and never played it until I saw somebody doing this idea on Facebook and I figured I'd give it a shot as well:

I let a wheel randomly land on one of my games I have not played in my Steam Library and I then play it for one hour and write an honest review.


This is a classic for sure; I enjoyed the lack of hand holding this game has as well as the difficulty; after playing it for an hour, I would say that this one is a great game, and I definitely would revisit this game again in the future to continue playing it. I can definitely see why this game won Game of the Year.

review:
Opposing Force is my favorite Half-Life expansion. I actually like it even more than the original game. It is one of those games I never get tired of playing over and over again. Being able to see the events of a game universe from the perspective of the enemy and understand their motivations is one of the reasons I love this game. Playing as a HECU soldier sent to cover up the events at Black Mesa is truly a completely different experience.

The training section at the beginning also does a good job of making us feel like a soldier. Here, we learn how to use Night Vision and how to climb and swing from ropes to jump across gaps. The sections where we fight alongside HECU soldiers are really fun. Fighting alongside the soldiers we constantly saw as enemies in Half-Life is a lot of fun this time. Even though the AI sometimes acts stupid.

In the “We Are Not Alone” chapter, we see Gordon Freeman passing through the teleport. Seeing this scene from Shephard's perspective this time is a really nice detail. When we go to Xen through the same teleport, we see Gordon there, and after falling down, we return to the previous save because of the paradox that occurs. The fact that this detail was actually thought out is really nice.

One of my favorite aspects of the game is the new weapons and enemies. The addition of Race X adds some nice variety to the game. The M249 Squad Automatic Weapon and M-40A1 Sniper Rifle are my favorite weapons. I especially love the feeling of power the M249 gives during firefights, and shooting enemies from long range with the M-40A1 is really enjoyable. The Displacer Cannon, one of the new weapons, is also different and cool thanks to its right-click ability. I compare it to the BFG9000 from DOOM. Being able to teleport enemies and, in some situations, send ourselves to a different location is a really nice idea. You need to use its ammunition carefully, but it is very satisfying when used at the right moment.

The only downside is that the game is short. I wish Race X had been explored a little more and that we had gotten a few more new chapters. It also disappoints me that Race X has never been mentioned in any other Half-Life game. Other than that, Opposing Force adds some great things to Half-Life despite being released one year after it, and it is an expansion worth playing on its own.

It has been 26 years since the game was released, but we still have no idea what happened to Corporal Adrian Shephard or Race X. I hope that if Half-Life 3 ever comes out, we get to see something related to them. Surely Valve wouldn't just leave Shephard forgotten somewhere in the interdimensional void. Even a small reference to the story of Opposing Force after 26 years would make me very happy. Despite all these years, it is still one of those games I keep coming back to.

review:
Opposing Force is without a doubt one of the strangest and most unique entries into the Half-Life canon in how different its goals as a game are. Unlike the Valve-produced HL games, Opposing Force isn't trying to be revolutionary or showcase any new crazy technology or push the medium of FPS to uncharted territory. Instead, it's focused on the expected: being a standard expansion pack providing us with more Half-Life. That actually makes Opposing Force and its expansion-pack brethren truly anomalous within the Half-Life canon, and you can see that present in everything from its game and level design to its atmosphere and aesthetic. The levels feel a bit too empty and compressed, attempting to mimic the immersive magic of the original game's portrayal of Black Mesa but being limited by its scope as an expansion pack. The story and its premise are brand-new and intriguing, but is executed with the exact same plot beats of the original.

What you get according to most people is a very derivative Half-Life game. But for me, its attempts to mimic Half-Life's magic quickly endeared me in it sort of gave a very uncanny valley vibe for me. It all feels a bit off and alien, which weirdly enough kinda fits the game's premise of giving us a new perspective of the Black Mesa incident. The weird new enemies that are exclusive to this game and not mentioned at all in base Half-Life give that similar underdog, scrappy vibe that extended-universe media tends to have when trying to add to the canon without being reciprocated by the original developers. For a lot of people that's a con, and understandably so! Maybe it's just from me experiencing and re-experiencing all the mainline Half-Life games and playing the expansion packs last, but the experimental (but not too groundbreaking) gameplay really struck a balance with me-- feeling new and fresh, but still undeniably Half-Life.

And that brings me to where this game shines despite being derivative in a lot of ways. The new stuff it does is just awesome. The brand-new weapons pack so much punch and have this deliciously impactful feel to them: the machine gun, wrench, weird green thingy that shoots spores. This is no doubt largely contributed to by the new Race X aliens, who are INSANELY tanky. I'm seeing others complaining about that fact and it did lead to a lot of frustrating deaths, admittedly, but defeating them remained a dopamine-inducing moment each and every time because of their tankiness.

You also get incentivized a lot more to actually ask NPCs to follow you, primarily because the majority of the NPCs you run into in Opposing Force are fellow Marines who are actually equipped with weaponry to handle the tougher enemies and all have awesome unique roles that honestly make you mourn them a bit when you lose them, contrasted to how comical/apathetic deaths in the original Half-Life could get.

Of course, not everything hits and there's an undeniable level of jank and lack of polish compared to the original Half-Life. You've still got buggy NPC pathfinding, frustrating save points, a few parts where it's insanely easy to get lost or not know what to do next, etc., etc. However, after finally playing Opposing Force for myself, I found it to strangely be a worthwhile and unique entry worth playing in the Half-Life canon despite it on the surface just offering "more Half-Life". In those attempts to be more Half-Life, I've found it kind of ends up being completely unique to the rest of the series, and in a really good way, too.

[h1]Great expansion pack that adds a lot to Half-Life :D[/h1]

Half-Life: Opposing Force, as the name might suggest, is an expansion pack to the base game, in which you play as an enemy Marine, Adrian Shephard, who is being sent into the Black Mesa facility along with other Marines to neutralize it. The gameplay stays relatively the same to the base game, but you get given a much larger variety of weapons, as well as more enemies. Because the expansion pack features important characters, I feel that it matters more to the overall story of Half-Life than the other expansion Blue Shift.
Starting out, the expansion pack already throws a decently sized roster of weapons that you can use your way, which honestly was fantastic, because most encounters with an enemy left you with an incredible amount of choices to how you want to go about it. I think Opposing Force might actually have more weapons than base Half-Life, which, coupled with the even shorter completion time, genuinely makes gunfights stay consistently fresh up until you pretty much beat the game. Some of the weapons also added creative mechanics that I wasn't expecting.
As opposed (haha, get it?🤓) to Blue Shift, the G-man comes has a more prominent role in the game, using him to get his dirty work done, similarly to how he used Gordon in the base game. Not to go too much into spoilery details, this makes Adrian an important character in the story overall, and I can only hope they utilize him for Half-Life 3 (if they ever make it)
All in all, the gameplay, weapons and enemies are all a fresh breath of air that make a worthwhile experience to any fan of Half-Life. There is more story relevance with this expansion pack, so I would definitely recommend this one to anybody who wants to find out what happens in the Black Mesa Research Facility!

review:
I think that despite me playing this game roughly 25+ years into the future, Half-Life 1, even in todays age, is a very good game. Although the graphics are quite clearly not the most latest and the mechanics & aesthetics are very old of the late 1990s when games weren't really all that much prevalent for computers, Half-Life 1 is really good because it was able to build a very interesting story that combined elements of Sci-fi and tried to push past what computers could do in the essence of video games at the time. It's really no wonder why I look at people and they are extremely nostalgic for the game; everything that I have described attributed to people really enjoying the game and being able to also play with others too. But the Sci-Fi & multiplayer aspects of it are not what make it an amazing game to me necessarily. It's kind of like a student studying history or archeology; for me, its looking at what this game did in those times and going through the 'remnants' of it that really brought it straight forward to me. The old aesthetics, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ movement that pissed me the ♥♥♥♥ off a large majority of the time, the 144p sound effects used for the game, the mechanics, seeing all of that packaged in one game created in 1998 is a kind of holy site to see as Half-Life 1 most likely inspired so many games that I love in todays age and, hell, even the damn sounds used for the game I have heard so many damn times in the past it really made me shocked at how changing the game was.

Overall, Half-Life 1 was a really nice experience and I would recommend it to those who are looking for a classic, see the past in present times, or just want a really good game for that matter. Half-Life 1 captivated the minds of so many games, and although I am not in my early 30s, I am happy to have had the experience of playing the game and see what so many people cherished and still do cherish to this day and age.

review:
Half-Life: The Day the FPS Grew Up
Before November 1998, first-person shooters were largely defined by the mold set by Doom and Quake: fast-paced, hyper-violent sprints through disconnected arenas to find colored keycards. Valve Software’s debut title, Half-Life, completely shattered that mold. It proved that a shooter could deliver a grounded, cohesive narrative and an immersive world without ever breaking the first-person perspective or relying on a single cutscene.

The Long Ride In
The genius of Half-Life is evident in its opening five minutes. Instead of dropping you immediately into a firefight with a shotgun in hand, the game places you on an inbound monorail tram. You play as Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist arriving late for work at the Black Mesa Research Facility.

During this unskippable ride, you don't shoot anything. You just watch. You see scientists walking with clipboards, security guards knocking on locked doors, and giant mechs loading cargo. This extended prologue does something revolutionary for the era: it establishes Black Mesa as a functional, mundane workplace before the disaster strikes. When the experimental Anti-Mass Spectrometer violently malfunctions and tears a rift to the alien dimension of Xen, the destruction hits much harder because you saw the facility when it was intact.

An Unbroken Perspective
From the moment Gordon steps off that tram to the final boss fight, the camera never cuts away. You never see Gordon from a third-person cinematic view, and you never lose control of your movement during dialogue. If a scientist is explaining a critical plot point, you are free to listen intently or wander around the room knocking over coffee cups with your iconic crowbar.
This unbroken perspective forces you to inhabit the character completely. You survive the disaster, crawl through flooded elevator shafts, and navigate radioactive coolant vats purely through your own agency. The environment isn't just a backdrop for combat; it is a sprawling, interconnected puzzle. Chapters flow seamlessly into one another—from the sterile laboratories of "Anomalous Materials" to the sun-baked cliff sides of "Surface Tension"—giving the facility a profound sense of scale and geographic logic.

The Illusion of Intelligence
Half-Life also redefined expectations for enemy artificial intelligence. Prior to 1998, enemies typically charged straight at the player until they died. When the government dispatches the Hazardous Environment Combat Unit (HECU) marines to silence both the aliens and the Black Mesa staff, the game shifts from a monster-closet shooter to a tactical battle of wits.
The marines act like a coordinated squad. They use covering fire, flush you out of cover with expertly lobbed grenades, communicate with each other via radio barks, and retreat when wounded. This dynamic AI forced players to completely rethink how they approached combat. You couldn't just circle-strafe in the open; you had to use the environment, funnel enemies into chokepoints, and make use of a wildly creative arsenal that evolved from a simple Glock to tripmines, biological alien weapons, and the devastating experimental Tau Cannon.

A Legacy Set in Stone
Half-Life did not just win Game of the Year awards; it became the new foundational text for game developers. Its highly modifiable GoldSrc engine gave birth to a community of creators who would go on to build industry titans like Counter-Strike, Team Fortress Classic, and Day of Defeat. By treating the player’s intelligence with respect and prioritizing seamless world-building over mindless action, Valve proved that video games were capable of delivering thrilling, cinematic narratives without abandoning the interactivity that makes the medium unique. Half-Life remains a masterwork of pacing and design that every fan of the genre needs to experience.

review:
Gonna start off by saying I forgot how long and challenging HL1 actually was. For a '90s FPS, this has so much going on, even compared to current games. Sure, there's a lot of filler and dead places, but there's also a lot of depth and charm that's missing from the genre today.

I grew up in the boomer shooter era and played most of them, but skipped HL1 until replaying it sometime after beating HL2. The way people talked about Half-Life back before Two was kinda like the niche, hipster indie darling of the FPS genre. It might not seem like it today, but when standing against its peers like Doom, Quake, and WWII shooters, Half-Life just felt more cerebral in comparison.

I think this is in part due to its stellar lighting and atmosphere. At a time when shooting a bullet at a wall and having it leave a mark to provide visual feedback was still a novel idea in game design, Valve took all the building blocks and just ran with them. Another part is probably due to its setting. You weren't fighting demons in hell or nazis in Normandy; you were fighting weird little aliens in a science lab. This just gave the whole thing a vibe that other shooters didn't have, creating more of a slow burn for a genre that was known for its fast-paced action.

I think a ton of progress was made here that raised the bar absurdly high. Just the amount of scripting in the game is something to marvel at if you have any game design or programming inclinations. It's a classic for a reason, and I think it holds up insanely well almost 30 years later. 

Can't wait to play some of the highly praised expansions for the first time!

Basically it's the same as Counter-Strike 1.6, but now with single player mode, just regular matches against where not only you need to win enough rounds and being in lead, but also complete challenges, which at first seemed they were optional, but that isn't the case.  Speaking about bots, bots they are as base game feature for this game, which can be turned on only by server host. Which is right have to have bots.
Back to about singe player mode. It works fine as the game training you for multiplayer matches, by making you to complete challenges, but only as counter-terrorists. Sure basic controls can applied to both teams, but it just doesn't let you experience playing as a terrorist. 
Sure making your own server and playing with bots you can do that. If you can find right servers, multiplayer can be fun, but at least for there isn't a lot of choice, epically which include English language for UI elements, but that's that server problem.

About Counter-Strike: Condition Zero Deleted Scenes, it is as a separate game to access missions. These missions can't be accessed from Condition Zero. However those are disconnected from each other. Because it's called Deleted Scenes then I guess it is understandable why. Basically it's about stopping the enemy from completing their goals, whatever they are. It also have original tools and basic stealth sections.
All missions are interesting of course with ups and downs. 
Well I encounter with some glitches only in the second mission, I was able to get where I shouldn't go, I found out about it, because I saw house texture missing from one side. At some point going back to the start location of mission, sleeping guard is gone, but snoring sound effect still plays out and then going where there was a guard counts as failed mission.

Yeah both games can give you enjoyable experience. Of course each give different experience.

review:
A fun spinoff of the counter trike series. The idea of a story mode for Counter Strike sounds wacky but this one does it pretty well. The levels are varied, quite beautiful and high quality, with a lot of scripted sequences and unique animations - and also a lot of easter eggs. Each one tells its own story and aren't connected in any way. There's even unique equipment you only see here, like a welding tool, deployable mines and a camera to see behind doors and around walls, which add to the tactical feel the game is going for. For some reason the campaign doesn't take you through all the levels, so you're gonna have to select the rest from the World Map option.
I felt all levels were very enjoyable, except maybe the ones were you have to fight a "boss" at the end which is just a bullet sponge. It's pretty tedious, but manageable.
This one was actually developed by Ritual Entertainment, not Valve - the same guys who made the SiN games and Legacy of Kain. I don't know why that isn't specified on the game's page, even if the studio was disbanded. I think they did a splendid job here. However they weren't pretty happy with their game being named "Deleted Scenes" - understandably so.
Highly recommend, especially if you love games like Half Life, as it's in the same vain lol.

review:
Half Life Blue Shift is a short, fun, and amazing expansion that covers everything that made the original Half Life perfect, but from the perspective of a security officer.

The story is short but interesting enough to make you care about what is happening around the player. It is also tied enough to the events of the original game, which makes the whole experience feel a bit more connected rather than just being a fully separate story.

The gunplay is essentially the same as the original Half Life, although sadly you have fewer weapons to play around with. One of the biggest changes is how body armor works, instead of relying on HEV charging stations or items, you recover armor by picking up helmets and  vests that are around the facility. Even though these pickups sometimes can be quite far apart, there are enough of them throughout the game to keep you always covered. The HEV charging stations also no longer work. This new type of armor works well enough for the shorter campaign.

Xen is also better executed here. It only lasts a few minutes, making good use of the enemies and environments without overstaying its welcome. It's a much more enjoyable version of Xen precisely because the game doesn't force you to spend too much time there.

Overall, Blue Shift is just a fun, short, and well developed Half Life expansion. It doesn't try to reinvent the formula, instead, it takes what worked in the original, puts you in the shoes of a different character, and gives you another run on the Black Mesa incident.

review: After becoming a soldier in Opposing Force, it was time to become a security guard in Blue Shift. In this game, we play as Barney Calhoun and hang out with the other Barneys at Black Mesa; I think they are all clones of Barney, except Otis, of course. At the beginning of the game, we can see Freeman passing by on a train, but I still don't understand why he glows like a lamp when he moves away. The biggest downside of the game is that it adds absolutely nothing on top of Half-Life and Opposing Force. There are no new enemies or weapons, and because the game is so short, we don't even get the chance to use most of the weapons; I usually use the .357 Magnum and Submachine Gun while playing. We can't use Suit Chargers either, so we have to get armor either from the environment or from our fallen friends. This must have been very traumatic for Barney. I also hate the HD models. Even if you use the original models, Dr. Rosenberg's model looks really out of place next to the other scientists. Overall, it isn't a bad game, but it feels quite underwhelming compared to Half-Life and Opposing Force. Its short length makes up for some of its shortcomings, but I still wouldn't recommend it as a Half-Life game. review:
Half Life Blue Shift is a short, fun, and amazing expansion that covers everything that made the original Half Life perfect, but from the perspective of a security officer.

The story is short but interesting enough to make you care about what is happening around the player. It is also tied enough to the events of the original game, which makes the whole experience feel a bit more connected rather than just being a fully separate story.

The gunplay is essentially the same as the original Half Life, although sadly you have fewer weapons to play around with. One of the biggest changes is how body armor works, instead of relying on HEV charging stations or items, you recover armor by picking up helmets and  vests that are around the facility. Even though these pickups sometimes can be quite far apart, there are enough of them throughout the game to keep you always covered. The HEV charging stations also no longer work. This new type of armor works well enough for the shorter campaign.

Xen is also better executed here. It only lasts a few minutes, making good use of the enemies and environments without overstaying its welcome. It's a much more enjoyable version of Xen precisely because the game doesn't force you to spend too much time there.

Overall, Blue Shift is just a fun, short, and well developed Half Life expansion. It doesn't try to reinvent the formula, instead, it takes what worked in the original, puts you in the shoes of a different character, and gives you another run on the Black Mesa incident.

review:
What more can be said? Absolute masterpiece.

Half-Life 2 elevated FPS and gaming in general to a level that is pretty difficult to match, and that's probably why there's still no Half-Life 3 as of 2026. 

As an FPS, it lets the gameplay tell its story with practically no interruptions, and it introduces new concepts like weapons and enemies fantastically by providing the right situations for you to experiment with and master progressively. Its distinctive color scheme, paired with great overall design, gives it a ton of personality and distinctive feel. Cities felt oppressive, wilder areas gave off that abandonment feel, and outskirts are a mix of both, with the most enjoyable and unexpected encounters. 

Shooting is fine. There are plenty of weapons to allow different approaches, and the gravity gun is immensely useful and fun to play with. Enemies are varied, although I wished there were more alien-like ones, but they are still dumb in their tactics and pretty easy to outmaneuver with movement or to force them to push you for an easy kill. Maybe it was just a result of the environment they were fighting in, but it felt like they were more organized later on. Resources like ammo and health are pretty abundant. Driving sections were cool, and I especially enjoyed how they played into the game's "controlled jankiness". Characters are interesting, but there were some bugs with their pathfinding leading to some resets. Soundtrack and sound design are both great and memorable. 

One of the problems that I think that I will find later on after spending more time with Half-Life 2 is that it has no real and concrete identity. After my first playthrough, since I last played some great years ago, I found that each section was defined by a specific style. Half-Life 2 but on a boat, Half-Life 2 but only with the gravity gun, etc. I'm afraid that when asked to present the final product, it will feel lesser, like its parts are greater than the whole, but I will see how that is explored in Episodes 1 and 2.

review:
Half-Life 2: The Blueprint of the Modern Shooter

When Valve released Half-Life 2 in 2004, it didn't just iterate on the first-person shooter genre; it completely dismantled and rebuilt it from the ground up. Over two decades later, stepping out of the train station into the oppressive, sun-bleached dystopia of City 17 remains one of the most defining moments in gaming history. Half-Life 2 is a masterclass in pacing, physics, and unspoken storytelling that still schools modern releases.

Welcome to City 17
The brilliance of Half-Life 2 begins with its world-building. Instead of relying on lengthy cutscenes or exposition dumps, the game drops you, as the silent protagonist Gordon Freeman, directly into an Eastern European city under alien occupation. The storytelling is entirely environmental and seamlessly integrated into the gameplay. 
You learn everything you need to know about the Combine empire by watching citizens being bullied by masked Civil Protection officers, listening to the chilling, omnipresent broadcasts of Dr. Wallace Breen, and gazing up at the monolithic Citadel that consumes the skyline. The atmosphere is thick with paranoia and Orwellian dread, creating a desperate setting that makes your eventual transformation from an unarmed fugitive to a legendary resistance leader incredibly earned.

A Physics Revolution
Before Half-Life 2, in-game physics were largely cosmetic—a few ragdolls or breaking boxes. Valve’s Source engine turned physics into a core gameplay pillar. Wood splinters, barrels float in water to solve puzzles, and heavy objects crush enemies. This mechanical leap is perfectly encapsulated by the Zero-Point Energy Field Manipulator, better known as the Gravity Gun. The Gravity Gun fundamentally changes how you view a digital environment. Suddenly, a radiator isn't just set dressing; it's a shield against incoming fire. A circular saw blade isn't just a prop; it's a lethal projectile waiting to be launched through a line of headcrab zombies. It transformed combat from a simple point-and-shoot exercise into an improvisational sandbox, encouraging players to experiment with their surroundings to survive.

Pacing Without Pause
Perhaps the game’s greatest triumph is its flawless pacing. Because there are no cutscenes, the camera never pulls away from Gordon Freeman's perspective. You are always in control, and the game constantly reinvents itself just before you can settle into a routine:
The Canals: A tense, high-speed chase on a heavily armed airboat while dodging hunter-choppers.
Ravenholm: A sudden, terrifying pivot into pure survival horror, forcing you to rely on gravity-gun physics and environmental traps to conserve ammunition against horrifying new zombie variants.
Highway 17: A sprawling, quiet road trip along a desolate coastline in a dune buggy, punctuated by intense skirmishes with Combine outposts and alien antlions.
Nova Prospekt: A full-scale tactical assault on a brutal alien prison, using pheropod pods to command an army of insectoid beasts.
Valve treats the player to a perfectly curated rollercoaster of tension and release. You are never doing the same thing for too long, yet the transitions between these wildly different chapters feel entirely logical and grounded within the world.

Characters Who Look Back at You
Half-Life 2 also revolutionized digital acting. The introduction of Alyx Vance provided players with an AI companion who felt genuinely human. Thanks to the Source engine’s advanced facial animation system, characters emote with subtle eye twitches, furrowed brows, and warm smiles. When Alyx looks at you, she actually tracks your movements. Paired with outstanding voice acting, the resistance members—from the brilliant Dr. Kleiner to the tragic Eli Vance—anchor the sci-fi spectacle with genuine emotional stakes.

Half-Life 2 is a rare anomaly in the gaming industry: a phenomenally hyped sequel that actually exceeded its impossible expectations. By marrying groundbreaking technology with meticulous, invisible design, Valve created a timeless adventure. It remains an essential, breathtaking journey that fundamentally changed what developers and players believed a video game could achieve.

review:
After finishing half life 2 and the two episodes, it has already become my 2nd favorite game of all time. The one thing that Valve absolutely nails and perfected in this game is the world and level design. City 17 looks incredible, the sky looks insane at times, the wilderness of the white forest, and locations like Ravenholm really make me never want to stop playing this game. The story is just remarkable and the characters (and voice actors/actresses) are incredible. Alyx  is a super likeable character, along with her Dad and Dog, and Gordon is, I mean, Gordon Freeman. 

The combat is nothing too crazy, but  it's simple enough to where you have no complaints. The enemy variety is good and some of them are challenging to take down, especially the Striders (won't reveal spoilers) at times. 

The "puzzles" or the ways to take on getting over, under, or across certain objects for secrets or vital ammo or health is really good and is extremely unique all these years later. The game doesn't hold your hand... There's no yellow paint or icons telling you what to do, instead they test your basic knowledge and common sense, which most games nowadays don't even do anymore. 

This game was an incredible experience, and I desperately need Valve to release a Half life 3.... You simply cannot end a game like that. 

Definitely a beautiful game that will stick with you. 10/10

review:
[i]Half-Life 2[/i] is a piece of gaming history with an amazing level of detail that seems wild even 20 years later. The dialogue is incredible, and the environments have love and care put into them. I was constantly driven to learn what's next in the story beats and shooter gameplay that was just plain fun. The Combine echo the soldiers from the first game with improvements that are so much cooler and immersive, it truly feels like an all-out-war and desperate effort to stop 'THE Freeman'. The environmental storytelling is masterfully done, and I especially like how the Combine react to Freeman with increasingly ferocity the further you tear through them. Its that combo of video-gamey-ness yet realism that makes this one of my more fun and memorable gaming experiences, so much more so than the original thanks to its added polish and optimization.

I would like to add some further notes regarding the two 'expansions' or DLC for this entry as they have some extra thoughts with each entry.

[u]Episode One[/u] 
While shorter and a little less impactful to me than its sequel, Episode One (and two) brings more of that wonderful gameplay and immersive story that made the main game so great. There's a ton of memorable moments like the elevator fight, and the horrifying strider at the end, that double as great visual as well as gameplay spectacles. It's also a nice development of Alyx's character throughout, with her and Gordon's bond deepening and us being able to see a more expressive and emotional side of her. For me at least, what really what only made this one weaker was how fast it was over. Otherwise, this is still a great continuation of the same overarching title.

[u]Episode Two[/u]
Episode Two took the potential that was already there and ran with it, and personally action is even cooler and cinematic than Episode One. G-Man remains a total delight despite raising some of the most important questions, and the gameplay sections stand out, strider bombing, dodging turrets, and the bug section being gross and awesome at the same time. The aliens are more horrifying too, and those stupid, relentless hunters. It feels like a lot of lore gets dropped even though it technically isn't much, and of course, we're left with more questions than answers yet again. Also, please make a sequel already. Same short-length complaint as Episode One though, even if it is technically longer, and hits even harder this time because of the crazier twist. 

[u]Overall[/u]  
All-in-all the Half-Life 2 'series' is a masterclass in detail, atmosphere, and physics-driven interactivity that still holds up today, the gravity gun alone never stops being fun. I know most of the things its praised for have become standard in today's top titles, but that doesn't stop it from being surprising, and a joy to play. The Combine invasion and G-Man's presence alone keep the mystery going strong throughout in the best way, and I was happy to find that the Episodes build on that with stronger character work for Alyx and great new gameplay sections.

Again both episodes are short, which with the plan they had in mind makes sense. But they really do leave you wanting that sequel that to this day, never came. That doesn't mean you shouldn't join me in that eternal hype too, though, experiencing it is a must.
[h3] Masterpiece; 10/10. [/h3]

review:
If we were to compare this game directly to CS1.6 and CS:GO right before CS:2, I would have to say this is easily the worst counter-strike game in the series. 

Textures are clear and crisp, and lighting effects have aged quite well, but maps are hilariously poorly lit and way too dark, the torch has visual bugs on a few maps and makes it harder to see than easier (double doors on aztec). The game runs excellently and has visually aged quite well, but low polygon count is highly noticeable, and I find the game is quite ugly to look at. It also went for a very cartoonish artstyle for character and weapon models, which clashes with the otherwise photorealistic style, likely photo-sourced textures. 

I only play with bots so I can't comment on multiplayer performance, but even when hosting your own server to play with bots, the extremely poor netcode is immediately and readily apparently. Characters have a delay before ragdolling after dying, shots can seemingly miss despite being clearly on target, and bots can fire at you behind walls and land non-wallbang kills. 

Regarding bots, their skill level varies considerably compared to 1.6. Whereas in 1.6/CZ, bots of a certain difficulty level would vary in skill level (you can tell by their name), that variance was small enough that most games would be fairly matched. In the case of Source, bots appear to vary in skill level considerably in a single skill bracket (I've only tested against Hard bots, unsure about other difficulties) and also vary in performance round-to-round. 
Bots have some improvements over 1.6 bots, including generally better pathfinding and decision making skills, as well as improved weapon control, but those are the extent of the positives. They frequently jump in place randomly, especially when turning corners, they occasionally throw their weapons away for no apparent reason (No weapons on the ground to pick up and replace), they sometimes shoot the ceiling for no reason, and they always shoot destroyable objects if they path into them, even if they can path around it. They also tap fire SMGs and have improved running accuracy, apparently. 

In terms of weapons, accuracy in general is significantly improved over 1.6 - Mainly, the AWP can actually be used, and long distance AK taps are possible now, which are simply not possible in 1.6. However, the spray patterns CS:GO players will be familiar with don't exist, so consistent and reliable full-mag spray prediction is impossible for most weapons. This is generally an improvement, although TTK is a bit too low for my tastes and the game can play a bit quickly with bots rushing in and standing still to die to a firing squad. 

Economy is simply broken. While it should be well known that 1.6's economy is poorly balanced, CS:S's appears to be even worse. T's can consistently buy AKs second round regardless of whether they won or loss, which is an utterly mind baffling balance decision. Since the only economic setting you can tweak is starting money, there is no feasible way to adjust this in game to fix it. Overall, due to economy alone, the game is rather T-sided in almost all cases, except for exceptionally poorly balanced maps. 

Almost all maps are source ports from 1.6, and follow a similar layout. Havana changes per round which is an interesting trick and can be fun to experience. Overall, they are their poorly balanced, early counter-strike selves. 

In general, I consider this game to be quite poor, although there are a large number of features to like about it. So, why the positive review? Well, it's not 2004 right now, and CS:S is not a game you buy and play for the gameplay of CS:S:
1. This game comes with the orange box, so you either already have it for free or can get it for cheap alongside other, more interesting games
2. The game's assets are required for some gmod maps, and although I don't play gmod, that alone is a good reason to buy it
3. It is still playable over 2 decades later on extremely low-end hardware due to impressive optimisation and bot support, and although the bots kind of suck to play with, they're better than nothing

With those considerations, it would be a bit pedantic and silly to give it a negative review just because the core game is of poor gameplay quality, given it's already marked as the black sheep of the counter-strike family and serves a different functional purpose as a game you purchase in the modern era.

review:
Valve’s 2004 Source engine remake that bridged the gap between 1.6 and Global Offensive.

The bad part is the altered hitboxes, floaty physics, and split competitive community. Props and barrels get in the way of firefights, and the oversized hitboxes make headshots feel far too easy compared to 1.6, which alienated hardcore purists for years.

The good part is the visual step up and the legendary custom server scene. The Source engine introduced dynamic ragdolls and clean map designs, but the real star was the community content that spawned peak surf, bhop, zombie escape, and jailbreak servers.

A classic shooter that traded raw competitive precision for massive modding flexibility.

review:
I really enjoyed Half-Life: Source. It's not perfect and definitely not better than the original Half-Life but it does add to the experience at times and play relatively okay.

Like I said it's not perfect, just to name a few bugs, the Houndeye can literally be passive at times with how broken it's A.I is, and the HECU isn't perfect either, the barnacle tentacles are also broken and you can't see if you're about to run into one unless you look up as the tentacle is wildly short for some reason, yet the hitbox is still long, there's also major graphical bugs on both Residue Processing & Surface Tension, the Apache hitbox on Surface Tension is also completely broken and I had to actually skip fighting it because my rockets were phasing through it.

By far the biggest crime this game commits is the SMG's recoil, most of the guns seemed to have gotten a recoil change, often looking more extreme but the SMG's recoil in particular is so bad it's almost un-usable, for some reason it orients the camera down and at medium to long distances it's basically impossible to use unless in single fire. This may be placebo or just insanity but I feel like the HD models (swapping the SMG to a Colt 727) preformed better and were easier to use but that doesn't make sense so I think I'm insane.

Aside from that, my experience was relatively smooth sailing, I enjoyed the new features like the source water, new 3d backdrops, ragdolls and particle effects. I think it's worth playing despite it's problems, there's mods like Half-Life: Source fixed that'll provide a better experience while getting the benefits of the source engine.

It's also a shame that this was completely abandoned by Valve and released without any real care

Half-Life: Source takes Valve’s foundational FPS classic and gives it the modern technical foundation it always deserved. Porting the original game into the Source engine introduces vastly improved ragdoll physics, dynamic water effects, enhanced lighting, and far smoother character movement. This technical facelift fixes many of the stiff mechanical frustrations of the 1998 release while keeping the iconic pacing, story, and level design completely intact. Taking the legendary **Half-Life (1998)** and bringing it into the engine that powered Half-Life 2 was something fans had been waiting to see.

The familiar Black Mesa Research Facility, Gordon Freeman, iconic weapons, enemies, and unforgettable moments were all there, but with improved water effects, lighting, physics, and visual details.

It may not be the definitive way to experience the original Half-Life, but there's something nostalgic about seeing this classic rebuilt in the Source engine.

For longtime Half-Life fans, Half-Life: Source feels like a snapshot of an important moment in the series' history—a bridge between the original game and the world of Half-Life 2.

the best out of all changes though I would say... was the flashlight. and the fact that you can also push items without it erratically going to some sides you do not want it to.

The game Is also very buggy which Is where all my complains go. 

remember the vending machines in OG half life? one of the coolest small details that brought life to the game, with colorful cans and allowing you to gain small health as you press all satisfying buttons.

however, I come across two issues. I sometimes could not use the can whenever I press the use button.

even the AI for enemies and other NPC's Is broken.

Overall. I would not recommend this game unless:

1: you want some new stuff added to gmod.

review:
I really enjoyed Half-Life: Source. It's not perfect and definitely not better than the original Half-Life but it does add to the experience at times and play relatively okay.

Like I said it's not perfect, just to name a few bugs, the Houndeye can literally be passive at times with how broken it's A.I is, and the HECU isn't perfect either, the barnacle tentacles are also broken and you can't see if you're about to run into one unless you look up as the tentacle is wildly short for some reason, yet the hitbox is still long, there's also major graphical bugs on both Residue Processing & Surface Tension, the Apache hitbox on Surface Tension is also completely broken and I had to actually skip fighting it because my rockets were phasing through it.

By far the biggest crime this game commits is the SMG's recoil, most of the guns seemed to have gotten a recoil change, often looking more extreme but the SMG's recoil in particular is so bad it's almost un-usable, for some reason it orients the camera down and at medium to long distances it's basically impossible to use unless in single fire. This may be placebo or just insanity but I feel like the HD models (swapping the SMG to a Colt 727) preformed better and were easier to use but that doesn't make sense so I think I'm insane.

Aside from that, my experience was relatively smooth sailing, I enjoyed the new features like the source water, new 3d backdrops, ragdolls and particle effects. I think it's worth playing despite it's problems, there's mods like Half-Life: Source fixed that'll provide a better experience while getting the benefits of the source engine.

It's also a shame that this was completely abandoned by Valve and released without any real care

For longtime Half-Life fans, Half-Life: Source feels like a snapshot of an important moment in the series' history—a bridge between the original game and the world of Half-Life 2.

review:
Even though I am able to play latest modern shooters without any issue, I find myself playing DoD time to time.

And I've pondered. "Why do I play this old game when I have bunch of other option?". I concluded that answer is [u]simplicity[/u]. Modern games are complicated thus overstimulating. 

In modern games you have to learn gameplay mechnanics (such as movement, gunplay etc.) to get somewhat competent. Modern graphics and level design are also tiresome to play. You have to deal with so many details and so many objects, which gets tiring after certain time.

Complexity isn't bad but sometimes you just don't care. You don't want to deal with bunny hopping, rocket jumping, sliding, wall riding enemies. You don't want to predict where bullet will drop. You don't care about how many polygons does bottle prop have. You don't care about how grass animate in wind, You don't care about raytracing/pathtracing. You don't want to wait for next round to spawn.

You just want to shoot the bad guys and move on. Nothing more, nothing less. DoD is good game if you appreciate simplicity. Gameplay is simple. Source engine is simple.

Half-Life 2: Deathmatch is... okay.

I wouldn't say it's a game I play every day, or even a game I would normally go out of my way to play, but it has a special place in my memories.

This was one of the first games I really started playing with one of my best friends. We spent some time messing around and fighting each other in this game before eventually switching over to Garry's Mod, which is now my favorite game.

As a game by itself, though, it can get pretty repetitive. The main gameplay loop is basically just fighting each other, dying, respawning, and seeing who comes out on top. review:
Score: 8.5/10

Half-Life 2: Deathmatch is a fast-paced multiplayer shooter built around the physics capabilities of the Source engine. Set in the world of Half-Life 2, it combines traditional gunplay with creative environmental combat, allowing players to turn everyday objects into deadly weapons.

What it does well

✅ Physics-Based Combat

The Gravity Gun completely changes how matches unfold.
Players can launch saw blades, explosive barrels, radiators, and other objects to eliminate opponents in creative ways.

✅ Fast and Fluid Gameplay

Movement feels responsive and satisfying.
Matches encourage quick reactions and constant repositioning.

✅ Iconic Weapons

The arsenal includes memorable weapons such as the crowbar, shotgun, crossbow, pulse rifle, RPG, and Gravity Gun.
Every weapon has a distinct role in combat.

✅ Creative Map Design

Maps feature environmental hazards, interactive objects, and vertical layouts.
Learning each arena rewards strategic movement and clever use of the surroundings.
Weaknesses

❌ Small Active Community

The player base is much smaller than it was during its peak years.

❌ Limited Game Modes

Most servers focus on classic Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch.

❌ Veteran Skill Gap

Experienced players often dominate public matches, making the learning curve challenging for newcomers.
Who will enjoy it?

You'll probably enjoy it if you like:

Arena shooters
Fast-paced multiplayer
Physics-based gameplay
Creative combat
Classic first-person shooters
Standout Features
Gravity Gun combat
Source engine physics
Classic Half-Life weapon selection
Interactive environments
Community servers
Fast competitive gameplay

It was a brief, bittersweet trip into the past. Let’s leave it at that.

review:
I don't like puzzle games, but Portal is something completely different for me. The game starts with us waking up from a Stasis Pod in the Short-Term Relaxation Vault. After GLaDOS welcomes us with the line, “We hope your brief detention in the relaxation vault has been a pleasant one.”, the game teaches us how to use its main mechanic, the Portal Gun. Later, we learn how to use the Weighted Storage Cube and other mechanics such as the High Energy Pellet. The puzzles are generally easy, with only a few of them making you think a little. As we progress, combining the mechanics we've learned makes the puzzles more interesting.

The Turrets' cute voices and GLaDOS's calm but manipulative dialogue give the game a unique atmosphere. I especially liked how she describes even dangerous situations as if they were completely normal, stays calm even when talking about the possibility of death and injury, and throws random nonsense into her serious speeches. Her constantly praising the Companion Cube while repeatedly reminding us that it cannot actually talk, along with details like “The Cake Is a Lie,” makes the game's dark humor even more entertaining. This humor and GLaDOS's way of speaking also fit nicely with Aperture Science's sterile and simple design. The strange writings outside the test chambers and the sound design also complement the atmosphere very well. Despite being released in 2007, the game still looks pretty good today. Thanks to the simple visual style of the Source Engine, it doesn't show its age too much. I also liked how it shows that it takes place in the same universe as Half-Life through a small reference. It's a nice detail that the universes of the two games are connected through such a small detail.

I also found the Bonus Maps that unlock after finishing the game more enjoyable than the sections in the main story. Especially the way some of the levels are made more difficult requires us to use the portal mechanic we learned earlier more carefully. The Challenge sections were much harder than I expected. I had to try some of them over and over to complete them. Completing all of them at 100% also took quite a lot of effort, and this process turned into a long and exhausting three-day marathon. In the end, I managed to get all the achievements as well. The achievement that challenged me the most was Aperture Science. Even though I was quite tired by the end, getting 100% completion in Portal was definitely worth it. I had fun and enjoyed it much more than I expected. A short game that takes 2–2.5 hours to finish, but one I really liked. It gives you the experience it wants to offer without unnecessarily dragging things out.

review:
Portal: The Flawless Triumph of Puzzle Design
Originally tucked away as a quirky, three-hour experiment in Valve's legendary The Orange Box compilation in 2007, Portal did not just steal the show—it redefined the entire puzzle genre. It is a rare, flawless gem of game design that strips away filler to deliver an experience where mechanics, narrative, and pitch-black comedy are perfectly intertwined.

Thinking with Portals
The genius of Portal lies in a single, mind-bending mechanic: the Aperture Science Handheld Portal Device. You shoot one blue portal, you shoot one orange portal, and they seamlessly link two points in space. But the portals are not just fancy doors; the game brilliantly teaches you to weaponize physics.
Portal forces you to unlearn how you navigate digital spaces. It operates on the rule of conservation of momentum—or, as the game puts it, "speedy thing goes in, speedy thing comes out." Falling from a great height into a blue portal on the floor will launch you out of an orange portal on the wall, allowing you to fling yourself across massive chasms.

The Passive-Aggressive Puppet Master
You play as Chell, a silent test subject trapped in the sterile, clinical environments of the Aperture Science Enrichment Center. Your only companion—and tormentor—is GLaDOS (Genetic Lifeform and Disk Operating System).
Voiced with deadpan, auto-tuned perfection by Ellen McLain, GLaDOS is arguably one of the greatest video game antagonists ever written. She doesn't scream or threaten you. Instead, she manipulates you with the promise of cake, passive-aggressive disappointment, and a bureaucratic indifference to your impending death. The script is razor-sharp, delivering laugh-out-loud moments amidst the creeping isolation of the facility.
Halfway through the game, the pristine, white test chambers give way to the rusted, gritty maintenance areas behind the walls. This environmental storytelling creates a brilliant narrative shift, turning a standard puzzle game into a desperate escape sequence.

A Bite-Sized Phenomenon
Despite its brief runtime, Portal left an enduring crater in pop culture. The game managed to make players feel genuine guilt over incinerating the Weighted Companion Cube—an inanimate metal box with pink hearts painted on it. Phrases like "The cake is a lie" became defining internet shibboleths for an entire generation of gamers. And just when you think the ride is over, the credits roll to Jonathan Coulton's "Still Alive," an incredibly catchy, passive-aggressive musical number that serves as the perfect victory lap.
Portal is a masterclass in restraint. It respects your time, leaving absolutely no room for bloated skill trees, repetitive combat, or padded fetch quests. It introduces a revolutionary mechanic, pushes it to its logical extreme, tells a perfectly contained sci-fi comedy, and bows out right before overstaying its welcome. It is, simply put, a perfect video game.

review:
[h1]Portal[/h1]
[b]First-person puzzle | ~3 hours[/b]

[h2]What it's about[/h2]
You wake in a glass cell somewhere inside Aperture Science, a research facility that appears to have been built by people with enormous budgets and no supervision. A calm computerised voice welcomes you and explains, with great warmth, that you are here to complete a series of tests.

The tests take place in numbered chambers, and the tool you're given for them is a gun that shoots doorways. Put one on this wall and another on that one, and the two openings become the same opening. Everything else follows from that: the puzzles, the jokes, and eventually the question of what happens to a test subject who finishes all the tests.

You walk, you look, you place two portals and rearrange the room around yourself. Every chamber is a space to be read: the answer is always in front of you, in the shape of the room.

[h2]What it does well[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]One idea, followed all the way down.[/b] The portal gun is a single mechanic with an unreasonable number of consequences, and the game finds nearly all of them. Sightlines become routes, falls become launches, and a wall you've looked at fifty times turns into a solution the moment you see the floor differently. Very few games get this much out of so little.
[*][b]It teaches without ever explaining.[/b] Each chamber introduces exactly one new idea, lets you use it until it's yours, then quietly combines it with the last one. Nothing stops to lecture you, there's no tutorial text to skip, and by the end you're doing things that would have looked impossible in the first hour.
[*][b]Comedy that still lands.[/b] The voice narrating your progress is polite, encouraging and increasingly hard to trust, and the humour comes from how long it keeps up the customer-service tone. Ellen McLain's delivery is the whole thing: perfectly flat, perfectly timed, never once winking at you.
[*][b]Not one wasted minute.[/b] Three hours, no padding, no filler chamber to hit a runtime. It starts, it escalates, it ends exactly where it should, and it's over before a single idea has a chance to go stale.
[/list]

[h2]Worth knowing[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]It's short.[/b] Three hours or so, and that length is the point rather than an oversight, but go in knowing this is an evening rather than a campaign.
[*][b]Culture got here first.[/b] Portal has been quoted, memed and referenced for nearly twenty years, so some of the best lines will arrive already familiar. The puzzles are untouched by that, and the tone survives it better than you'd expect.
[*][b]The later chambers ask for hands as well as heads.[/b] A few solutions near the end need decent timing and aim once you've worked out what to do, and falling through your own portal repeatedly can be disorienting if you're prone to motion sickness.
[/list]

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Portal is as close to a perfect game as anyone has made. One mechanic, taught flawlessly, explored completely and dropped the moment it's done, wrapped in a script funnier than most things written for any medium. It's a comedy, a puzzle game and a quietly unsettling story about a building, and it manages all three in about the time it takes to watch a film. Nearly twenty years on, nothing about it feels like a period piece.

[b]Still the best three hours in games. If you've somehow never played it, start tonight.[/b]

I really like how each puzzle that comes after the other forces you to use the knowledge/skill you gained from the last puzzle to solve the next. you really have to use your brain on a lot of the puzzles. There are a lot of simple ones but some puzzles genuinely had me going “What the ♥♥♥♥ am I supposed to do here?”, then after I’d figure out I’d go “Oh, duh!”, I can only blame that on my brain being slow. It’s also helpful knowing that in the middle of the screen, it indicates the last portal you put down so you don’t get confused and forget like my stupid brain sometimes did until I noticed it. 

The game starts you off waking up in a sort of cell until you are let out to do a series of tests/puzzles, and as you play through the game you notice your character has no dialogue, and I feel like playing any game where your character has no dialogue, it makes you feel more immersed in the game, as if the character is you. This is my second play through of the game but I remember on my first play through, I didn’t expect there to be a bigger plot until I got nosey and explored a crack in the wall, what I found was a hidden room and there it reveals the truth about what’s to come later in the game written all over the walls from whoever the last test subject was. The AI that is having us go through the tests on 2 or 3 occasions brings up the fact that we get a cake at the end of the testing. If you’ve played enough video games, you’d feel a bit sceptic about whether there actually is a cake or not. The room i mentioned before with all the writings on the wall reveal “THE CAKE IS A LIE!!”, so upon seeing this, you wonder what’ll happen once you finish the testing. Well what happens is you are about to get incinerated, but the AI’s mistake was forgetting you still had the portal gun in hand so what do you do? You escape. What I loved about the escape is that even though the testing was over, the game stayed true to its puzzle game title and had you figuring out how to get from one room to another using the portal gun and the skills you learned doing the tests, even to the end of the game when you destroy the AI, you have to do some maneuvering to defeat it with the skills you learned and I really liked that.

The most surprising part about this game is that it released in 2007. I was 4 years old at the time and honestly, you can’t even tell it was made all that time ago, the game has held up very well for its age. Pretty high frame rate, good resolution, and the graphics look like it was made in the early 2010s rather than the late 2000s. I feel like anyone who enjoys puzzle games and an interesting plot would enjoy this game a lot.

Trying to figure out how to get through each puzzle can be fun and exciting once you figure out how to get past it, and the plot gets very interesting once you find out the truth about the rumored cake. Though the plot was interesting, they didn’t open up more about it such as how we ended up there, what the company is doing, and why there is no other human besides us there? there’s a lot of unanswered questions that I really wish were explored, and because of that, I give the game a 9/10. I hope in the second game, a lot of my questions are answered, but this first game was really fun and enjoyable and I’d recommend this game to anyone looking for an interesting puzzle game with a bit of plot. 

If you read this to the end, Thank You and I love you!

review:
Left 4 Dead 2: The Immortal King of Co-op Zombie Shooters
When Valve released Left 4 Dead 2 in 2009, barely a year after its predecessor, skeptics wondered if it was too soon for a sequel. Fast forward to today, and the game stands as an undeniable masterpiece that has stubbornly refused to age. It isn't just one of the best zombie games ever made; it is the definitive cooperative shooter experience, setting a gold standard that countless studios have tried—and failed—to replicate.
The AI Director 2.0: The Puppet Master
The beating heart of Left 4 Dead 2 is its dynamic pacing, governed by the ingeniously upgraded "AI Director 2.0". This system observes how well your team is performing and alters the level layout, item spawns, weather, and enemy waves on the fly. If you are breezing through a level, the Director might summon a torrential downpour to ruin your visibility, followed immediately by a devastating horde. If your team is limping toward the safehouse with single-digit health, the Director might show a rare moment of mercy, spawning a clutch bottle of pain pills in a side room. This mechanic ensures that no two playthroughs of the same campaign ever feel identical, creating an endless loop of unscripted, water-cooler moments.  
 A Masterclass in Audio and Enemy Design
To survive the apocalypse, you have to listen. Valve's sound design in Left 4 Dead 2 is nothing short of brilliant, serving as both atmosphere and a vital gameplay mechanic. Every Special Infected has a distinct audio cue that triggers pure panic: the hacking cough of a Smoker, the shrill screech of a Hunter, the gurgling of a Boomer, or the terrifying, screen-shaking roar of an incoming Tank.   The sequel introduced three new Special Infected that completely changed the tactical landscape:
The Charger: A hulking brute that punishes teams who bunch up in narrow corridors, charging through them like bowling pins.  
 The Spitter: A terrifying area-denial zombie that forces survivors out of tight, defensive corners with pools of burning acid.   
The Jockey: A manic, giggling gremlin that leaps onto your back and steers you directly into danger or off ledges.
The synergy between these monsters means players are constantly forced to communicate. If a Smoker drags your medic away while a Spitter cuts off your path to save them, your team has mere seconds to adapt or die.
Carnage with Character
The game trades the original's grim, cinematic darkness for a sun-drenched, blood-soaked road trip through the American South. The new cast—Nick, Rochelle, Coach, and Ellis—bring an endless amount of charm and wit to the grim setting. Their banter feels natural and evolves as the campaign progresses, seamlessly providing lore and comic relief without slowing down the action.  

 Combat also received a massive, visceral upgrade with the introduction of melee weapons. Swapping out a pistol to carve through a horde with a katana, a fire axe, or a roaring chainsaw is incredibly satisfying and completely alters close-quarters combat. The dynamic gore system makes every shotgun blast and frying pan swing feel heavy, chaotic, and impactful. 

A Legacy That Refuses to Die
Perhaps the most staggering thing about Left 4 Dead 2 is its immense longevity. As of late 2026, the game is still averaging tens of thousands of active players every month, routinely hitting concurrent peaks of over 40,000 players. It even reached an all-time peak of over 100,000 concurrent players years after its release.   This immortality is heavily driven by the game's flawless integration with the Steam Workshop. The modding community has turned the game into an infinite sandbox of creativity. Want to play a meticulously crafted, custom 5-part campaign? It's there. Want to replace all the common zombies with Teletubbies, the Tank with Shrek, and your weapons with Minecraft swords? You can do that in two clicks.   Left 4 Dead 2 is pure, unadulterated adrenaline. It perfectly balances terror and comedy, punishing difficulty, and triumphant teamwork. review:
Left 4 Dead 2 is a game about teamwork, survival, and discovering exactly how quickly four people can completely abandon the concept of teamwork.

The premise is simple.

You're trapped in the middle of a zombie apocalypse.

There are thousands of infected.

You have guns.

Your objective is to get from point A to point B without becoming zombie food.

Easy.

Until you play with friends.

The game starts off fairly calm. You grab a weapon, pick up some supplies, and start walking through whatever horrible place the survivors have been thrown into this time.

Then someone shoots a car.

Everyone looks at them.

“Why did you shoot the car?”

“I didn't know it would make noise.”

The alarm starts.

Hundreds of zombies appear.

Everyone starts screaming.

Welcome to Left 4 Dead 2.

The special infected are what make the game so much fun. Regular zombies are bad enough, but then you hear a noise and realize something much worse is coming.

Smoker?

Someone's getting dragged away.

Hunter?

Someone's getting tackled.

Boomer?

Congratulations, you're covered in vomit.

Charger?

There goes your teammate.

Jockey?

Someone is being ridden into a wall.

Tank?

RUN.

The Tank is the game's way of asking whether your team has actually been paying attention.

Usually, the answer is no.

You hear the music.

Everyone freezes.

“Tank.”

Someone says it quietly.

You all immediately start running in different directions.

One person gets separated.

Someone falls off a ledge.

Another person forgets to heal.

The Tank punches someone through a wall.

Now you're down a player.

Great teamwork.

The campaign design is also fantastic. Every level feels like a journey rather than just a collection of rooms, and you're constantly moving toward some kind of safe room while trying to survive whatever the Director decides to throw at you.

And that's one of the best parts of the game.

The game seems to know exactly when you're getting comfortable.

You haven't seen anything dangerous for a while.

Your health is good.

You have plenty of ammunition.

You start thinking:

“This is going pretty well.”

Then the Director decides that you're having too much fun.

A horde appears.

A Witch is nearby.

A Tank spawns.

The lights go out.

Someone screams.

Your entire team collapses.

You make it to the safe room with 12 HP and absolutely no supplies.

Perfect.

The AI Director keeps every game feeling slightly different, which is a huge reason L4D2 has remained so replayable.

You can play the same campaign multiple times and still have completely different experiences.

Maybe you get an easy run.

Maybe you get attacked by three special infected simultaneously.

Maybe your friend gets dragged into a hole and you have to rescue them.

Maybe someone accidentally triggers the alarm and turns the entire level into a zombie festival.

You never really know.

And then there's versus mode.

This is where friendships go to die.

Playing as the survivors is one thing.

Playing as the infected is something completely different.

You get to become the exact creatures that have been ruining everyone's day.

You hide around a corner.

You wait.

You see a survivor walk past.

You spawn.

You attack.

You get killed immediately.

You respawn.

You try again.

Eventually you manage to pull someone off a roof as a Smoker and feel like a tactical genius.

Then a shotgun deletes you.

Back to the respawn screen.

The game is also ridiculously fun with friends because the chaos creates stories you'll remember long after the match ends.

You don't remember every normal round.

You remember the time your friend got launched off a bridge.

You remember someone accidentally shooting the Witch.

You remember hiding in a closet while a Tank destroyed everything outside.

You remember the guy who refused to heal because he was “saving the medkit.”

You remember him dying thirty seconds later.

And somehow, despite all the chaos, the game still rewards actual teamwork.

Stick together.

Share supplies.

Cover each other.

Revive your teammates.

Watch for special infected.

Don't wander off.

It's incredibly simple advice.

Nobody follows it.

Someone always runs ahead.

Someone always gets grabbed.

Someone always says, “I got this.”

They do not have this.

Left 4 Dead 2 is one of those games that feels timeless because it doesn't need complicated progression systems or endless grinding to stay fun.

You pick a campaign.

You grab a gun.

You shoot zombies.

You survive.

You die.

You laugh.

You restart.

And somehow you're still playing hours later.

It's chaotic, funny, tense, and one of the best examples of co-op gaming at its absolute best.

10/10.

I've survived the zombie apocalypse countless times, but I've never survived playing with my friends.

Left 4 Dead is an absolute blast with friends.

There’s something special about getting a group of friends together, jumping into a campaign, and watching everything go completely off the rails. The game is already incredibly fun on its own, but the real magic comes from its modding community.

If you love messing around with mods, custom maps, ridiculous character replacements, completely over-the-top weapons, and anything else you can throw into the game, Left 4 Dead gives you endless ways to make every session feel different. One minute you're trying to survive a normal zombie outbreak, and the next you're fighting through some completely absurd custom map with mods that make absolutely no sense—and that's exactly what makes it so much fun.

The best moments aren't even the ones you plan. They're the random, chaotic situations that happen because of the combination of your friends, the game, and whatever ridiculous mods you've installed. Every playthrough can turn into its own story that you'll be laughing about afterward.

If you enjoy co-op games, messing around with friends, or love modding games and seeing just how ridiculous you can make them, Left 4 Dead is absolutely worth playing. It's one of those games where the fun comes from the game itself, but the community and the endless possibilities with mods and custom maps make it something you can keep coming back to for years.

review:
This game is a 16-year-old piece of software that still somehow runs better than half the modern live-service slop being released today. Congrats, Valve. Your ancient zombie shooting gallery from the Obama administration still hits harder than most $70 “AAA experiences.”
The AI Director will either drown you in a tidal wave of Special Infected the second you dare to breathe near a safe room, or it will fall asleep and leave you wandering empty streets like a lonely sad bastard for ten minutes. The Specials still have the pathfinding intelligence of a concussed raccoon. Smokers will drag you through walls. Chargers will yeet you into the void. Jockeys will ride you like you’re their personal mechanical bull while your teammates watch and laugh. And the Tank? The Tank will clip through geometry, no-scope you from three maps away, and then despawn out of pure spite.
Versus mode is a gladiatorial arena of pure toxicity where half the lobby is cheating, the other half is throwing, and everyone is screaming racial slurs in voice chat. It’s beautiful.
Yet here I am. 121 hours later. Still loading up this dusty old relic every time I want to feel something. Because when the chaos clicks—when your team is coordinated, the Director is on one, and you’re screaming while a Tank is chasing you through a burning building with a chainsaw—nothing else comes close.
It’s janky. It’s old. It’s held together with duct tape and Valve’s pure refusal to let it die.
And I still love it.
10/10 would get charged into a wall by a 500-pound zombie again.
