And then there's the Workshop, custom maps and all the community content, which basically gives the game an almost endless amount of stuff to play.

For a game this old, it's honestly crazy how well it still holds up. The gameplay is simple enough to pick up but has a lot of depth once you actually get into Versus and higher difficulties. Definitely one of those games where you can come back years later and still have a great time.

review:
Science, Sarcasm, and Spuds: The Enduring Brilliance of Portal 2

Portal 2 is that rare, perfect sequel that takes a flawless, bite-sized experiment and expands it into a sprawling comedic masterpiece of puzzle design. Where the original 2007 game was a tightly wound, sterile gauntlet that redefined first-person physics, Valve’s 2011 follow-up shatters the pristine testing chambers, dragging players through the overgrown ruins and deep historical bowels of Aperture Science.

Physics and Fluidity
The core mechanic remains untouched: shoot a blue portal, shoot an orange portal, and step through to bend space. The genius of Portal 2 lies in how it iterates on that foundation. Valve introduces a suite of new testing elements that turn the environment into a dynamic playground rather than a static puzzle.
Thermal Discouragement Beams, Hard Light Bridges, and Excursion Funnels force you to think about trajectory and timing in three dimensions. But the true game-changers are the Mobility Gels. Bouncing across a room coated in blue Repulsion Gel or sliding at breakneck speeds across orange Propulsion Gel transforms the cerebral puzzle-solving into exhilarating, momentum-driven action. It perfectly executes the series' golden rule: speedy thing goes in, speedy thing comes out.

A Masterclass in Writing and Voice Acting
A puzzle game shouldn't be this genuinely funny, yet Portal 2 features some of the sharpest comedic writing in gaming history. The narrative succeeds on the backs of three phenomenal performances:
GLaDOS (Ellen McLain): Deposed and forced into a humiliating new form, GLaDOS shifts from a cold, passive-aggressive overseer to a reluctant, deeply sarcastic ally. Her psychological warfare is as sharp as ever, but her character arc reveals a surprising, tragic depth.
Wheatley (Stephen Merchant): The bumbling, fast-talking personality core is a triumph of animation and voice acting. Merchant’s erratic, deeply insecure delivery makes Wheatley an unforgettable companion whose sheer incompetence is both hilarious and terrifying.
Cave Johnson (J.K. Simmons): As you fall into the sealed, 1950s-era underground testing spheres, you are guided by the pre-recorded voice of Aperture’s eccentric founder. Simmons delivers a bombastic, unhinged performance, culminating in a legendary rant about combustible lemons that remains a high-water mark for video game monologues.

The World as a Storyteller
Aperture Science is the game's true main character. You start in a facility reclaimed by nature—vines tearing through the sterile white panels, testing chambers violently reassembling themselves in real-time. As you plummet into the salt mine depths, the aesthetic shifts to a retro-futuristic, atomic-age aesthetic. The environmental storytelling is flawless, charting the company's descent from a well-funded, optimistic scientific powerhouse into a bankrupt, morally bankrupt madhouse.

The Cooperative Campaign
Rather than simply bolting two players into the single-player story, Valve crafted a distinct, full-length cooperative campaign starring two lovable testing androids, Atlas and P-Body.
Managing four portals instead of two exponentially increases the complexity of the puzzles. The co-op campaign is a brilliant test of communication, spatial reasoning, and trust. It requires players to execute synchronized aerial maneuvers and trust their partner to place a portal perfectly while they are in mid-air. GLaDOS actively tries to drive a wedge between the two players with personalized insults, turning the cooperative experience into a hilarious meta-game of mutual sabotage and eventual triumph.
Portal 2 remains a monumental achievement. It took a concept that seemed impossible to improve upon and built a world with emotional weight, impeccable pacing, and unparalleled mechanical ingenuity. It isn't just one of the best puzzle games ever made; it is one of the definitive experiences of the medium.

Portal 2 is one of the best games I've ever played. It manages to combine a captivating story, an incredible atmosphere, amazing voice acting and genuinely innovative gameplay into one unforgettable experience.

review:
Portal 2 is a simple game, but it is also a very well-executed one. After playing the first Portal, I expected the sequel to mostly repeat the same formula with better graphics and some new mechanics, but that is not what happened. Portal 2 actually continues the story of the first game and builds on what was already established instead of simply replacing it with a new scenario. That was probably the biggest surprise for me, especially because I was not expecting the two games to be connected as directly as they are.

The gameplay remains the strongest part of the experience. The concept is simple, but the game constantly uses the Portal Gun and its mechanics to create different situations without making the puzzles unnecessarily complicated. Personally, I didn't find the puzzles difficult at all. They are generally very easy to understand, and the game does a good job of teaching the player how each mechanic works before asking them to combine it with something else. For some players, the lack of difficulty might be a problem, but for me it is actually an advantage. Portal 2 has a very fast pacing, and making the puzzles significantly harder would probably slow the entire experience down and make the game much more frustrating than it needs to be.

That pacing is one of the reasons I enjoyed it. The game doesn't constantly stop you to make you solve one puzzle for a long period of time, and it doesn't feel particularly punitive when you make a mistake. You experiment, understand what the game wants you to do, solve the puzzle and move forward. The result is an experience that remains consistently entertaining instead of becoming exhausting.

The story is also much more important than I expected. Portal 2 doesn't just use the first game as a loose reference; it continues what was established previously and gives the overall Portal story an actual conclusion. The humour is also much more present here, with more voice acting, more dialogue and plenty of ridiculous moments that give the characters much more personality. It makes the campaign feel more alive without taking away from the gameplay. By the end, it genuinely feels like the Portal story has reached its conclusion rather than simply stopping because the campaign is over.

Visually, Portal 2 still looks good, but graphics were never what I was looking for from this game. The important part is that the presentation supports the gameplay and the atmosphere without getting in the way. The same applies to the cooperative side of the game. Having friends to play the co-op with can add another layer of fun to the same basic concept, especially because solving puzzles together changes the way you approach them.

Portal 2 is not a game that tries to be unnecessarily complex. It takes a simple concept, adds more mechanics, continues the original story and keeps the pacing fast enough that the experience never becomes boring. It is not a masterpiece for me, and my opinion remains very close to what I had with the first Portal, but it is a good puzzle game that knows exactly what it wants to be and delivers that experience without dragging it out.

★★★★★

Portal 2 is one of those games that starts as a puzzle game and somehow ends up feeling like a story about loneliness, failure, friendship, and learning to let go.

Every test chamber feels like you're solving more than just a puzzle. You're constantly being told that you're not good enough, that you're replaceable, that you will fail—and yet you keep going. Not because someone promises you'll succeed, but because you want to see what's on the other side.

The humor makes the darker moments hit even harder. The characters are ridiculous, but somehow their relationships feel strangely human. By the end, leaving the facility feels less like finishing a game and more like saying goodbye to a place you've spent too much time in.

And then there's the penguin.

I don't know where the penguin came from. I don't know why it's here. Maybe it knows something I don't.

Maybe we're all just penguins trying to find our way out of Aperture.

10/10. Sometimes the hardest puzzle is knowing when to leave.

review:
The original 2009 Unreal Tournament mod turned standalone shooter that started the entire franchise with a grittier, darker survival horror vibe.

The bad part is the outdated engine movement and painful perk grinding. Movement feels stiff and slow compared to modern shooters, making getting cornered by a sudden Scrake or Fleshpound an instant death sentence. Levelling up perks like Support or Demolitions requires absurd amounts of grinding, forcing you to deal millions of damage or weld doors for hours just to rank up.

The good part is the legendary, suffocating atmosphere. Unlike the arcade polished look of the sequel, the original London streets, underground labs, and abandoned hospitals feel pitch black, dirty, and genuinely terrifying. The combination of haunting ambient dark ambient music, eerie industrial noise, blood spattered corridors, and the terrifying screams of Zeds lurking in the dark creates pure dread that modern coop games fail to replicate. Door welding actually matters for map control, and weapons like the Handcannon pack an incredible amount of punch.

A classic, raw survival horror shooter that holds up for fans who prefer pure nightmare atmosphere over fast action.

review:
Killing Floor is one of those games I wish I had played sooner. It’s a co-op survival horror FPS from Tripwire Interactive that originally released in 2009, and even though it’s an older game, I actually had a pretty good time with it.

The main thing I like about Killing Floor is how simple the idea is. You’re basically fighting through waves of enemies, getting better weapons and equipment as you go, and trying to survive until the final boss. You can play by yourself, but the game is really designed around co-op, with up to six players working together.

I also really like the different classes, or Perks, because they give you different ways to play. You can specialize in things like healing, support, explosives, or different types of weapons. It gives you a reason to keep playing and leveling up your character.

The weapons are also pretty fun. There are a lot of different weapons to use, and shooting the enemies feels satisfying. The enemies can get pretty crazy too, especially when you start getting into the harder waves. The game can go from being manageable to completely chaotic really quickly.

One thing I wasn't expecting was how much content there actually is. There are a ton of maps, weapons, achievements, and community content, and Steam currently lists 285 achievements for the game.

The graphics definitely show the game's age, though. This is a 2009 game, and you can tell. Some of the character models, environments, and animations look pretty dated compared with newer games. But honestly, I don't think that takes away too much from the experience.

I also like that Killing Floor doesn't try to be something it isn't. It's mainly about jumping into a game, shooting monsters, surviving waves, and having fun. There's a story and a setting behind everything, but the gameplay is definitely the main focus.

Overall, I enjoyed Killing Floor. It's an older game, but it still has a lot of fun gameplay, especially if you have friends to play with. If you like zombie games, survival games, or games where you fight through increasingly difficult waves of enemies, I think Killing Floor is definitely worth checking out.

review:
The original 2009 Unreal Tournament mod turned standalone shooter that started the entire franchise with a grittier, darker survival horror vibe.

The bad part is the outdated engine movement and painful perk grinding. Movement feels stiff and slow compared to modern shooters, making getting cornered by a sudden Scrake or Fleshpound an instant death sentence. Levelling up perks like Support or Demolitions requires absurd amounts of grinding, forcing you to deal millions of damage or weld doors for hours just to rank up.

The good part is the legendary, suffocating atmosphere. Unlike the arcade polished look of the sequel, the original London streets, underground labs, and abandoned hospitals feel pitch black, dirty, and genuinely terrifying. The combination of haunting ambient dark ambient music, eerie industrial noise, blood spattered corridors, and the terrifying screams of Zeds lurking in the dark creates pure dread that modern coop games fail to replicate. Door welding actually matters for map control, and weapons like the Handcannon pack an incredible amount of punch.

A classic, raw survival horror shooter that holds up for fans who prefer pure nightmare atmosphere over fast action.

review:
While i wouln't call this game complete or essential by any stretch of imagenation, just dismissing it as "Half Life 2 with boobs" would do it a injustice (cinematic mod has you covered on that front).
The music is really good, the diverse enemy types like the Jetpack troopers are interesting and while it dont exactly look like CSGO, for being one of the first 3rd party source games it looks pretty impressive.

Unexpectedly after also having tactical mechanics like Aim Down Sights & Shiftwalking, this game also has some of the easiest & best Bhopping i've ever seen in a source game where just chaining jumps (nevermind airstrafing) pulls you away at march 3, way faster than any source game designed to be fast like Fortress Forever or Smashball.

While its always disappointing to see a unfinished game with untapped potential be cancelled (especially when so short), this game didn't really make me sad about missing out on a sequel/DLC as the foundation didn't show that much promise compared to HL2 or even to modern indie titles. Its not bad, but its also not great so what we got was probably as good as it was gonna get.
Same goes with the story and characters. While i didnt find the supporting characters annoying, i also didnt care about them as much as Alyx Vance or Meryl Silverbough due to the lack of time spent with them.

The "insane levels of interaction" is a overexaggeration even by 2004 standards both in terms of tactical utility or immersive simulation. You cant even pour a cup of coffie from the countless coffie makers you encounter, though you can turn on water taps and pull out hankerchiefs so i guess A for effort.
Its about the same level of interactability as Dystopia with ingame touch screens.

Its not a hidden timeless gem but its also not offensively bad. Like i said, its not a must have, but if you are a source collector like i am, go ahead and buy it although in that case do it on a sale as it gets riddiculously cheap on discounts and that price is more representative of its runtime than the normal base price..

review:
I know people compare it unfavorably to Half-Life 2 but there was something cool here. I wish they got to continue the story; but I guess that's what happens with these episodic games. Very good presentation and some fun shooting. It's a very short run-time, but that's to be expected with only 1 episode. Because of that though it's definitely worth playing. Stock-generic weapons but again this was supposed to be the beginning of the game, and they're fun to use. Really satisfying to use the pistol specifically imo. I like just poking around in the environment and looking for secrets in these Source Engine games. Also I really enjoy the world of the SiN games. Elexis is a great villain, Blade is a fun protag, and you gotta love JC for 90's/2000's "hacker" charm. The Mobster Boss guy (forgetting his name but I believe it's the same guy from the SiN expansion pack) is really entertaining. I love the biopunk/cyberpunk aspects where you have this corrupt city ruled by corporations and you're fighting people who've mutated along with maybe turning into a monster yourself. I was hooked by the setup for the story here and it would've been cool to see Freeport under martial law; plus find out what Elexis has planned for Blade. I do wish Blade actually talked a bit more like the original though.

"What's the world come too?" Truly.

review:
While this is a positive review, I will say it's not from the perspective that some of the others have. For starters, this clearly suffered the curse of "Half Life was popular", stripping its ID away to create another silent protagonist "linear action sequence" game. This does somewhat undermine it as Blade is now just a nobody with mentions of his past, no actual personality, and it leaves some set pieces feeling empty. Furthermore, there's a very obvious Half Life mimicking involved, which no doubt hurt the game further. The combat varies from laughable easy to "just throw more enemies than there is ammo, it'll be fine" and the maps are no different being "realistic work space" to "weirdly mangled mess". Plus the doorways on the tanker aren't slanted with the tanker's hull, which is somewhat annoying...

BUT. Despite me finding obvious flaws in it, I can't deny that the graphics (provided you don't focus on the NPCs which have a bit of a texture issue) do still look pretty good for when they were made, maybe more than Half Life 2. And while the guns are basic with a basic secondary fire, they do have some kick to them as a single headshot is enough to kill low level soldiers if you don't jack up the challenge level, the shotgun doing the same, and a dedicated grenade and melee button certainly show they wanted combat to be fluid unlike Half Life's "swap to melee, swap to gun, swap to grenade" weaponry. There's also an adjustable AI narrator, similar to Left 4 Dead, where you can alter how quickly or slowly the game will come to your aid if it senses you struggling by dropping medi packs or ammo, going beyond just simple difficulty.

I can't comment on the story given technically there isn't any, especially with this being the only episode and what little we get here is clearly ground work stuff so far from being deep lore, but the voice acting of the main characters is pretty good and you can see where they wanted to be different with the health function, the mutagen slowing time (which was the style of the time!) and it's just a product of that Bond/Matrix/Edgy early 2000s era for gaming.

This is far from a great game, but it's unique for what it is and has a great main menu theme. I would certainly recommend everyone try it at least once, because then you can see why it was originally hyped in the past but also why it failed. The game is, funny enough, somewhat shameless in showing its pros and cons. Though personally, I feel if they spent less time modelling HUGE BREASTS on the main villain and a little more time working on the game they could've had a better result (I swear she has the most high res model...)

review:
[h1][i]"You're clones. I mean, you're human, but you just—you're not real. You're not, like, a real person. Like me. You're clones."[/i]
~ The Island, 2005[/h1]

Looking back at the [b]SiN[/b] series, it's hard not to notice how incredibly unlucky it was. I mean, come on. Who cares about [b]SiN[/b] nowadays? Well, the old geezers who still managed to have some fun with it back in the day probably do, but in general, it's one of those things that became completely forgotten. Yet at one point? It was a huge deal.

What started with a big exodus from [b]3D Realms[/b]—with lots of people behind [b]Duke 3D[/b] (from [b]Richard[/b] "[b]Levelord[/b]" [b]Gray[/b] to [b]Mark Dochtermann[/b]) leaving to pursue more independence, creative freedom and, well, justice ([b]Levelord[/b], for example, claimed his work wasn't getting enough credit)—was supposed to compete with [b]Half-Life[/b] itself.

And you know what? On paper, [b]SiN[/b] was supposed to win. While [b]Half-Life[/b] was using a modified version of the original [b]Quake[/b]'s engine, [b]SiN[/b] had all the power of [b]Quake II[/b] behind it, while also offering things like a complex, immersive environment and, most importantly, non-linear gameplay. After failing to fulfill an objective, instead of getting a "game over" screen, we were supposed to keep playing, just with a different outcome. Which was unprecedented back in the day. Still is, actually.

As usual with overly ambitious projects, though, [b]SiN[/b] ended up being ridiculously buggy (even today, many patches later, it still has both enemies and the player getting stuck in the geometry) and even came with a huge day-one patch. Which was another unprecedented thing at the time (remember, it was only 1998, and the internet was still considered a luxury that not even all adults had access to).

Also, [b]Ritual[/b] (that's how our guys decided to be called from now on) didn't have the privilege of “it'll be done when it'll be done” that [b]Quake II[/b] had. And as a result, the non-linear part wasn't nearly as satisfying as it was supposed to be (we still got "game over" screens now and then, too), while the immersive part became one of those annoying things that exist only to stand between you and your frags, making everything less fun. [b]Half-Life[/b] won. End of story. Or is it?

See, [b]Half-Life[/b] was not the only thing [b]VALVe[/b] was doing. There was also that funny lil' thing called [b]Steam[/b]. Yeah, [i]that[/i] [b]Steam[/b]. The one where you're reading this text. And [b]VALVe[/b] co-founder, [b]Gabe Newell[/b] ([i]praise [b]Gaben![/b][/i]), had some ideas for its future. The 2000s were a weird period. It was a time before the indie revolution, yet it had already become quite obvious that a massive 4+ year development cycle for video games could be a huge problem for everybody. [b]Gabe[/b]? He thought he had a solution for that.

The solution was—episodic releases. Instead of making one long game, it sounded like a much better idea to produce shorter and cheaper releases every few months. It'll keep players busy, it'll fuel the store (which did need that at the moment), etc. Everybody's happy. On paper, at least. In reality, the whole thing flopped pretty fast. The episodic approach did find its own niche with adventure games (let's admit it, we all have at least some of [b]Telltale[/b]'s releases in our libraries), but for first-person shooters? It was a flop.

Even [b]VALVe[/b]'s own juggernaut, [b]Half-Life 2[/b], failed to meet expectations with its episodes, which were canceled after only two installments. [b]SiN[/b]? It was dead right after the first one. Why? Well... You see, the original [b]SiN[/b] was many things. But it was never a copycat. [b]SiN Episodes[/b]? It was just a [b]Half-Life 2[/b] clone.

While [b]JC[/b] (the main character's partner, who kept giving him instructions) was still there, [b]Blade[/b] also got himself one of those “girls with an attitude.” Because apparently, all the cool guys were getting those. And let's just be honest, the so-called [b]Jessica Cannon[/b] was just a reskin of [b]Alyx Vance[/b]. The setting? They didn't even bother reskinning it. It was [b]City 17[/b], copied as is, with all of its post-soviet vibes. Heck, they even copied [b]Half-Life[/b]'s chargers! Both functionally and visually!

And no, I am not exaggerating. Even the enemies feel like a [b]Half-Life[/b] rip-off. And when you think about it, it's ironic as F. I mean, I get it—[b]Ritual[/b] desperately tried to survive back in the day, so it's not like I'm complaining 'bout 'em partnering with [b]VALVe[/b] and going episodic. It's just... they left [b]3D Realms[/b] to pursue creative freedom. Yet what they did here is a shameless, “[i]we so-o-o don't care![/i]” kind of rip-off.

To be completely fair, though, I must say I like the pace here. I actually like it much more than what we had in [b]Half-Life 2[/b]. I mean, [b]Half-Life 2[/b] was a major achievement and had a really cool multiplayer mode. review:
This year's likeliest winner of the Yeah It's Nice (Throwback Edition) award. The last couple of levels are a pair of nutcrackers to say the least - I caved and used ol' reliable (impulse 101) a couple of times after I gave up on tackling the finale proper - but overall, what's here [i]is[/i] neat, and I [i]am[/i] sad that Ritual never got to do anything else with this, even if for just another episode or two. I'd also argue that Ritual made [b]astonishingly[/b] good use of the Source Engine to the extent that I feel they outdid Valve themselves in any number of aspects. In interactivity, at the least.

Relevant example: Healing in this game functions similarly to Half-Life 2. You have small spray-dispensing pickups found in supply boxes + on the bodies of fallen grunts (usually; I think they only drop if your HP is below a certain value), and you have wall-mounted HP stations. The former isn't particularly interesting. The latter is. Healing stations operate on disposable canisters - again akin to HL2, where you can only heal for as long as the station has its 'charge'. The difference is that SiN allows you to [i]eject[/i] the canister, and if there's a fresh (or mostly full) one nearby, you can slot that one in and keep going as necessary. That's neat enough on its own, but now let's assume for the sake of the argument that you have a full canister next to you. You do NOT, however, have a healing station in the room. Say it's a few doors away and there's like five grunts between here and there, and your HP's not looking great as-is. In which case, you can [i]break the canister open and allow the spray to disperse,[/i] healing you for about half the value that the station would. This also allows for bits of minor, but tense decision-making in certain parts later on - if you're low on health and chance upon a canister but no station, and there's a good chance that the game'll sic some more grunts on you soon, do you break the canister there and take your chances with a lower return on health, or do you carry it around for a while in the hopes you can get the most out of it?

This is all just one part of the core gameplay, bear in mind. A lot of what's there, in that regard, feels like HL2 But A Bit More Interesting, imo. Like you only get three weapons (pistol, shotgun, AR), but each one has its use at any given point and they all have secondary firing modes which use their own sort of ammo. There's iron sights that display an orange reticle around the sight itself whenever you're pointing at an enemy from any distance so that you have a better idea of when to fire, instead of potentially wasting your bullet(s) on an obstacle or wall. Melee is embedded in the guns themselves; you hit Q to bash at will. Your incendiary grenades are proper throwables instead of being a separate entity, predictably set to G. So on and so forth. These details and design decisions aren't particularly ground-breaking or anything, but I do think they make for an experience that plays better than if it were based entirely on the HL2 framework.

I won't say much about the story since I think it's a fun little B-movie romp best experienced blind on your own time (with or without knowledge of what happened in the prior SiN entries; I've yet to play those myself, but I didn't have an issue following along), but I do have a few passing comments:
[olist]
[*]How the hell did they bag Jen Taylor for the semi-obligatory 'preppy heroine' role while she was between Halo 2 and Halo 3?
[*]The reviews calling the game horny or pornographic because Elexis is a femme fatale that shows up like four or five times throughout the whole thing is equally funny and squint-inducing.
[*]The Radek boss fight that would've been in like Episode 3 or 4 would've been awesome. Alas.
[/olist]

Unfortunate that things turned out the way they did. A year after they put this lovely little piece out, Ritual was bought out and folded into MumboJumbo, who went defunct in 2018 and (visibly) did nothing with the IP in all the years in between. It's not the first company to suffer such a fate and it's hardly the last, either.

What's the world come to?

And you know what? On paper, [b]SiN[/b] was supposed to win. While [b]Half-Life[/b] was using a modified version of the original [b]Quake[/b]'s engine, [b]SiN[/b] had all the power of [b]Quake II[/b] behind it, while also offering things like a complex, immersive environment and, most importantly, non-linear gameplay. After failing to fulfill an objective, instead of getting a "game over" screen, we were supposed to keep playing, just with a different outcome. Which was unprecedented back in the day. Still is, actually.

As usual with overly ambitious projects, though, [b]SiN[/b] ended up being ridiculously buggy (even today, many patches later, it still has both enemies and the player getting stuck in the geometry) and even came with a huge day-one patch. Which was another unprecedented thing at the time (remember, it was only 1998, and the internet was still considered a luxury that not even all adults had access to).

Also, [b]Ritual[/b] (that's how our guys decided to be called from now on) didn't have the privilege of “it'll be done when it'll be done” that [b]Quake II[/b] had. And as a result, the non-linear part wasn't nearly as satisfying as it was supposed to be (we still got "game over" screens now and then, too), while the immersive part became one of those annoying things that exist only to stand between you and your frags, making everything less fun. And [b]VALVe[/b] co-founder, [b]Gabe Newell[/b] ([i]praise [b]Gaben![/b][/i]), had some ideas for its future. The 2000s were a weird period. It was a time before the indie revolution, yet it had already become quite obvious that a massive 4+ year development cycle for video games could be a huge problem for everybody. [b]Gabe[/b]? He thought he had a solution for that.

The solution was—episodic releases. Instead of making one long game, it sounded like a much better idea to produce shorter and cheaper releases every few months. It'll keep players busy, it'll fuel the store (which did need that at the moment), etc. Everybody's happy. On paper, at least. In reality, the whole thing flopped pretty fast. The episodic approach did find its own niche with adventure games (let's admit it, we all have at least some of [b]Telltale[/b]'s releases in our libraries), but for first-person shooters? It was a flop.

Even [b]VALVe[/b]'s own juggernaut, [b]Half-Life 2[/b], failed to meet expectations with its episodes, which were canceled after only two installments. [b]SiN[/b]? It was dead right after the first one. Why? Well... You see, the original [b]SiN[/b] was many things. But it was never a copycat. [b]SiN Episodes[/b]? It was just a [b]Half-Life 2[/b] clone.

While [b]JC[/b] (the main character's partner, who kept giving him instructions) was still there, [b]Blade[/b] also got himself one of those “girls with an attitude.” Because apparently, all the cool guys were getting those. And let's just be honest, the so-called [b]Jessica Cannon[/b] was just a reskin of [b]Alyx Vance[/b]. The setting? They didn't even bother reskinning it. It was [b]City 17[/b], copied as is, with all of its post-soviet vibes. Heck, they even copied [b]Half-Life[/b]'s chargers! Both functionally and visually!

And no, I am not exaggerating. Even the enemies feel like a [b]Half-Life[/b] rip-off. And when you think about it, it's ironic as F. I mean, I get it—[b]Ritual[/b] desperately tried to survive back in the day, so it's not like I'm complaining 'bout 'em partnering with [b]VALVe[/b] and going episodic. It's just... they left [b]3D Realms[/b] to pursue creative freedom. Yet what they did here is a shameless, “[i]we so-o-o don't care![/i]” kind of rip-off.

To be completely fair, though, I must say I like the pace here. I actually like it much more than what we had in [b]Half-Life 2[/b]. While i wouln't call this game complete or essential by any stretch of imagenation, just dismissing it as "Half Life 2 with boobs" would do it a injustice (cinematic mod has you covered on that front).
The music is really good, the diverse enemy types like the Jetpack troopers are interesting and while it dont exactly look like CSGO, for being one of the first 3rd party source games it looks pretty impressive.

Unexpectedly after also having tactical mechanics like Aim Down Sights & Shiftwalking, this game also has some of the easiest & best Bhopping i've ever seen in a source game where just chaining jumps (nevermind airstrafing) pulls you away at march 3, way faster than any source game designed to be fast like Fortress Forever or Smashball.

While its always disappointing to see a unfinished game with untapped potential be cancelled (especially when so short), this game didn't really make me sad about missing out on a sequel/DLC as the foundation didn't show that much promise compared to HL2 or even to modern indie titles. Its not bad, but its also not great so what we got was probably as good as it was gonna get.
Same goes with the story and characters. While i didnt find the supporting characters annoying, i also didnt care about them as much as Alyx Vance or Meryl Silverbough due to the lack of time spent with them.

The "insane levels of interaction" is a overexaggeration even by 2004 standards both in terms of tactical utility or immersive simulation. You cant even pour a cup of coffie from the countless coffie makers you encounter, though you can turn on water taps and pull out hankerchiefs so i guess A for effort.
Its about the same level of interactability as Dystopia with ingame touch screens.

Its not a hidden timeless gem but its also not offensively bad. Like i said, its not a must have, but if you are a source collector like i am, go ahead and buy it although in that case do it on a sale as it gets riddiculously cheap on discounts and that price is more representative of its runtime than the normal base price..

This also allows for bits of minor, but tense decision-making in certain parts later on - if you're low on health and chance upon a canister but no station, and there's a good chance that the game'll sic some more grunts on you soon, do you break the canister there and take your chances with a lower return on health, or do you carry it around for a while in the hopes you can get the most out of it?

This is all just one part of the core gameplay, bear in mind. A lot of what's there, in that regard, feels like HL2 But A Bit More Interesting, imo. Like you only get three weapons (pistol, shotgun, AR), but each one has its use at any given point and they all have secondary firing modes which use their own sort of ammo. There's iron sights that display an orange reticle around the sight itself whenever you're pointing at an enemy from any distance so that you have a better idea of when to fire, instead of potentially wasting your bullet(s) on an obstacle or wall. Melee is embedded in the guns themselves; you hit Q to bash at will. Your incendiary grenades are proper throwables instead of being a separate entity, predictably set to G. So on and so forth. These details and design decisions aren't particularly ground-breaking or anything, but I do think they make for an experience that plays better than if it were based entirely on the HL2 framework.

I won't say much about the story since I think it's a fun little B-movie romp best experienced blind on your own time (with or without knowledge of what happened in the prior SiN entries; I've yet to play those myself, but I didn't have an issue following along), but I do have a few passing comments:
[olist]
[*]How the hell did they bag Jen Taylor for the semi-obligatory 'preppy heroine' role while she was between Halo 2 and Halo 3?
[*]The reviews calling the game horny or pornographic because Elexis is a femme fatale that shows up like four or five times throughout the whole thing is equally funny and squint-inducing.
[*]The Radek boss fight that would've been in like Episode 3 or 4 would've been awesome. Alas.
[/olist]

Unfortunate that things turned out the way they did. A year after they put this lovely little piece out, Ritual was bought out and folded into MumboJumbo, who went defunct in 2018 and (visibly) did nothing with the IP in all the years in between. It's not the first company to suffer such a fate and it's hardly the last, either.

review:
With the remaster finally launching I guess I'd better finally leave some thoughts on the OG version. [i]SiN[/i] is one of those games I always expect to be a little worse than it is, but then I play it and realize "Wait this is awesome" but then I get to one of the more gimmicky levels that tries something that doesn't quite work and I go "man I wish this was over" only to go back to one of the good levels and be right back into it all over again.

I've played through this release twice, one being the first steam release which just had the base game and was censored. Around 2020 they did kind of a "Half-Remaster" that got the game more stable, fixed a few bugs, uncensored a few things, and biggest of all added the [i]Wages of SiN[/i] expansion pack (which I do still need to play). I started a playthrough when that came out and in the past few days I realized I never finished it so I took the past few days to finish the final few levels.

The downside is while they did touch it up to run well, it's not hte most friendly to higher resolution screens. If you play on anything higher than 1080p the UI will basically be the size of your fingernail tucked away in the corner of the screen, though the game itself is still basically playable. There's a source port called Dominatrix you can install that apparently lets you scale the UI so if you're gonna play this version of [i]SiN[/i] that might be the play though I've heard it can break some of the rope climbing mechanics in the expansion so it's not a perfect option. I imagine SiN Reloaded will be the way to go for technical aspects but this is still here if you want the [i]most[/i] original experience (also for some reason after I closed out my latest session of the game it re-enabled mouse acceleration in my windows settings so make of that what you will. I think maybe because the game crashed and games tend to un-set it that option on a proper close).

Jank aside, the game itself is, I think, the truest successor to [i]Duke Nukem 3D[/i]. Not just because one of the level designers from that game was the lead designer on this (Rich "Levelord" Gray), l but the whole philosophy of the level design. The levels are full of weird little knick-knacks to mess with, if you press a button something cool will probably happen and exploration is always [i]deeply[/i] rewarded. There's always [i]something[/i] around every corner if you look and sometimes you'll even stumble into a whole alternate level, a new path, or something you do in one level will affect something that happens in another level. In some ways it kind of feels like if one of those insane notorious feature creep games like [i]Duke Forever[/i] or whatever Peter Molyneux's latest zany scheme is actually shipped on time and mostly delivered on its promises. There's cool stuff like in-game PC's with command lines that actually work with DOS commands like DIR and CD. The weapons themselves are a ton of fun and feel great to use and John Blade is one of the great underrated protagonists of 90's shooters. On the surface he's a bit like Duke and even has some of the same one-liners but there's kind of this unspoken but intentional thread that he's not [i]quite[/i] as cool as he seems, like a more competent Jack Burton. Some of his one-liners are less "tough" and more "He couldn't come up with something clever on the spot so he said something totally whack" and that humanizes him in a way you don't get from your typical 90's tough guy protagonists. For all the issues [i]Phantom Fury[/i] had I think it is telling that Blade has at least stayed in the conversation long enough to have a cameo in that game, he's just got a certain charming "something" that makes him lovable.

That said it's not a perfect game and you can kind of see why it lost out to [i]Half-Life[/i]. I think it's a much closer battle than some made it out to be but the Day 1 release was also pretty buggy from what I understand. Some levels have a gimmick like riding a motorcycle or something, and while it's impressive that it's there [i]at all[/i] the vehicle controls are [i]exceptionally twitchy[/i]. Some levels will take away your weapons and force you into a long stealth sequence that doesn't work well, some stretches of the game just feel [i]long[/i]/ Like I get wanting quantity but this game has a [i]lot[/i] of levels and whenever it feels like you're nearing the climax chances are [i]you probably aren't[/i].

Still, there's a lot to like, some of it almost feels like a proto [i]Deus-Ex[/i] immersive sim, especially when they let you disable security systems, and it genuinely feels like you have some degree of freedom in how to approach solving things. There's no "wrong" path to take and you won't see everything on the first playthrough.

Visually the maps and models look quite good for their time, particularly the lighting and weapons. Since this is a Quake II engine game your hands and basically every character wobbles around like Jell-O because of the loose way it handles floating point math but it's part of the charm and I dare say this game is a far more interesting use of the Quake II engine than... the actual Quake II.

Whether this particular version of the game retains any merit compared to Reloaded remains to be seen but if you've already got it and just want to play the game it's still an option.

Really fun and charming game with cool environments, funny and memorable characters, and great visual style. The only thing is that it takes a little bit of work to get it working normally with a reasonable UI and menu size. Below I have written a small guide on how to do it:

I would recommend installing the "Dominatrix" mod, which lets you play in normal resolutions / UI scale with a normal (ish) sized menu, adjust the FOV and max framerate, and it also gives you a weapon switch wheel which makes the game feel a lot smoother to play. Go to this website: https://rohit.itch.io/dominatrix Then scroll down to the downloads section and download the version for your computer's operating system (for windows its the "mingw" one, the second to last option). Then open the .zip file and drag all the mod files into the game directory. From now on, run the game through the dominatrix.exe instead of the normal exe - You can set the exe to be what steam launches by going into the "general" tab of the game's steam properties (access this by right-clicking the game in your steam library and clicking properties), then in the launch options field, type the file path in quotation marks, for example "C:\Steam\steamapps\common\SiN 1\dominatrix.exe" and then put a space and write %command% afterwards (with no quotation marks on that part). So it should look like this (but with your own file path instead): "C:\Steam\steamapps\common\SiN 1\dominatrix.exe" %command%

In the game itself, you control the menu with arrow keys and the enter key. You can go to the Dominatrix settings (to bind your weapon wheel, and change the UI scale, FOV, and framerate) by going to Controls (yeah the settings are all called controls for some reason) > game options > dominatrix extra settings. In the video settings, make sure to set the resolution that you want. ALSO, MAKE SURE TO SET THE SCREEN SIZE IN VIDEO OPTIONS TO BE LESS THAN MAXIMUM, OTHERWISE THE HUD WILL BE GONE IN-GAME!

Another thing that helps a lot with this game is binding a quicksave and quickload button. Open the console by pressing the ` key (the key to the left of the 1 key) and then type bind f5 "save quick" and then hit enter, but replace the f5 with whatever key you want. Same for quickloading but instead of "save quick" it's "load quick"

You can test to see if everything is working before starting the actual game by going to Game > New Game > Training

I played the demo for Sin before the game released.  That must have been back in 1998.  I liked it quite a bit.  Starting off the game manning a heavy machine gun from a helicopter before going in on foot seemed pretty cool.  Fresh.  The game looked good and utilized the Quake 2 engine well.  The game also seemed challenging and so I got a surprising amount of play out of what was merely a demo.  And that was that.  I never got the full game.  I couldn't tell you why.  Perhaps I was influenced by some negative reviews or perhaps it's true that the game suffered heavily from being overshadowed by Half-Life.  Whatever the case was after picking up the game on Steam in 2026 I can tell you that it was for the best.  For whatever the comparison may be worth, I also completed Far Cry 1 in 2026 and THAT game is a masterpiece.  So having played shooters since I picked up Doom in 1994 I do like to think that I can give old games fair consideration.  

First of all if you're going to play the game pick up the Dominatrix mod.  Search for it.  It'll fix some resolution issues.  The reason I enjoyed that demo so much back in the day may have very well been because that first level might have been the best level in the game!  The levels seem to get worse and worse and it seems like the game must have been rushed or something.  I see reviewers complaining about the snipers but they didn't bother me that much.  I found the underwater divers much more annoying.  These annoying enemies are juxtaposed with levels that were FAR too easy towards the end of the game.  The few vehicles in the game control poorly.  You might find yourself taking damage from locker doors and cupboards closing on you.  Yes, little wooden cupboard doors will harm you in this game while you find yourself looking for items. 

The game isn't all bad and some of the shooting is fun enough.  I enjoy the little bits of humor here and there and the game does get a few style points.  There seems to be this sentiment that Sin was unfairly overshadowed by Half-Life.  I've seen people call it a "gem".  A "classic".  "Underrated".  It's not.  It's really not.  It's basically an average shooter.  I would give it a 6/10.  Maybe even somewhere between a 5 and a 6.  It's not a bad game but I cannot recommend it.

review:
Barely recommended. This was really on the verge on whether I should put thumbs up or down for this one.

SiN is an FPS game with usually fun combat, wacky characters and severe deliberate oversexualisation that becomes a satire of its own. Normally, I push hard against heavily sexualised games, but this one mostly makes jokes out of it, so I guess I'm not complaining. Even without over-the-top sexualisation other aspects are over-the-top as well. Humour and dialogues are so cheesy, corny and dated. It's so lame that it works, quite amusing. Reminds me of those 80s and 90s cheesy action films like Steel (1997), or Tango & Cash (1989), Blade (1998) too haha. The music here is very good though, similar music could be heard in already mentioned Blade and The Matrix (1999).

As for the gameplay, there is quite a lot of variety in levels. both quality and pace. Most of the stealth levels are ranging from pretty bad to very bad. There are some okay water levels, they're not good, but toleratable. Some of the best levels are the very first levels of the game, although there are still many good levels later on. Unfortunately, most of the levels in the last third of the game are atrocious. Full of snipers who can easily kill you even on easy difficulty, most enemies are insane bullet sponges which makes combat a lot less fun, the environments are poorly lit, but the level design in many of those late game levels is garbage. The jungle levels, the levels where you play as someone else so to say, and the lab levels are really bad. At least, the final few levels were pretty good.

Now as for expansion, it is a lot better than the main game. While, there were some levels I liked less than others, overall there wasn't a single awful level, and most were good. It's a lot more action-oriented than the main game. Final boss battle was terrible though...

Another aspect which quite annoyed me in this game is how illogical and cryptic it is sometimes. The dumbest one is that in one building in which the game preferred you to get in stealthily and unnoticed, you need to activate the alarm manually in order for one door to open from which the alarmed guards come in. And in that room there is a keycard which you must get. So, basically in order to proceed you have to fail the approach what you thought the game preferred you to perform... Luckily, in both, the main game and the expansion combined there were only about 3-5 moments which I had no idea how was I supposed to figure out.

Overall, SiN is a heavily flawed FPS game. The wide variety of weapons and dismemberment makes combat fun, but numerous bad levels bring this game down a lot, to the point that I can only barely recommend it.


7/10

For all the issues [i]Phantom Fury[/i] had I think it is telling that Blade has at least stayed in the conversation long enough to have a cameo in that game, he's just got a certain charming "something" that makes him lovable.

That said it's not a perfect game and you can kind of see why it lost out to [i]Half-Life[/i]. I think it's a much closer battle than some made it out to be but the Day 1 release was also pretty buggy from what I understand. Some levels have a gimmick like riding a motorcycle or something, and while it's impressive that it's there [i]at all[/i] the vehicle controls are [i]exceptionally twitchy[/i]. Some levels will take away your weapons and force you into a long stealth sequence that doesn't work well, some stretches of the game just feel [i]long[/i]/ Like I get wanting quantity but this game has a [i]lot[/i] of levels and whenever it feels like you're nearing the climax chances are [i]you probably aren't[/i].

Still, there's a lot to like, some of it almost feels like a proto [i]Deus-Ex[/i] immersive sim, especially when they let you disable security systems, and it genuinely feels like you have some degree of freedom in how to approach solving things. There's no "wrong" path to take and you won't see everything on the first playthrough.

Visually the maps and models look quite good for their time, particularly the lighting and weapons. Since this is a Quake II engine game your hands and basically every character wobbles around like Jell-O because of the loose way it handles floating point math but it's part of the charm and I dare say this game is a far more interesting use of the Quake II engine than... the actual Quake II.

Whether this particular version of the game retains any merit compared to Reloaded remains to be seen but if you've already got it and just want to play the game it's still an option.

review:
Barely recommended. This was really on the verge on whether I should put thumbs up or down for this one.

SiN is an FPS game with usually fun combat, wacky characters and severe deliberate oversexualisation that becomes a satire of its own. Normally, I push hard against heavily sexualised games, but this one mostly makes jokes out of it, so I guess I'm not complaining. Even without over-the-top sexualisation other aspects are over-the-top as well. Humour and dialogues are so cheesy, corny and dated. It's so lame that it works, quite amusing. Reminds me of those 80s and 90s cheesy action films like Steel (1997), or Tango & Cash (1989), Blade (1998) too haha. The music here is very good though, similar music could be heard in already mentioned Blade and The Matrix (1999).

As for the gameplay, there is quite a lot of variety in levels. both quality and pace. Most of the stealth levels are ranging from pretty bad to very bad. There are some okay water levels, they're not good, but toleratable. Some of the best levels are the very first levels of the game, although there are still many good levels later on. Unfortunately, most of the levels in the last third of the game are atrocious. Full of snipers who can easily kill you even on easy difficulty, most enemies are insane bullet sponges which makes combat a lot less fun, the environments are poorly lit, but the level design in many of those late game levels is garbage. The jungle levels, the levels where you play as someone else so to say, and the lab levels are really bad. At least, the final few levels were pretty good.

Now as for expansion, it is a lot better than the main game. While, there were some levels I liked less than others, overall there wasn't a single awful level, and most were good. It's a lot more action-oriented than the main game. Final boss battle was terrible though...

Another aspect which quite annoyed me in this game is how illogical and cryptic it is sometimes. The dumbest one is that in one building in which the game preferred you to get in stealthily and unnoticed, you need to activate the alarm manually in order for one door to open from which the alarmed guards come in. And in that room there is a keycard which you must get. So, basically in order to proceed you have to fail the approach what you thought the game preferred you to perform... Luckily, in both, the main game and the expansion combined there were only about 3-5 moments which I had no idea how was I supposed to figure out.

Overall, SiN is a heavily flawed FPS game. The wide variety of weapons and dismemberment makes combat fun, but numerous bad levels bring this game down a lot, to the point that I can only barely recommend it.


7/10

review:
Iron Warriors: T-72 Tank Command is an old-school armored warfare simulator built around the idea that operating a tank should involve much more than pointing a cannon at an enemy and firing. Developed by Crazy House and published by Strategy First, it approaches tank combat with an emphasis on simulation, crew responsibilities, ballistics, and tactical positioning. Its age is immediately apparent in its presentation and interface, but beneath those dated elements is a surprisingly ambitious military simulation aimed at players who enjoy learning how armored vehicles function rather than simply using them as oversized weapons.

One of its strongest qualities is the selection of playable Soviet-designed tanks. The T-34-85, T-55A, and T-72B represent different generations of armored warfare, allowing the game to explore machines with noticeably different capabilities. Players can take control of individual crew positions rather than having every function conveniently condensed into a standard action-game control scheme. review:
People call this a poor man’s Oblivion, but it's closer to Gothic or Riven. I’m pretty sure the Oblivion Killer thing was some marketing gimmick in a magazine and people just rolled with it.

It does have it’s problems.

It can crash, randomly, but this seems to be caused by the autosave feature. If you save manually often and stick the maximum amount of time between autosaves, it seems to be much more stable. The animations are janky, they seem to run at around 24-30fps while the game around it will run at 60+, and the voice acting can be sketchy.

However, the things it does well, it does really well.  It has an almost Diablo style loot system. Loads of different equipment, from basic sticks to fanciful swords. There’s no durability so you don’t have to worry about replacing weapons. Different weapon categories are better at different things and you can imbue your weapons with an element (Lightning, Ice, Fire, Poison, and Spirit). Different enemies are more vulnerable to different weapon types and elements, so it’s worth picking up equipment as you go and experimenting.

Enemies don’t level up with you either, certain zones will be very hard in the early game, especially if you wander too far south, so it’s worth taking it slower and exploring, doing odd jobs before becoming a god-killing machine. But, if you play your cards right you can get overpowered really quickly.

The music is very good, it’s a shame Harold Faltermeyer hasn’t done more games. I would listen to the Two Worlds soundtrack regardless if there was a game attached to it.

I’ve always had a soft spot for it. I bought it at launch back in 2007 and have a disc copy, but I had the hankering to buy it again and beat it. If you can get it on a sale and can get past the jank, and enjoy it for what it is, you’ll have a good time.

review: Dark Messiah is endearing for both its flaws and strengths. Certainly the DNA of Arkane is here: slick levels, clever gameplay, a story with twists (though some are not surprising, like who’s surprised that what the succubus wants turns out to be bad!?), and atmosphere that comes through even the dated presentation. But with all that, the flaws are there too: janky physics, awkward dialogue, and the use of the Source engine that makes it look and feel like a Half-Life mod. A really good mod. I love that it looks like a Half-Life mod. It’s modest that way. But oh so ambitious too. The jank is also a sign of ambition, and it gives a physicality and spontaneity to the game is sorely missing in many of today’s games. The dialogue, especially from the female characters, can be goofy and poorly delivered, but I don’t care because the story is doing something different.  There’s a wave of homage games coming around lately, paying dues to Dark Messiah, and I can see why. They just don’t make ‘em like they used to.

review: Dark Messiah is endearing for both its flaws and strengths. Certainly the DNA of Arkane is here: slick levels, clever gameplay, a story with twists (though some are not surprising, like who’s surprised that what the succubus wants turns out to be bad!?), and atmosphere that comes through even the dated presentation. But with all that, the flaws are there too: janky physics, awkward dialogue, and the use of the Source engine that makes it look and feel like a Half-Life mod. A really good mod. I love that it looks like a Half-Life mod. It’s modest that way. But oh so ambitious too. The jank is also a sign of ambition, and it gives a physicality and spontaneity to the game is sorely missing in many of today’s games. The dialogue, especially from the female characters, can be goofy and poorly delivered, but I don’t care because the story is doing something different.  There’s a wave of homage games coming around lately, paying dues to Dark Messiah, and I can see why. They just don’t make ‘em like they used to.

review:
This game is a bit of a forgotten gem. The main highlight of it is its incredibly satisfying melee combat focused on improvisation rather than facing enemies head on. The environments are masterfully designed, where each element can be used to get an upper hand over your opponents. The feeling you get, if you manage to plan ahead and utilize each kick, throw and trap to win some very tough fight, is incredible.

That said, the story and lore are uninspiring. The Might and Magic setting is pretty much as generic as it can get, when it comes to fantasy. I also did not really care about the characters. The tension between Xana and Leanna was probably the strongest point, but the rest of the cast are mostly just random NPCs that happen to get a name for the sake of some one-off quest here and there.

The technical problems are also present. Climbing ropes can phase you into walls, larger maps can crash the game on higher video settings, random crashes out of nowhere happen as well, and so on. These are expected from a two decade old game, but for the sake of your own sanity I recommend quick-saving a lot.

I also want to mention Arx Fatalis. Dark Messiah was supposed to be its sequel, but the things didn't go quite according to the original plan and we eventually got this Might and Magic series spin-off. Personally, I think it's a bit of a shame, because Arx had a far more interesting setting and I very much enjoyed its semi-open underground world with all of its immersive elements. Both of these are unfortunately gone. Instead Dark Messiah offers better visuals and a far more focused experience with refined combat, smoother character progression and clearer objectives. It's probably a good trade for most players.

So overall, it's a good game, albeit with some issues. For the current price, it's absolutely worth it, even more so on a discount.

review:
For a nearly twenty-year old game - a short one, my twelve hours is probably standard for a playthrough- Dark Messiah is the right mix of mechanics and complex sections for an RPG. The kicking mechanic alone is fun -forget FUS-RO-DAH! And you can set your arrows, and objects, and bodies, on fire -if you don't want to just ragdoll your enemies. There's plenty of climbing, and swimming, and hidden places to find. But getting to those secrets can be fatal, you'll take many a wrong step off a high perch and miss that rope or chain. There's not a lot of lore, though, and a relatively small selection of weapons and armour, dependent on you chosen skills. The game is very linear, with only three or four choices towards the end. Enemies are hit sponges and you're fairly soft: straight up whacking at monsters can be tough, use the environment. 

YES, the game needs a few tweaks to get it working on modern systems. YES, it is well known for crashing. 

BUT...Dark Messiah has kicking. It has personality. You can use your imagination. If you want to clear your gaming palate between playthroughs of Skyrim and Assassin's Creed, this is one you might want to try.

review: This game is definitely dated, but for its age still looks pretty good. One of the reasons for this is that the character models are quite good. Another reason is that it runs on Valve's Source engine featured in great games like Half-Life 2 and Arcane's own Arx Fatalis. The game has some of the most unique combat that essentially encourages you to not fight fair. You can go sword-to-sword with enemies, but it's much easier to use the environment against them. Kick them off a ledge, throw a barrel at them, cause a platform to collapse and fall on their head, cast a freeze trap on the ground and watch them slip off the edge of a cliff, etc. The developers put in a lot of details that make the game feel weird and different. When maimed, some enemies will try to limp away and call for help. Once dead their corpse attracts flies. As you level up you can gain magical abilities that will make some difficult areas much easier, but you have to select where to apply points. You won't get new abilities automatically. At first glance the game might look a little like Morrowind, but it's way different. Where Morrowind is a big open world, this game is much more linear and has a much simpler story. The single-player campaign story is divided into chapters. But I don't think you play this game for the story so much as for the unique combat. The game had a multi-player mode which seems like it would've been fun, but from what I understand that's pretty dead. Bottom-line there are so many games out there that just copy the same mechanics from other popular games, but this one has unique mechanics that makes it stick out in the crowd as something really special.

review:
PC Gaming Through the Years: A Survey - #12 (2006) 
I'm attempting to finish one game with a Steam release date from every year from 1990 to the present. This had been sitting in my backlog for five years, and hadn't checked off 2006 yet, so I gave it a shot. It was fun! The combat was not for me, but the stealth was well implemented (even without individual enemies having visible detection meters), so you didn't actually have to do too much until the late game. Whoever said you see hints of Dishonored was right, though this is still a rougher, less experienced Arkane. So, kind of perfect for my 36-year survey of PC gaming. 
I don't think any reviews here have actually called it an "immersive sim," because it's not, and... it's really not. It's somewhat like on-rails Dishonored with stealth options about 60-70% of the time (and probably magic stuff too, though I never really tried that). That being said, it does force you into combat a lot more than Dishonored, which really dampened the experience for me. Especially at one particular point where you are not only forced into a duel but also practically banned from using magic. That being said - normal difficulty wasn't too bad. And it was cool to see Arkane's development from their earlier years.
Graphics were nostalgic, seemed standard for '06. Refreshing to see beautiful women in games. 
I didn't need mods or anything to run it on my PC (Windows 10), but there was a glitch where it would crash when I would alt-tab out to check something when it was first starting up.

review:
Quake III Arena is probably the greatest multiplayer game ever made.
Though, for modern systems, Quake Live is probably the best way to play it. The only real difference (aside from Quake Live's hundreds of maps and training course) is that Quake III Arena has a sort of "singleplayer campaign" where you verse bots on multiplayer maps.
This campaign is fun for the same reason as the multiplayer, and therefore I'd recommend—albeit with one notable exception. The campaign on Nightmare mode took me about 10.8 hours, but most of this is on the final boss fight, Xaero. Xaero is easily the hardest boss fight I've ever faced in a video game, and it's not even close. It's barely a matter of skill—the fight is just straight-up unfair. Xaero effectively instant-kills you with the Railgun if he sees you for a split moment. You have to kill Xaero in spite of his overpowered hit-scan abilities 10 times before he can do the same. The difficulty spike is absurdly steep. Though I was able to beat Xaero on Nightmare, I wouldn't recommend it unless you're willing to endure the rage.
Either way, I could never give Quake III a negative review. This game is the PEAK of multiplayer.

review:
This is genuinely the only multiplayer game that doesn't make me mad while I play. I never even get the urge to strangle my opponents. Despite coming out in 1999, it's still incredibly fun to play, and the visuals have aged surprisingly well they don’t look jarring at all. 

The core gameplay is exactly what an arena shooter should be. Every weapon in your arsenal has a specific, highly tactical purpose. The movement is really smooth; you can double your speed by strafe jumping, and rocket jumping is a staple Quake mechanic that needs no introduction. 

The combat loop is perfectly balanced: you can use the Plasma Gun for slight wall-climbing tricks or long range harassment, pick off low-health targets with the Machine Gun, or shred them up close with the Shotgun. The Railgun is your long-range damage dealer a guaranteed two-tap on unarmored targets while the Rocket Launcher is really great for map control and prefiring corners. Then there’s the Lightning Gun, which melts enemies at mid-range but demands rock-solid tracking aim.

There’s no real story mode or a campaign unfortunately, but the basic lore is some bored gods called the Vadrigar abducting the greatest warriors from across the universe to fight for their entertainment in the Arena. That's all the context you need.

Honestly, I have no idea how id Software managed to create such an immortal masterpiece back in the day. I mean, the games they made were masterpieces anyway, but you know what I mean. It’s a timeless classic that aged real well. Do yourself a favor and give it a try.

review:
Quake III Arena is probably the greatest multiplayer game ever made.
Though, for modern systems, Quake Live is probably the best way to play it. The only real difference (aside from Quake Live's hundreds of maps and training course) is that Quake III Arena has a sort of "singleplayer campaign" where you verse bots on multiplayer maps.
This campaign is fun for the same reason as the multiplayer, and therefore I'd recommend—albeit with one notable exception. The campaign on Nightmare mode took me about 10.8 hours, but most of this is on the final boss fight, Xaero. Xaero is easily the hardest boss fight I've ever faced in a video game, and it's not even close. It's barely a matter of skill—the fight is just straight-up unfair. Xaero effectively instant-kills you with the Railgun if he sees you for a split moment. You have to kill Xaero in spite of his overpowered hit-scan abilities 10 times before he can do the same. The difficulty spike is absurdly steep. Though I was able to beat Xaero on Nightmare, I wouldn't recommend it unless you're willing to endure the rage.
Either way, I could never give Quake III a negative review. This game is the PEAK of multiplayer.

review:
This is genuinely the only multiplayer game that doesn't make me mad while I play. I never even get the urge to strangle my opponents. Despite coming out in 1999, it's still incredibly fun to play, and the visuals have aged surprisingly well they don’t look jarring at all. 

The core gameplay is exactly what an arena shooter should be. Every weapon in your arsenal has a specific, highly tactical purpose. The movement is really smooth; you can double your speed by strafe jumping, and rocket jumping is a staple Quake mechanic that needs no introduction. 

The combat loop is perfectly balanced: you can use the Plasma Gun for slight wall-climbing tricks or long range harassment, pick off low-health targets with the Machine Gun, or shred them up close with the Shotgun. The Railgun is your long-range damage dealer a guaranteed two-tap on unarmored targets while the Rocket Launcher is really great for map control and prefiring corners. Then there’s the Lightning Gun, which melts enemies at mid-range but demands rock-solid tracking aim.

There’s no real story mode or a campaign unfortunately, but the basic lore is some bored gods called the Vadrigar abducting the greatest warriors from across the universe to fight for their entertainment in the Arena. That's all the context you need.

Honestly, I have no idea how id Software managed to create such an immortal masterpiece back in the day. I mean, the games they made were masterpieces anyway, but you know what I mean. It’s a timeless classic that aged real well. Do yourself a favor and give it a try.

review:
Quake 4 is great Quake game, but it is certainly not without its flaws. Unlike prior Quake games, Quake 4 is clearly interested in delivering a narrative and having characters. It continues from the events of Quake II, but with a new protagonist. The story, though by no means the most profound, kept me interested throughout my entire playthrough.
This game took me roughly 9.5 hours on Nightmare difficulty (or whatever Quake 4 calls it). There's a lot of content here, and unlike Quake II, there's a decent amount of environmental variety. For a game from 2005, the visuals hold up remarkably well. The new enemies are great, and I'm a fan of some of the redesigns.
That all being said, Quake 4 has a handful of notable problems. First, this game is a bit janky to play on modern software. High graphic settings won't work unless you force them to in the config text file.
Second, the movement feels dull. This is a Quake game. Movement is pretty important to the franchise. At first I thought there was some sprint feature I didn't know how to use because of how painfully slow the movement was. There are stat upgrades throughout the game that make you faster, but the movement never feels great. Ironically, Quake 4's multiplayer completely nails the movement.
Third, the weapon balancing feels like a downgrade from all the other Quake games. Not only do weapons feel weaker, but all enemies are bullet sponges (especially on Nightmare). It's to the point where the boss fights don't even feel that different than some of the standard enemies. This all being said, the weapon sandbox offers good variety and will force you to use them.
Overall, the gameplay loop may not be as strong as Quake II, but the narrative far exceeds it. The problems do not ruin Quake 4, and it's still a great, underrated game that I'd recommend.

review:
This game is basically Quake II-2 but it's a narrative driven game with a lot of waiting around for NPCs to do stuff. The first 2 hours are boring as sin but the game gets slightly better when you're able to move quicker and get access to the rest of the guns. There isn't much in terms of variety in this game. It's a lot of metal hallways and shooting a lot of the same enemy only for a bigger enemy to spawn to break up the monotony occasionally. Sometimes you think you're in for a boss fight only to be let down when it's just a set piece that lasts 30 seconds and disappears.

As for positives; the game looks good provided you patch it to make ultra graphics settings work. If it has anything going for it, it's got good enemy design and a bleak body horror atmosphere so if your favorite Doom is Doom 3, maybe you'll enjoy this game? If you want something similar but with better weapons, gameplay, characters and way more personality, maybe track down Prey (2006) and play that instead.

As it stands Quake 4 is not a good Quake game. Don't make this your first experience with the series because Quake 1 and 2 are so, SO much better and there's a reason this game is mostly forgotten outside of one scene in particular.

review:
Quake 4 is the only Quake I've played. First about 20 years ago. Then replayed it several times since. It's basically about 7 hours of concentrated shooter. You pretty much just press W and shoot. That's probably why I never tried to get into the Quake series in the first place - I want something more from a shooter. But if that's your thing, look no further. It's also much more fast-paced than you'd expect from an old shooter.

But it doesn't have any of that useless out-of-place ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like parries, annoying ammo economy, or “specific weapons only kill specific enemies” mechanics in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ “boomer shooter” of all things. Some modern “boomer shooters” do exactly that while mocking the source material without actually understanding it. That's probably why playing actual old shooters like this one can be a better experience than playing some of the modern so-called “boomer shooters”

I'd advise against buying it on Steam, though. They put basically zero effort into making it work out of the box on modern PCs, so you have to go through guides and edit INI files just to make it playable. I can't really approve of that practice. The full price is also kind of too much for what I'd personally pay for Quake 4 today, after replaying it several times and knowing exactly what to expect. If you're charging this much for a game this old in this year, at least make some effort to make it work properly.

The game still got it after 20 years. It's short (less than 10 hours, i think), it switches pace, doesn't give you fatigue of doing same stuff, it's atmospheric, no BS cutscenes or guiding hand tutorials. It's the game you lock in to and beat in couple of evenings like Prey.
Gunplay is amost fine. The only thing i hate is machine gun. Other guns are pretty much solid.

Real con i see is that it's takes some hoop jumps to run every Id tech 4 game properly: set custom height, width, aspect ratio, screen refresh. Also r_multisampling turned out to be antialiasing, not texture filtering which i cranked up to 16 and been wondering why game's lagging (Id Tech is bad with Anti-Aliasing so set multisampling to 0 or 2 at best).

review:
DISCLAIMER: I initially brushed this game off too fast and refunded it on steam. However, I felt bad afterwards for not giving it an honest try and remembered that I had the game on GoG. I've since played through most of the game on GoG and felt like writing a review here too. 

With that out of the way... 

Quake 4 feels very much like ID's answer to Half-Life. 

The game starts off really slow and the textures did not age nearly as well as Half-Life but once it gets going its actually a pretty good ride and some portions of the game as well as the shield mechanics feel kinda like early Halo games. 

I think its a very interesting game since its really nothing like the other Quake games at all, besides some loosely connected thematic elements from Quake II. It really plays and feels like a weird cross between Half-Life and Halo CE which is kinda cool. 

The beginning is a little boring, but once you get past the exposition and find a few more weapons (about 15-20 mins into it) the game actually really shines. The vehicles and boss fights are pretty cool as well. 


I will say though this game has several pretty intense horror sections with lots of gross-out mutilation and other body horror stuff so absolutely keep that in mind if you're not a fan of that stuff. Those portions don't last too long but it would be dishonest to say that they weren't a huge part of the game. Quake has always been a gory franchise but ID kinda took it to a whole new level here, haha.


I don't think I like this game better than Half-Life or Halo CE but its enjoyable and a pretty interesting direction for a Quake game. Kinda wish it were possible to rescue more of the friendly NPCs. 

<< Potential Spoilers >> but often it feels like the game just kills them off for fun and shock factor which kinda makes you numb to it since some sections of the game kill off minor characters before you can feel any sort of emotion towards them. I kinda preferred the early game portions in this regard since the other characters didn't just feel like cheap expendable trash and had enough personality to be interesting.

If you like gory boomer shooters with some half-life 1 inclinations, you will probably like this game.

Not bad but not particularly good.  I cannot bring myself to recommend it.  Some people love it.  I'm not one of those.  Maybe if I had played it 2005 I would have.  In contrast I played Far Cry 1 before this and liked it a lot.  The combat was just more fun and the conclusion more satisfying.
