Having said that, this game was designed for lower-rez screens, and could really use a remaster.

Why its a decent shooter for its time.
- There's some gnarly and interesting lore behind the enemy, the Strogg
- The game actually had a writer. Not an amazing one, but the story is okay
- The graphics were pushing the limits for the generation they came from
- The unbroken first-person narrative is handled quite well
- The gameplay is pretty good, if not a little slow, most of the time.

How it s**t the bed
- It is not a Quake game, slow, a little clunky, weapons feel a bit underwhelming compared to previous masterclasses in design
- It only really gets enjoyable a quarter-way in
- I want the story of Quake 1 to continue. Stop with the space marines.
- The turret and tank sections are just the worst things in the industry. Luckily they are few and short

It's not a bad game, it even holds up. But there is also nothing special about it. The runt of an overachieving litter. Every entry in the Quake series before this one had something new to bring to the gaming industry. This one, kind of just rehashed everything else going on at the time. 

Not Raven's finest work, but still better than most of the stuff I would consider bad. 
It does what it needs to and leaves the room without anyone really even noticing.

With that out of the way... 

Quake 4 feels very much like ID's answer to Half-Life. 

The game starts off really slow and the textures did not age nearly as well as Half-Life but once it gets going its actually a pretty good ride and some portions of the game as well as the shield mechanics feel kinda like early Halo games. 

I think its a very interesting game since its really nothing like the other Quake games at all, besides some loosely connected thematic elements from Quake II. It really plays and feels like a weird cross between Half-Life and Halo CE which is kinda cool.

Those portions don't last too long but it would be dishonest to say that they weren't a huge part of the game. Quake has always been a gory franchise but ID kinda took it to a whole new level here, haha.


I don't think I like this game better than Half-Life or Halo CE but its enjoyable and a pretty interesting direction for a Quake game. Kinda wish it were possible to rescue more of the friendly NPCs.

review:
Quake 4 is great Quake game, but it is certainly not without its flaws. Unlike prior Quake games, Quake 4 is clearly interested in delivering a narrative and having characters. It continues from the events of Quake II, but with a new protagonist. The story, though by no means the most profound, kept me interested throughout my entire playthrough.
This game took me roughly 9.5 hours on Nightmare difficulty (or whatever Quake 4 calls it). There's a lot of content here, and unlike Quake II, there's a decent amount of environmental variety. For a game from 2005, the visuals hold up remarkably well. The new enemies are great, and I'm a fan of some of the redesigns.
That all being said, Quake 4 has a handful of notable problems. First, this game is a bit janky to play on modern software. High graphic settings won't work unless you force them to in the config text file.
Second, the movement feels dull. This is a Quake game. Movement is pretty important to the franchise. At first I thought there was some sprint feature I didn't know how to use because of how painfully slow the movement was. There are stat upgrades throughout the game that make you faster, but the movement never feels great. Ironically, Quake 4's multiplayer completely nails the movement.
Third, the weapon balancing feels like a downgrade from all the other Quake games. Not only do weapons feel weaker, but all enemies are bullet sponges (especially on Nightmare). It's to the point where the boss fights don't even feel that different than some of the standard enemies. This all being said, the weapon sandbox offers good variety and will force you to use them.
Overall, the gameplay loop may not be as strong as Quake II, but the narrative far exceeds it. The problems do not ruin Quake 4, and it's still a great, underrated game that I'd recommend.

review:
As someone who had not played Wolfenstein prior, if you are expecting Doom with a WW2 skin you are in for a rude awakening. The first 3 episodes are incredible no doubt, however the prequel levels (4-6) leave a lot to be desired. For the prequels it feels like they really upped the difficulty to the point of them being unfair at several points. The game was never shy from putting in mazes even in the first 3 levels but it really felt like in episodes 4-6 that became the primary theme. I especially found episode 6 to be an absolute chore to get through both due to confusing level layouts and frustrating enemy placement/layout.

Another flaw of the game is the packaging. Put simply, the packaging is awful, it's just like how Doom used to be packaged before the unity port, which is to say that it uses DOSBox. DOSBox is a fine application but source ports for Wolfenstein exist which make the game vastly more accessible and gives plenty of quality of life feature improvements, I think Wolf 3D would be much better if it were packaged with a source port with DOSBox available as an option rather than vice versa. Ultimately this isn't a huge deal, there are tutorials for setting the game up with ECWolf and you can just copy the map files outside of steam and use ECWOLF but it's still ♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Probably the largest flaw for most people is the lack of inclusion of the SoD lost missions. Spear of Destiny used to be on Steam but then they merged Spear Of Destiny with this release, the problem being that Spear of Destiny only has 1 mission in this release when the original contained 3 missions. That said, this does not bother me personally as I bought SoD before it got delisted so I have all missions.

TLDR:
Overall, Epsiodes 1-3 alone make the game worth. Episodes 4 and 5 are decent but flawed and Episode 6 is substantially worse and more frustrating than the rest of the game. And play on a source port.

Been playing Wolf since the beginning almost, when all I had was a black and white display and "PC Speaker" sounds. I think it still holds up great for the most part. Everybody knows about this game, so instead I'm gonna talk about this Steam release of it.

Better yet, ECWolf. ECWolf makes the experience a lot better. with fast and smooth performance while not breaking anything (Ghost Hitler fireballs are not slowed down, pushwalls move two spaces always, etc.). It also implements better controls (proper mouse turning), higher resolutions and a map system similar to the one on ROTT. It's by far the best way to play the game. That being said I still play the DOS version for nostalgia and because I'm weird.

Calling it a cafe is generous, as it was really just a dimly lit basement crammed with PCs and masked by a strong cigarette smell. but it was there, where my love for gaming began. review:
I feel like the world does owe a lot to John Romero and John Carmack with the incredible minds behind many games. With a small group of people and team they've managed to always optimize and sell products only with high quality as it was in their quota, especially considering how with the early technology they've boosted Super Mario 3's existence into bloom assisting Nintendo back in the day. So if you wanna praise for what Mario got and received back in the day then these two are the ones to be blamed for. Thus Wolfenstein 3D and DOOM being the big boomer shooter games out there, evolving into bigger and badass with the gameplay and gunplay and still aging too well that still gets the very ease of recognition.

Wolfenstein 3D is the first adaptation where it tries to go for full 3D experience with a World War II theme where you fight against Nazi enemies and escaping the grasp of the very castle itself with Hitler lurking from the deeper levels ahead. Objective is simple, kill all of the henchmen, find loot and arsenal scattered across to help in your journey and finish the mission (and eliminating Hitler along the way). For its time it's still satisfying to see how you can use knife, pistol, smg and a minigun to your premise for obliterating troopers being an obstacle to you in each corner. You can push off secret walls to find and obtain treasures, caches and loot. For its time it does have a great sense of arcade as well, especially with crisp and well sounding voices of enemies giving indication what's happening in the surrounding with every action you do. Whole campaign consists of 6 main campaigns with 9 floors to complete along 10th floor being the secret. There are also few Easter Egg levels to complete if you try your best to go and find them.

Now I should also mention that this game comes with Spear of Destiny being an expansion combined for Steam release. Though Spear of Destiny was separate thing- until Wolfenstien 3D got an update and the expansion got delisted for awhile now. Regardless it adds more content to this little game. Same goes for its Lost Levels both 2nd and 3rd chapters. (You'll need to download these separately if you want more content).

Though game still has its own hindering problems, game doesn't come with a map on this version and I may be wrong but I checked it isn't there. Which does slow down your progress trying to memorize where you've been making it more challenging to go through where you've been. Hitboxes for enemies can be odd and sometimes enemies fire faster than you ignoring shots that would stagger them. Mutants or Zombies whatever you wanna call them are the most evil thing the devs brew for all titles across this little bundle cause holy heck they're such a pain in the neck, they never make a sound if they're approaching you and can juggle gunning you down easily. Hitboxes on secret walls is also stiff and very specific. Sometimes the game is confusing where you pushed a wall and you either have to do it from another side or go all across the other section to reach back there and push behind but no hints are given due to an old game, it's really aggravating to maneuver through secrets if you want some extra dough to help yourself. Sometimes enemies can shoot through walls and curves you cannot see through or through doors that barely fully opened. I've lost count how many times these examples did hinder or annoy my experience but I suppose I can't blame it due to limitations, it's still well optimized and gives me enough adrenaline to keep on pursuing with enough difficulties to try on, whichever suits you really.

Once again Wolfenstein 3D is a staple for what it is and still ages well after so many years later. It's worth a try if you're fancying to killing baddies and bosses.

DOOM 1993 is practically perfection in classic/boomer shooters from what I've played thus far. Great enemy roster, a solid arsenal selection, and reasonable difficulty on HMP/UV. I've played through the modern trilogy on Nightmare and beat UN for Eternal and Dark Ages, so I'm a more seasoned DOOMer, your mileage may vary.

DOOM II takes a step down in quality in map design and it truly shows with the maps not being designed by Romero. Despite this, I still found the game to be highly enjoyable! The addition of the Super Shotgun is massive, and it's easily my most used weapon with the damage output for how relatively cheap it is so long as you're staying on top of ammo pickups. The additional enemies are great, though I do wish the Hell Knights had some more variance from the Barons. It can be REALLY difficult to tell what's a Baron and what's a Knight if you're unfamiliar with their sound cues. The shading causing Barons to look brown from a distance definitely doesn't help. A handful of the maps can be pretty confusing, but I was able to do most without help (the city and palace/fortress were the main exceptions that come to mind.)

Overall, DOOM + DOOM II is a must-buy if you're a fan of the modern trilogy and especially if you're a fan of boomer/retro titles. It's reasonably inexpensive and an even better deal when it (rather frequently) goes on sale for less than $5!

Though DOOM and DOOM II are not the only things in this bundle. Other fan-made games are packaged here which I played as well. For the most part, these are very fun as well. No Rest for the Living offered challenging but still fun levels, Sigil and Sigil II offered brand new areas with new textures and music with an interesting storyline to boot, and Legacy of Rust completely expanded the game to its limits with brand new enemies and weapons that I had a blast with. The other three modes (Master Levels for DOOM II, TNT: Evilution, and The Plutonia Experiment) were alright, nothing much to say about those but I still had a mostly good time.

This Quake port is in a weird place, where it doesn't have enough quality of life features, but at the same time it takes too many liberties with altering the original experience. TL;DR: If you don't own Quake, buy it, but run it with a good source port instead of playing the Steam version.

Quake 1 is such a game that even today’s games—whether big or small—contain a piece of it. That’s because it was built using the “Quake Engine,” a game engine that the team behind Quake 1 developed from scratch specifically for the game. Today, it’s known as “Id Tech 2,” and this game engine is such an engineering marvel that it’s the sole reason games like Half-Life 1 & 2, Counter-Strike 1.6, Source and 2, Left 4 Dead 1 & 2, Portal 1 & 2, Titanfall 1 & 2, Apex Legends, DOOM 2016 & Eternal, and many others—all of these games owe their existence to Quake 1. The game engines for the titles I’ve listed were built and developed on top of the Quake Engine (Id Tech 2).

We simply cannot overlook such a marvel of mathematics and physics in a game engine. Considering how clunky today’s game engines are, with their problematic physics and optimization issues, Quake 1 & 2 truly possess an amazing game engine. I’d like to thank “John Carmack,” the man who developed the game and its engine that inspired and made all these games possible.

Most notable is the unique gothic atmosphere which has rarely been attempted again and truly differentiates this from the many disciples of sister franchise Doom (and even Quake's own sequel). Clever but decipherable map designs, unity of themes & game design concepts, movement & pace of combat, weapon variety, score, all great. I'd recommend playing on Easy for new players, Normal difficulty is actually quite difficult by modern standards.

If you're an fps fan you simply need to play Quake at some point. The amount of content available, and the level of modern polish, is simply absurd for the low asking price.

review:
[h1][b]Quake[/b][/h1]

[h3][b]Time Played:[/b][/h3]

2.5 Hours

[h3][b]Last Played:[/b][/h3]

2nd of September, 2026

[hr]

Fresh off the experience of Nodebuster being a bit of a dud, the Steamy™ refreshed my “Play Next” shelf, and had this as the first item.

Seeing as how Dusk and ULTRAKILL both directly-cite this as inspiration, it just celebrated its 30th anniversary, and was updated with a new campaign from Machine Games...about breaking a cycle to escape a hostile dimension, allegedly, this fit the current ambition for my life in its entirety.

Thus, I did-eth the play.

[h3][b]Yay:[/b][/h3]

+ Before you can even see the titlescreen, you are treated to some gameplay videos.

+ You get some accessibility features, but can also turn them off.

+ The atmosphere was notably-high.

+ Very-much a “boot up and dive right in” kind of game.

[h3][b]Meh:[/b][/h3]

~ I didn't immediately grasp the logo shown on “Unbind” was “Q” until I saw it listed among the bindings.

~ The game never tells you it has a quick-save and load system outside of the keybinds. I missed this my first, frustrating, 37 minute play attempt.

[h3][b]Nay:[/b][/h3]

- I had it randomly keep registering the right key input for over a minute. Reasons unknown, but it was not an issue with the keyboard.

- Even with the quick save feature being known, I almost hard-locked myself by mis-pressing, so that really wasn't more than a patch of duct tape on a split ship.

- This means that unless you full-save at the start and/or end of every level, you can totally screw yourself over, unless you bind Quick-Save, and loading to a key/mouse button on two inconveniently-distant keys/buttons.

- Episode 1's secret level was one of the most obnoxious things I've put myself through, having almost 0 cover, low gravity, and three hit-scan enemies that I swear I was hit through the floor by more than once.

- I did not enjoy dealing with literally any of the enemies, and the environments seemed purpose-designed to corner you in as many ways as they could.

- Lack-of-clarity was also had to me over when I took damage, with some enemies seemingly having hit-boxes that extended past their models.

- When not that? Absolutely swarming you with some of the cheapest placements of them I've ever seen in a game.

- Adding on to these gripes, many of them have hit-scan projectiles you absolutely cannot even try to dodge.

[hr]

[h3][b]Verdict:[/b][/h3]

Though my initial impressions were overwhelmingly-negative, on realising it may have been a product of its time, and included a quick save, I delved back in with high hopes that were almost-immediately dashed to the ground, then flattened by a steam roller.

This may have been utterly-revolutionary in 1996, but that was 30 years ago, and to a player without any nostalgia for it, I can confidently-state all it did for me was make me appreciate how much games have evolved since then.

Simply put, I did not a single minute of the 2.5 hours put into this, so while hardcore FPS players may find it to be utterly-amazing, that was the exact antithesis of my opinion on it, me not seeing myself coming back for a third session of head-to-metaphorical-brick-wall bashing.

[h3][b]Placed in:[/b][/h3]

5: Dourly-Dismissed.

review:
WTF how have I not written a review for this game yet? It's simply one of the best games ever made, it literally defined the FPS genre. I've been playing almost since it came out in 1996 and have yet to tire of it. If you aren't already familiar, id Software created their own flavor of game with this masterpiece (which ironically almost destroyed the company and was rushed to release), setting the stage for dark-fantasy medieval Lovecraftian horror action-hero shooters. All of the classic FPS tropes started here: rocket-jumping, teleporting, explosive pixelated gore, arena-style deathmatch...there's a good chance that you will recognize influence from this game in just about any shooter you've played.

While this Steam release doesn't necessarily offer anything the community hasn't already delivered over the last 30 years, it's been done incredibly well and boasts an excellent new episode that was created by some of the most talented and recognizable names in the mapping community. All of the official content has been neatly packaged into this release with some nice graphical upgrades, all while maintaining the old-school Quake vibe. It's well worth the price, if nothing more than to help fund the retro-shooter resurgence. It's also compatible with the literal thousands of hours of community-made maps, episodes, and mods (such as Arcane Dimensions), making this the most cost-effective $10 you've ever spent.

If you have expectations for modern tactical shooting, this ain't it. But if you want frantically-paced retro arcade action, it can't be beat. And once you play all of the official content and start diving into the world of mods and maps, you may find yourself joining the ranks of content-creators yourself. 

Also, shoutout to my RMB -> walk forward homies. Pretty sure that archaic keybind dates back to this game.

+mlook, over and out.

review:
The best $10 you'll ever spend on Steam. Seriously, this remaster is fantastic in ways that bring classic Quake neck-and-neck with modern titles. Let's go over exactly what you're getting, and hopefully it'll convince you to dive into what I consider an essential purchase.

-The original Quake campaign's 4 episodes- 30 levels.
-The fantastic Scourge of Armagon pack's 3 episodes- 18 levels.
-The cult classic Dissolution of Eternity pack's 2 episodes- 16 levels.
-The modern continuation, Dimension of the Past's 10 levels.
-The second part to the modern continuation, Dimension of the Machine's 12 levels.
-And the latest 30th anniversary pack, Dawn of the Machine's massive 19 levels (With metaprogression and NG+!)
(The raw level count includes Hubs and secret levels.)
-Also packed in is full online multiplayer support, complete with a server browser and no-hassle lobby creation. You can run public or code-based private lobbies off NightDive's servers instead of trying to set up your own from scratch... which is a huge deal for a game this old. Multiplayer modes include classic TDM, DM, CTF, a full Co-Op mode for every previously mentioned campaign, and a Horde mode.
-Plenty of modern accessibility settings including full no-hassle bind reassignment, HUD customization, and comfort options like a weapon wheel if you aren't confident in memorizing the number keys.
-A full refresh of the game's graphics, remaining faithful while upping fidelity and resolutions.
-On top of that is an entire vault of concept art, interviews, and playable pre-release demos and playtests.

The last thing really worth mentioning is the incredibly active modding scene. Quake is known for its easy modding and insane quantity of high-quality user made content... you can easily double or triple your playtime exploring impressive full conversion campaigns, map packs, and gamejam packs. 

TLDR. Play it.

review:
I've had a bit of a rough year, and this was a comforting boomer shooter. Quake II was the first Quake I ever played, and the remaster is nice. The changes are small and show good judgment for the most part. For me, the campaigns, ranked from my most favorite to least:

1. Call of the Machine: Nice, more challenging than the other campaigns (Corpse Run and especially the Caseli Effect are the highlights). The "every unit is a fresh start" gimmick means that you aren't weighed down with too many advantages against the bosses. I liked seeing many more enemies per level. I only saw one Power Shield in the whole campaign. They make good use of the Mutants, very dangerous in packs. I think Ruined Earth is inspired by Half Life 2, which is pretty cool.

2. Ground Zero: The best attempt at making Quake II more challenging on classic hardware. I think the turrets and the Medic Commanders are good additions, and I like that the game-breaking Power Shield only shows up very late in the game.

3. Quake II 64: I like the bite-size maps that evoke original Quake II set pieces without copy-pasting them. I also really like that Quad Damage applies instantly rather than being stored in inventory, honestly this is how it should have been.

4. Quake II: The original, it's fun but eventually you have too many advantages piled up. You can just apply a saved-up quad damage and invulnerability and hose down the final boss.

5. The Reckoning: It's fine, but it's not too much different than Quake II.

Back in the day, Quake 2 was the reason I bought a Voodoo 2.  I remember saving up allowance, eventually being able to buy the thing, then installing it into my computer.  When all was said and done, I fired up the game and wondered why everything still looked and ran the same.  That's when I learned that I had to manually switch the renderer.  That experience of switching from software rendering to hardware rendering and seeing the colored lighting for the first time was mind-blowing.  I spent the next year playing nothing but Quake 2.

This is still a great game.  It might not have the legacy of Quake 1 or 3, but I probably spent over a thousand hours playing Q2 multiplayer and I still love it.  This remaster looks great, feels good, and has a small but active multiplayer community.

Original Quake 2 and its expansions were alright and fun enough, but they were clearly lacking some things and unfinished. But this remaster by Nightdive? It's top-notch 90s fps gaming, even better than Quake 1. It has various qol improvements, ranging from adding unused attacks to enemies, an objective marker (thank god), graphical improvements that don't stray far from the original look and various gameplay balances that are all for the better. Aside from the base game and the expansions from the 90s you also get the Nintendo 64 campaign and Call Of The Machine, the latter of which was designed specifically for this remaster and takes advantage of modern hardware with larger levels and it throwing huge amounts of enemies to you at once. All of the campaigns are super fun to play in this remaster, with the good old typical old-school fps gameplay being present.

I rate the og Quake 2 a 7/10 and the remaster a 9/10. It really makes the game that much better

review:
A really fun, fast-paced shooter that lacks depth and something that makes it unique/memorable. First of all, I really love this game's almost constant fast-paced action. It's genuinely really fun & rarely exhausting (until maybe the final units). I do think it has most of Quake 1's strengths with the fun movement & decent weapon design. It does seem to have more variety in terms of things, but those things feel like they have less depth compared to Quake 1. Most enemies feel the same in the way you play against them, so it can get a bit repetitive at times. The weapon selection is fine, it's mostly similar to Quake 1 but with I believe more weapons; however, weapons like the grenade & rocket launchers don't feel as fun to use as Quake 1's (the ray-gun is definitely a really fun addition though). Again, there is more  but not as much depth/fun factor. Similar to Quake 1, you'll also have weapons that have a direct upgrade & make the previous ones basically useless. The level design is good for the most part & pretty fun but nothing super special. It definitely gets weaker near the end. One example was unit 9 being full of tank commanders at everyone corner; this enemy placement slowed down the combat a lot for no reason. It's not a fun challenge or anything as you can easily corner peak with a ray-gun. Still, this game was super fun to play. 

The designs of the Strogg enemies are cool, but nothing special. The overall aesthetic is a generic sci-fi aesthetic, and doesn't have the same memorability of Quake 1's. I do really like the metal soundtrack & it fits with the fast-paced combat.

Overall, Quake 2 is a super fun fast-paced shooter that retains most of what makes Quake 1 super fun, but it isn't as memorable. I know Quake 2 wasn't meant to be a Quake 2 sequel, but it isn't as ground breaking or memorable as Doom 1 or Quake 1.

review:
I know it's different from the first, but it works. The first game was a creepy fast paced dungeon crawler that just so happened to feature revolutionary technology that forever changed the industry. Its story was vague at best, but the combat was relentless, and with its expansions, it pushed the limits of the engine even further. This game doesn't necessarily have the same strengths as the original, but it helps it feel distinct. 

The original campaign relies entirely on the strength of its combat. As opposed to 1, enemies here are more reactive, flinching when you hit them enough, and they take visible damage on their bodies. Sure, it's primitive by today's standards, especially compared to something like the Resident Evil 2 remake, which has possibly the most brutal gore system in a game. But the rhythms have aged exceptionally well. You have a strong, large arsenal, and each weapon is well suited to specific situations and enemies. For instance, little guys gib easily, so one blast from the super shotgun will do them in. Probably want to pull out the rail gun for flying enemies, though, because they're far away and that thing is basically a shotgun in sniper form. The levels are all pretty standard corridors, meaning that like the first game, there isn't any one part that stands out, but it's an enjoyable piece of shlock and does at least tell a pretty simple, coherent narrative. It sort of set the template for the following decade of miltary scifi shooters, but as I said, the fast combat has helped it age well, and the arsenal is great. It's also worth noting that the enemy gallery is just as iconic as the original game's; the Strogg are a creepy force, biomechanical nightmares who are all designed distinctly and therefor serve specific purposes in combat.

The Reckoning is a side story about a different marine also who is the sole survivor of his squad and as such, he must do The Thing on his own. This pack introduces some new enemies like forest creatures, and gives you three new weapons; an energy weapon that fires bouncing projectiles, a pump action rocket launcher that fires in two round bursts, and a land mine you can place by hand. This one also features more outdoor environments, a nice touch. At first it's a little monotonous, but the difficulty ramps up quite a bit, introducing enhanced versions of base game enemies that are more difficult to kill, and absolutely fiendish level design that will have you paranoid for just about every single corner. It also doles out resources more sparingly, meaning that it can be a real ball buster. It's a good continuation, though, and expands the world of the conflict in some interesting ways.

Ground Zero is just as difficult an expansion, and gives you a whole bunch of new weapons to make up for it, including a laser beam that gibs enemies, a land mine launcher that's especially useful against monster traps and new wall crawling enemies, an automatic weapon that heavily resembles the Nail gun from the first game (sadly nowhere near as useful), and an electric land mine that's quite useful against the hordes. Much like The Reckoning, this one can be brutal in its enemy placements and the levels are also very, very long. It's still good though, and the enhanced challenge is welcome. 

Quake 2 64 was a nice pallet cleanser after the uber tough previous expansions. It's a PC port of the Nintendo 64 version of the game, and while it follows more or less the same plot as the base game (lone marine going and messing things up for the Strogg), this one plays most similarly to the original title. The repurposed engine is used for more colorful environments that are also much, much shorter than anything in the previously mentioned campaigns, with dense, recursive environments and much less aggressive enemy numbers. Where the base game could have upwards of 150 enemies in a level and the expansions could go much higher beyond that, here I think the most amount of enemies plateaus at 80. So while it's a smaller, simplified version of the game, it has the same excellent combat sandbox and satisfying environments to navigate. 

The final campaign in this is the new one added for the 2023 remaster, Call of the Machine. Much like Dimension of the Machine from the 2020 release of Quake, this had Machine Games staff members utilize the Kex engine to deliver much bigger, much more devious and atmospheric levels than anything in the prior campaigns and expansions. The result is easily the best part of Quake 2. The over all goal is to defeat the Masters of the Machine, one of the big things that is making the Strogg. Rather than playing as a lone marine, you are a marine in a teleportation center using Strogg computers to send in other Marines to find data discs that will help find the Masters. Like Dimension of the Machine, you can tackle the levels in any order you wish, but because of this narrative of deploying different marines, each levels sees you start with just a pistol, and you rebuild your arsenal using a mixture of weapons from the base game and the original expansions, depending on the level.

It's great stuff. The Kex Engine took a game known for fairly drab but intricate level design and breathes new life into it, allowing each level to feel like a modern day game. Theming is clear and distinct between each level; one area leans into cosmic horror by traipsing through a mine that leads somewhere mysterious, while another starts you in a space prison with just a pistol and a BFG10k right at the start. These levels have without a doubt the highest amount of enemies, and there are moments of gigantic set pieces in large areas that truly feel like a desperate war zone. Sometimes the tone is able to shift to full on horror, too, thanks to enhanced lighting and far more variety in the environments. It's an absolutely fantastic cap to the story of the game, and ties into the lore of the first in ways that were unexpected. I loved how Machine Games was able to take a game known for pushing the standard forward in terms of environmental storytelling and make it feel brand new, more well realized take on the ideas of the original. 

I know this game has its detractors, and considering how different it is, I guess I can see why. But the combat is absolutely air tight, filled with moments that feel cinematic without ever wresting control from the player, and the end result is a game that's aged surprisingly well. Call of the Machine alone is worth the purchase, but this is a mountain of content for a game that plays to its strengths well.

review:
Developed by Outerlight Ltd. and published by Blazing Griffin, The Ship: Murder Party remains one of Steam's most unusual multiplayer experiences. Released during an era dominated by traditional arena shooters and military-themed action games, it dared to build its entire identity around social manipulation, stealth, and calculated murder. Set aboard a collection of luxurious ocean liners inspired by the 1920s, the game places players into a deadly contest orchestrated by the mysterious Mr. X. Every passenger aboard is trapped in a twisted game where survival depends as much on observation and patience as it does on pulling a trigger.

The central mechanic is brilliantly simple yet endlessly entertaining. Each player receives a target to eliminate while another participant is assigned to hunt them. This creates an ever-present atmosphere of tension where no encounter feels entirely safe. A seemingly harmless guest standing near a staircase may be waiting for an opportunity to strike, while the person casually following you through a dining hall could be your assigned hunter. Unlike most first-person games that reward aggressive play, The Ship encourages restraint. Timing, positioning, and maintaining appearances become the keys to success, turning every match into an unpredictable battle of wits.

The game's cruise ships play a significant role in establishing its identity. Lavishly decorated interiors, elegant lounges, restaurants, and private cabins provide a fitting backdrop for the unfolding chaos. Although the Source Engine visuals clearly show their age, the artistic direction continues to hold up surprisingly well. The contrast between the sophisticated environments and the brutal acts committed within them gives the game a distinctive personality. Few titles can match the absurdity of quietly pursuing your quarry through a ballroom while attempting to avoid suspicion from every other guest in attendance.

One of The Ship's most memorable features is its character needs system. Players are required to monitor hunger, sleep, and hygiene throughout a match, adding an extra layer of strategy to the experience. Ignoring these needs results in penalties that can leave players vulnerable at the worst possible moments. It is an unconventional mechanic that initially feels out of place, but it ultimately reinforces the game's unique approach to multiplayer design. Managing your physical condition while simultaneously tracking your target and avoiding your pursuer creates a level of multitasking rarely seen in the genre.

The game also includes a story-driven tutorial campaign that introduces players to its mechanics and the sinister premise behind Mr. X's murderous entertainment. While the single-player content is relatively brief, it succeeds in establishing the tone and preparing newcomers for the complexities of multiplayer matches. The narrative may not be particularly deep, but it provides enough context to make the entire experience feel like participating in an elaborate mystery novel with deadly consequences.

Naturally, The Ship shows its age in several areas. Its interface and controls reflect design conventions from the mid-2000s, and technical issues occasionally remind players of its vintage. More significantly, the multiplayer population is nowhere near what it once was, meaning prospective players will likely need to coordinate games with friends or seek out dedicated community groups. Nevertheless, these limitations are easier to forgive when considering how innovative the title remains. Many modern games have borrowed elements of social deduction and player-driven storytelling, yet few have combined them as effectively as The Ship.

What ultimately makes The Ship: Murder Party memorable is its originality. Every session generates stories that feel uniquely personal, whether it is narrowly escaping an assassin in a crowded corridor or executing a flawless plan without attracting attention. The game trusts its systems to create memorable moments rather than relying on scripted events, and that philosophy continues to pay dividends years after release. It stands as an example of how creative ideas can outlast technological advancements and remain relevant long after their initial debut.

For players willing to overlook its age and gather a group of friends, The Ship: Murder Party offers an experience unlike anything else available on Steam. Its combination of stealth, social deduction, and dark humor ensures that it remains a fascinating piece of multiplayer history and a genuinely enjoyable game in its own right.

Rating: 8/10

Developed by Outerlight Ltd. and published by Blazing Griffin, The Ship: Murder Party remains one of Steam's most unusual multiplayer experiences. Released during an era dominated by traditional arena shooters and military-themed action games, it dared to build its entire identity around social manipulation, stealth, and calculated murder. Set aboard a collection of luxurious ocean liners inspired by the 1920s, the game places players into a deadly contest orchestrated by the mysterious Mr. X. Every passenger aboard is trapped in a twisted game where survival depends as much on observation and patience as it does on pulling a trigger.

The central mechanic is brilliantly simple yet endlessly entertaining. Each player receives a target to eliminate while another participant is assigned to hunt them. This creates an ever-present atmosphere of tension where no encounter feels entirely safe. A seemingly harmless guest standing near a staircase may be waiting for an opportunity to strike, while the person casually following you through a dining hall could be your assigned hunter. Unlike most first-person games that reward aggressive play, The Ship encourages restraint. Timing, positioning, and maintaining appearances become the keys to success, turning every match into an unpredictable battle of wits.

The game's cruise ships play a significant role in establishing its identity. Lavishly decorated interiors, elegant lounges, restaurants, and private cabins provide a fitting backdrop for the unfolding chaos. Although the Source Engine visuals clearly show their age, the artistic direction continues to hold up surprisingly well. The contrast between the sophisticated environments and the brutal acts committed within them gives the game a distinctive personality. Few titles can match the absurdity of quietly pursuing your quarry through a ballroom while attempting to avoid suspicion from every other guest in attendance.

One of The Ship's most memorable features is its character needs system. Players are required to monitor hunger, sleep, and hygiene throughout a match, adding an extra layer of strategy to the experience. Ignoring these needs results in penalties that can leave players vulnerable at the worst possible moments. It is an unconventional mechanic that initially feels out of place, but it ultimately reinforces the game's unique approach to multiplayer design. Managing your physical condition while simultaneously tracking your target and avoiding your pursuer creates a level of multitasking rarely seen in the genre.

The game also includes a story-driven tutorial campaign that introduces players to its mechanics and the sinister premise behind Mr. X's murderous entertainment. While the single-player content is relatively brief, it succeeds in establishing the tone and preparing newcomers for the complexities of multiplayer matches. The narrative may not be particularly deep, but it provides enough context to make the entire experience feel like participating in an elaborate mystery novel with deadly consequences.

Naturally, The Ship shows its age in several areas. Its interface and controls reflect design conventions from the mid-2000s, and technical issues occasionally remind players of its vintage. More significantly, the multiplayer population is nowhere near what it once was, meaning prospective players will likely need to coordinate games with friends or seek out dedicated community groups. Nevertheless, these limitations are easier to forgive when considering how innovative the title remains. Many modern games have borrowed elements of social deduction and player-driven storytelling, yet few have combined them as effectively as The Ship.

What ultimately makes The Ship: Murder Party memorable is its originality. Every session generates stories that feel uniquely personal, whether it is narrowly escaping an assassin in a crowded corridor or executing a flawless plan without attracting attention. The game trusts its systems to create memorable moments rather than relying on scripted events, and that philosophy continues to pay dividends years after release. It stands as an example of how creative ideas can outlast technological advancements and remain relevant long after their initial debut.

For players willing to overlook its age and gather a group of friends, The Ship: Murder Party offers an experience unlike anything else available on Steam. Its combination of stealth, social deduction, and dark humor ensures that it remains a fascinating piece of multiplayer history and a genuinely enjoyable game in its own right.

review:
It's not a good game. But weirdly, I think people should play it. Partly for the janky charm of mid 2000s sci-fi, and for the ridiculous challenge the game offers.

I found this game to be unreasonable. The enemy aim and awareness is incredible, and your guns and health are pretty underwhelming. The shotgun is decent, but you have to be so close that the enemies will nail you well before you can get in range. The machine gun is also not bad but feels really lame to use because you don't get enough ammo and have to play perfectly for it to be useful. I'm almost convinced this game was meant to be played with cheats.

This is my main gripe with the game - you have to play pretty much perfectly to be able to make smooth progress. There are so many times even in the first half of the game that I found myself in a tight spot and had to rely on quicksaves to make sure I was making the perfect moves so I could progress. It started to feel like a turn-based game. It isn't fun.

The story is kind of interesting, actually very acceptable for an FPS game, although the main character is not a convincing action hero, he is just a regular guy who is somehow capable of overcoming robots and special forces. 

I think at the price, it's worth going for, if only for the ridiculous intro cutscene and to get absolutely destroyed by the aimbots a few times. I think playing games like this helps contextualize what aspects of gameplay are actually vital for a game to be successful and fun.

review:
One of the "typical scifi FPS from 2000's borrowing gameplay features from other successful titles" games that flooded the market after 2000's and kept coming for a while.

If you are looking for something like that, I can recommend this game but only with the fan made patch. With it the game feels complete, without it, the enemies are aimbots and the game doesn't feel that finished, altough it can be still fun.

Game takes place on a mining asteroid where you have to find your (once was?) friend after being asked by your ex. There you have to shoot your way through the game, moving objects with drag & drop, sometimes hack cameras, terminals and other stuff, but almost always just shooting.

You can slow time so the inspiration for this one is clearly FEAR, altough this is NOT a horror game, but a scifi action game.

Also the game can be finished in about 3 hours. For me it took 2x as that because without he fan made patch it was more...challenging...and after patching it up I've started a new game - glad I did.

The dialogues are sometimes cheesy and the dialogue sound quality is strange but this only adds to the "popcorn B movie" feeling.

Yes, the game is far from perfect and you'll se LOTS OF negative reviews talking about perfectly valid points so before playing it, consider them.

And don't forget the fan made Dominus Patch because most of those reviews are based on the non-patched state of the game.

review:
I should write a super long and detailed review. My souls wants to say a lot about this. I'm afraid I don't know any words in the English lexicon that could physically describe the depths of my love for this game and the World of Darkness.

Long and short: The game is a garbage, buggy mess without a few patches, which make the game immediately amazing. The writing is funny, simple and still full of undertones and jabs, it's to my taste at least. It probably will be to anybody that's in any way gothic or alt leaning. That's all the comments I will make on the game itself. Buy it, add patch, play game, you'll have fun.

Just on a more personal note.

This game fundamentally shaped me as a person. It's, at times, a hyperbolic and analogous comparison to the real world, its people and it's politics at their absolute worst, dumbed down to the lowest point. It's kinda how the world always *felt* to me if you took out all the social and political acting to make everyone seem smarter and in greater condition than they really are. Kinda like I'm doing now with this long ass buzzword-esque review, I know.

Somebody, somewhere is always suffering though. I think this game acknowledges that. It made me acknowledge that.

In a mass of lights in any vast city, it will be the best or worst time of somebody's life on almost any given day.
The world is a deceptively dark place. Stay safe, kindred. I'm thinking of all of you.

review:
In 2004, we had two completely world-changing revolutions in video games (among several you might have heard of). In one of them you could pick up hookers, bang them in your custom ride, kick them out, kill them and then beat them for your money back and then some before driving away to engage in unlimited levels of crime fantasy in a civilization in the American West that never apparently stopped being Wild no matter how many fences went up or train tracks got laid down; where right around the time you knew the game, a whole new category of, "Oh ♥♥♥♥," hit the narrative. In another one you could W Undead Rizz hookers into following you into a secluded location and give them the Big Succ instead of you getting it, draining them of their blood to fuel you in your Vampire Jyhad for survival and supremacy within a ruthless supernatural world where there are things that can make even a super-predator feel fear. In both cases, the women involved were actually sexually and physically appealing and generally the men were as well. If you need to guess which game this review is for by now, your birthday year probably begins in a, "20," and/or you might be too intellectually deficient for an actual RPG.

Somehow, both games took place in fictional renditions of LA - the most shocking feature of which was that both, believably, portrayed the urban Pacific Coast of the United States as really awesome places to live and just maybe the pinnacle of standards of living combined with an absolutely mind-melting level of personal freedom. Also neither one of of them lectured you about Current Events. Also, both games can be reliably modded (which we did back in the day with zero corporate interference or pointless updates that seem literally designed to kill modding and don't really accomplish much else) to transfer one setting over into the other. In fact, I'll be surprised if there isn't a WoD/VtM mod for San Andreas already - I know there's one for GTA V for a multiplayer server. Do with that information what you want.

We really did used to have it all. We really were once a proper country and Gaming was once a proper hobby.

Buy this Modern Gothic & Punk Fantasy Gem and be reminded of that fact. Stellar gameplay (don't listen to the haters, it's just slightly dated with a small learning curve and how you spend your EXP on the character sheet actually matters for your performance), peak introduction to an endlessly fascinating setting that reminds you of another fact you should've retained from your youth if not the fact you experienced the high watermark of this sub-culture that predates Steam itself: all the things you thought were cool as a kid (Vampires, Gangsters, Werewolves, Grim Grinning Ghosts, Edgy Hard AF Music, Samurais and Ninjas, Pirates, the Italian and Russian Mafias, Dark Sorcery, Zombies, Lovecraftian Entities, Secret Government and/or Corporate Black-sites, wild and loud firefights, Modern-Day Crusader Van Helsing clones, lethal Special Forces Operators and a bit of believable if unrealistic gory and bloody comic book violence) are still cool. Plenty of mods for this game exist, made by a devoted and amazing fanbase that not only keep the game running even better than it was twenty years ago but also add planned yet removed content and entirely unique fan creations to the game - there's even a few Conversion Mods that add entirely new stories in the same setting for you to check out.

never saw anyone talk about how racist this game gets in the final act. it's so disappointing. for the first ~2/3rds it was one of the sickest rpgs i've ever played. vampires, murder, and goth clubs in early 2000s LA?? are you kidding?? then i got to chinatown.

[b]edit:[/b] beneath all the praise i was finally able to find some comments written by actual asian-americans, along with this article. i strongly recommend reading what they have to say, as i can only point out/understand so much:

https://www.thegamer.com/vampire-the-masquerade-bloodlines-2-racism-orientalism/

from an rpg, worldbuilding, and gameplay perspective, so much of bloodlines is sooooo good. my experience with the first half was so exciting, but too much of the grime i loved in the beginning is losing its charm after seeing whatever tf happened in chinatown. the writing felt so self aware, despite occasionally being problematic; now i'm not so sure.

as soon as i saw "the orient" i was reminded that this is very much a game from 2004. offensive stereotypes and accents galore. [b]then there's lines like the one where you tell a japanese woman "are you lost? japan is that way."[/b] [i]whhaaaaaat.[/i] whyyyyyyy duuude. this is probably a malkavian only line (malkavians are known for their insane/incoherent rambling), but no way can i excuse it, especially considering it was [i]required[/i] to progress the quest. i think i blocked the rest of the godawful writing in that quest out of my mind. it arguably gets worse.

chinatown also introduces a major player in the story, ming xiao, a vampire-like being called a kuei-jin. at this point, the game starts drawing a line between "western" and "eastern" vampires. all the supernatural beings in LA find the "eastern" vampires scary and foreign and unsettling blahblahblah. ming herself seems presented as a manipulator and deceiver who immediately looks down on you and the other LA night creatures. it also felt like my dialogue options only steered my character toward disliking her. the way its all presented wrongly rubs me that much more considering the rest of the writing that comes with it.

there's also the subject of fat larry, one of the [i]two[/i] black characters. he sells you weapons and gets you involved in a gang dispute. considering the rest of the writing i can't possibly be cool with this, even though he was such a welcome presence in the side cast.

at first it also felt like a game for the strange women n sinister queers out there, but no, not really.

random example: i was talking to this nosferatu woman (vampires that are physically more monstrous) who was a model before she turned. she was NOT a girl's girl, and was tearing down this other model's appearance. i hoped it'd be an interesting bit of writing about internalized misogyny until i read my dialogue option blaming all of this on her "monthly curse." i think that's when i finally looked up who wrote the game.

other example: you can find "blood dolls" in bars, random npcs you can talk to and eventually drain for blood. all of them are women. playing this as someone who prefers to interact with women, it took me a moment to notice these things. as someone occasionally attracted to men, though?? why can't i bite that depressed bar owner guy???

it also felt at first like it was sexualized in a more palatable way given all the subcultures present and what i thought were interestingly written women. now i'm wondering if i was deluding myself out of seeing what could easily have been usual the fetishization. there may still be much to appreciate if you're not the wrong kinda weirdo and have a proper, healthy, respectful understanding of things like goth and bdsm culture, along with where and when they do and don't intersect. the real question is whether the writers do.

pretty much everybody/everything in bloodlines ranges from morally grey to awful, semi-optionally including you. that grime, again, felt so self aware in the beginning and was part of what hooked me on the world. now it doesn't look so cute.

is it possible to enjoy the good parts of bloodlines, knowing all this? i don't know. i'm not sure i have the energy, nor would it feel right to stay in like with the first half. maybe i'll play through it to see how i feel about the early writing, but i might not even do that. it feels tainted in a way that makes me just think "ugh, whatever, time to move on."

review:
A very flawed albeit very charming and well written RPG (mostly) that could have been a true GOAT if Activision didn't treat it like ♥♥♥♥. 
I'll start with the things I liked:
- Immersive with a great atmosphere that reminds me of Blade and Underworld, with that 2000's edge and grunge
- A moody, great soundtrack 
- Some great writing, with a story that starts strong but ultimately falls flat by the end
- Roleplaying is strong, and don't let anyone tell you to not play malkavian for a first playthrough cause I had a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ blast
- Great voice acting
- Some cool abilities and skill system
- That early Source engine jank that I find charming, but it can be frustrating too sometimes

Now for things I didn't like:
- Even with the unofficial patch, which is mandatory, I still had crashes and stuttering, though nothing terrible
- As I said before the story starts strong, but ultimately you get railroaded through it eventually, and the faction quests feel unfinished and half baked, which is a shame. Plus the ending is... very abrupt
- Combat sucks honestly and is far more frequent and mandatory than the game tells you (Jack literally says early on that Guns are useless), and you get less and less opportunities to talk your way through situations the further in the story you get. Invest a bit in melee early game as its just better, but once you get to Hollywood start fully going in on Guns and ranged, it's just faaaar stronger for the 2nd half
- A lot of unfinished and cut content, which can't be helped, but it does leave parts of the game feeling rushed or downright underwhelming (like heather feels like a huge missed opportunity to me)
- Some frustrating jank, like NPC's blocking your path in alleyways which happens a lot, wish you could just phase through them, and awkward cutscene directing (weird and funky camera angles and editing)

I really wanted to fall in love with this, and I sort of did? But the flaws are just very apparent and haunt you through the entire experience. Yet there's nothing quite like this game at all, even its sequel failed to capture its magic despite being technically an improvement in some places.

Somebody, somewhere is always suffering though. I think this game acknowledges that. It made me acknowledge that.

The world is a deceptively dark place. Stay safe, kindred. I'm thinking of all of you.

"8/10." One of the very first games I played on PC as a kid, so coming back to it was basically a nostalgia trip from start to finish. I remembered the campaign being much longer as a kid, though — this time I absolutely flew through it.

The Stalingrad missions still hit just as hard as I remember, especially Red Square. Charging up that hill with nothing but a clip of Mosin-Nagant ammo (and yeah, I did get lucky) while watching soldiers being sent forward with barely any chance of survival is genuinely disturbing. Seeing the way their own people were treated makes those missions feel less like a typical WWII shooter and more like a small glimpse into just how brutal that war actually was. And unfortunately, some of those scenes feel uncomfortably relevant even today.

A true classic and one of those games that will always have a special place in my gaming memories. Coming back to it after all these years was absolutely worth it. The one that started it all.

review: Where it all began. At the time, this game definitely gave the Medal of Honor series a run for its money. Sure you were fighting against the same old Germans. But you were playing as 3 soldiers from each of the 3 major Allied Nations (United States, Great Britain and the Soviet Union). You start the game in basic training as member of the U.S. Army's 101st Airborne Division the day before deploying to Normandy. Later on you play as a British Royal Commando and finally defend Stalingrad as a member of the Soviet Red Army who eventually takes part in the fall of Berlin. What set the original game from other shooters at the time was of course the player aiming down the sight of their weapon. Voice acting was good. Firefights felt intense. And a lot of the weaponry was fun to use. Who would've thought this would turn into a massive franchise spanning over 20 years with settings beyond the Second World War. Overall, say what you will about the series today, but you HAVE to add the original game to your library if you're a true FPS fan like me

review:
I so desperately want to like this game.

It has a much more grounded feel compared to even just the sequel CoD 2... let alone whatever the bastardized thing modern CoD is supposed to be. It's somewhere between CoD 2 and something like a Brothers in Arms game. I really want a modern singleplayer WW2 game with this kind of pacing and difficulty. 

However, I can't. The level design is super ass. review:
My negative review is not because of the game itself. The original Call of Duty is actually a very well made game with engaging gameplay and a story on-par for a WWII game in the vein of Medal of Honor. Plus, its multiplayer mode, while I've never fully explored it, has proven impactful in the world of multiplayer FPS games and I cannot deny its influence. 

My negative review is because of Activision. Without modifying the game's files, the experience you get playing is unenjoyable. You have to deal with brightness bugs, limited 4:3 resolutions, and even with the patches so generously given in guides, you could very easily run into other issues such as inverted colors or other graphical artifacts that ruin gameplay. This is expected with a lot of old games, and while developers are not required to update their games for modern systems, it's quickly becoming an industry standard. 

The killer is not just the bugs, however. The killer is also the price, which over 20 years after release still remains at $20. I know perfectly well of the notoriety of the Call of Duty series, how much money it brings Activision, and how in spite of seemingly diminishing returns people will continue to buy the latest installment of the series. This does not condone the price-gouging behavior apparent from Activision with this game. Buy a physical copy of this game second-hand, do your research on patches, and I think you'll enjoy the Call of Duty that started it all. Don't buy it for $20 or even on the measly -25% sale that I bought it on. Do as I say, not as I do.

review:
Call of Duty® is a foundational WWII FPS that still carries historical weight in the genre, even if its mechanics feel dated by modern standards.

The campaign structure is the standout: instead of a single perspective, it rotates between American, British, and Soviet soldiers, which gives the war a broader narrative scope than most shooters of its era. Missions are linear, but tightly designed, and the pacing is consistently strong; rarely does it overstay its welcome.

Gunplay is where age shows. Weapons feel functional rather than tactile, recoil and feedback are minimal by today’s standards, and AI behavior can swing between competent and unintentionally comedic. That said, enemy encounters still work because the level design does most of the heavy lifting.

Audio design deserves credit: weapon sounds and ambient battlefield noise still sell immersion better than 
expected for a 2003 title. The orchestral score also helps elevate otherwise simple objectives.

With some tweaks in the .cfg file, I was able to remove the graphics limitations and run the game in 4K with improved visuals at 120FPS

Verdict:
Historically important and still playable if you appreciate classic linear shooters. Not something that competes with modern FPS design, but a strong example of how the genre was shaped.

The start of the Soviet campaign is a great piece of interactive video game storytelling from the first person view.

It took me awhile to get adjust without this modern conveniences mainly to avoid grenades...or the POTATO MASHERS! Also, as expected, Captain Price is a badass like his MW counterparts. 

After completing the game, [spoiler]when the end credits were rolling, I got the treat of watching an epic mini movie of a squad of Americans lauching a daring rescue of Captain Price from captivity. [/spoiler]

Highly Recommened 10/10, especially for WWII history buffs and enthusiasts. I also do want to note that this game confirms that there are no cows were harmed in the making of this game if you are concerned about the issue.

review:
Call of Duty: United Offensive is a substantial expansion to the original Call of Duty, taking its cinematic World War II combat and increasing the scale of almost everything around it. Developed by Gray Matter Studios and published by Activision, the expansion focuses on larger battles, additional weapons, vehicle sequences, new multiplayer modes, and three distinct Allied campaigns. Although its technology and mission design clearly belong to an earlier generation of PC shooters, its energetic presentation and relentless battlefield atmosphere still make it an enjoyable piece of classic first-person shooter history.

The single-player campaign contains 13 missions divided between American, British, and Soviet soldiers. This structure gives the adventure considerable variety, taking players through conflicts associated with the Battle of the Bulge, Sicily, and Kursk. Switching perspectives also changes the atmosphere regularly. One moment may involve fighting through frozen defensive positions, while another can involve pushing across open terrain under heavy enemy fire. The campaign rarely allows the action to become comfortable, constantly introducing artillery, armored vehicles, machine-gun positions, and large groups of soldiers.

One of the expansion's strongest qualities is its ability to make battles feel larger than the player. Instead of portraying every encounter as a solitary mission, United Offensive frequently surrounds the player with friendly troops who advance, defend positions, and exchange fire with enemy forces. Explosions, artillery strikes, vehicle movements, gunfire, and shouted commands create an appropriately chaotic environment. Modern games can obviously produce far more sophisticated battlefields, but the carefully scripted presentation remains surprisingly effective considering the game's age.

Gunplay follows the straightforward style of the original while expanding the available equipment. Rifles, submachine guns, explosives, and other period weapons are complemented by heavier options, including flamethrowers and deployable machine guns. Artillery mechanics add another dimension to certain engagements. Weapons are uncomplicated by modern standards, but their direct handling suits the fast pace of the campaign. Enemies can still punish careless movement, encouraging players to make use of cover and friendly soldiers rather than simply charging into every position.

Vehicle gameplay contributes considerably to the expansion's variety. Tanks, jeeps, motorcycles, and aircraft sequences break up extended stretches of infantry combat. These sections are intentionally accessible rather than simulation-heavy, allowing the campaign to deliver spectacle without forcing players to master complicated vehicle systems. Some vehicle sequences have aged better than others, but they help give United Offensive a broader sense of warfare than a campaign built exclusively around fighting on foot.

Multiplayer was another significant part of the package. The expansion added 11 multiplayer maps alongside modes including Capture the Flag, Domination, and Base Assault. Objective-focused modes provide more structure than simple elimination matches, with Base Assault being particularly appropriate for the expansion's emphasis on large-scale warfare. The main issue for modern players is population rather than design. As an older multiplayer title, finding active matches can be considerably less reliable than it was during the game's prime years, making the single-player campaign the more dependable attraction today.

Presentation is naturally where its age becomes most obvious. Character models are basic, environments use relatively simple geometry, animations are limited, and visual effects cannot compete with contemporary shooters. Even so, the art direction remains effective enough to communicate the harshness and disorder of its battlefields. Smoke, snow, fire, explosions, military vehicles, and groups of soldiers create atmosphere despite the primitive technology. Audio remains particularly important, with artillery, gunfire, explosions, engines, and battlefield chatter providing much of the intensity.

The mission design can also feel restrictive by modern standards. Encounters are heavily scripted, enemy behavior is sometimes predictable, and progression occasionally depends on reaching specific locations before the next event activates. Players accustomed to open environments or highly dynamic artificial intelligence may find this approach dated. United Offensive works best when accepted as a tightly directed military action experience rather than a sandbox battlefield.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially listed as Unsupported. Players primarily interested in experiencing it on Valve's handheld should keep this limitation in mind rather than assuming that the simple controls automatically guarantee full compatibility. Its design may appear ideal for portable play, but the official Deck classification does not currently provide that assurance.

Another important consideration is that United Offensive is an expansion and requires the original Call of Duty. Viewed in that context, however, it provides a generous continuation rather than a minimal collection of extra missions. The new campaigns, weapons, vehicles, multiplayer maps, and gameplay additions meaningfully broaden the original formula while preserving its distinctive emphasis on fighting alongside other soldiers.

Call of Duty: United Offensive remains a compelling experience for anyone interested in the early years of the franchise or classic World War II shooters. Its graphics, artificial intelligence, scripted progression, and technical conventions have aged considerably, but its sense of battlefield scale remains impressive. The constant mixture of infantry engagements, defensive battles, vehicle sequences, artillery, and cinematic set pieces gives the campaign an energetic rhythm that still works. It represents an era when expansion packs could significantly extend and enhance an existing game rather than simply adding a handful of isolated extras.

Rating: 8/10

review:
Call of Duty: United Offensive is a substantial expansion to the original Call of Duty, taking its cinematic World War II combat and increasing the scale of almost everything around it. Developed by Gray Matter Studios and published by Activision, the expansion focuses on larger battles, additional weapons, vehicle sequences, new multiplayer modes, and three distinct Allied campaigns. Although its technology and mission design clearly belong to an earlier generation of PC shooters, its energetic presentation and relentless battlefield atmosphere still make it an enjoyable piece of classic first-person shooter history.

The single-player campaign contains 13 missions divided between American, British, and Soviet soldiers. This structure gives the adventure considerable variety, taking players through conflicts associated with the Battle of the Bulge, Sicily, and Kursk. Switching perspectives also changes the atmosphere regularly. One moment may involve fighting through frozen defensive positions, while another can involve pushing across open terrain under heavy enemy fire. The campaign rarely allows the action to become comfortable, constantly introducing artillery, armored vehicles, machine-gun positions, and large groups of soldiers.

One of the expansion's strongest qualities is its ability to make battles feel larger than the player. Instead of portraying every encounter as a solitary mission, United Offensive frequently surrounds the player with friendly troops who advance, defend positions, and exchange fire with enemy forces. Explosions, artillery strikes, vehicle movements, gunfire, and shouted commands create an appropriately chaotic environment. Modern games can obviously produce far more sophisticated battlefields, but the carefully scripted presentation remains surprisingly effective considering the game's age.

Gunplay follows the straightforward style of the original while expanding the available equipment. Rifles, submachine guns, explosives, and other period weapons are complemented by heavier options, including flamethrowers and deployable machine guns. Artillery mechanics add another dimension to certain engagements. Weapons are uncomplicated by modern standards, but their direct handling suits the fast pace of the campaign. Enemies can still punish careless movement, encouraging players to make use of cover and friendly soldiers rather than simply charging into every position.

Vehicle gameplay contributes considerably to the expansion's variety. Tanks, jeeps, motorcycles, and aircraft sequences break up extended stretches of infantry combat. These sections are intentionally accessible rather than simulation-heavy, allowing the campaign to deliver spectacle without forcing players to master complicated vehicle systems. Some vehicle sequences have aged better than others, but they help give United Offensive a broader sense of warfare than a campaign built exclusively around fighting on foot.

Multiplayer was another significant part of the package. The expansion added 11 multiplayer maps alongside modes including Capture the Flag, Domination, and Base Assault. Objective-focused modes provide more structure than simple elimination matches, with Base Assault being particularly appropriate for the expansion's emphasis on large-scale warfare. The main issue for modern players is population rather than design. As an older multiplayer title, finding active matches can be considerably less reliable than it was during the game's prime years, making the single-player campaign the more dependable attraction today.

Presentation is naturally where its age becomes most obvious. Character models are basic, environments use relatively simple geometry, animations are limited, and visual effects cannot compete with contemporary shooters. Even so, the art direction remains effective enough to communicate the harshness and disorder of its battlefields. Smoke, snow, fire, explosions, military vehicles, and groups of soldiers create atmosphere despite the primitive technology. Audio remains particularly important, with artillery, gunfire, explosions, engines, and battlefield chatter providing much of the intensity.

The mission design can also feel restrictive by modern standards. Encounters are heavily scripted, enemy behavior is sometimes predictable, and progression occasionally depends on reaching specific locations before the next event activates. Players accustomed to open environments or highly dynamic artificial intelligence may find this approach dated. United Offensive works best when accepted as a tightly directed military action experience rather than a sandbox battlefield.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially listed as Unsupported. Players primarily interested in experiencing it on Valve's handheld should keep this limitation in mind rather than assuming that the simple controls automatically guarantee full compatibility. Its design may appear ideal for portable play, but the official Deck classification does not currently provide that assurance.

Another important consideration is that United Offensive is an expansion and requires the original Call of Duty. Viewed in that context, however, it provides a generous continuation rather than a minimal collection of extra missions. The new campaigns, weapons, vehicles, multiplayer maps, and gameplay additions meaningfully broaden the original formula while preserving its distinctive emphasis on fighting alongside other soldiers.

Call of Duty: United Offensive remains a compelling experience for anyone interested in the early years of the franchise or classic World War II shooters. Its graphics, artificial intelligence, scripted progression, and technical conventions have aged considerably, but its sense of battlefield scale remains impressive. The constant mixture of infantry engagements, defensive battles, vehicle sequences, artillery, and cinematic set pieces gives the campaign an energetic rhythm that still works. It represents an era when expansion packs could significantly extend and enhance an existing game rather than simply adding a handful of isolated extras.

It’s an X game... If you want the definitive sandbox experience of the classic X3 era, Terran Conflict is honestly the better choice. I am moving over to it the second I finish the Bala Gi missions (I just need to buy my TL and the trading station, otherwise I'm completely done).
The only real reason to play Reunion today is if you are deeply interested in the lore and want to see the conclusion of the original Brennan trilogy (X: Beyond the Frontier, X2: The Threat, and this one). Ironically, this campaign feels like the longest but easiest in the trilogy, and unfortunately, the least fun.
Personally, I still prefer X:BtF because it felt tighter, simpler, and more like a true space adventure. X2 didn't quite feel like an Alpha, but it did feel like a Beta. I liked X2's visual style more because it feels less empty, more colorful, and much more lived-in and atmospheric—especially with its cool cockpits. X3 feels a bit dull and colorless by comparison, and it completely lacks cockpits. X3 trades that unique charm for a more 2000s modern, Homeworld-like ship design. There is nothing wrong with that look, but I honestly prefer X2's 90s-style toy spaceships.
It makes me sad that Egosoft never put enough effort into their story campaigns to make them tight and genuinely fun. It always feels like they had a mountain of very cool ideas and features in mind that they simply never implemented. I bet there was originally a much bigger adventure game segment buried in the design—complete with dialogue choices, puzzles, mini-games, more varied missions, and better fleshed-out characters (I very much got that impression from playing X2). I genuinely liked the premise of the Brennan plotline, but it is sadly just a very unpolished, rushed story that was completely abandoned after this game. With that said, I do appreciate the banter between the characters in X3 (even if it's a bit buggy), and it was nice that Egosoft actually gave Julian a voice actor.
In Reunion's main story, you don't actually need to grind or trade much. If you capture or steal an upgraded M3 fighter, you are set, but you could honestly finish the entire narrative in your starting Buster with a bit of luck. The campaign has a very "alpha," unpolished feel and isn't particularly engaging, but at least it's relatively quick and doesn't force a massive grind on you. For both the main plot and Bala Gi, I highly recommend keeping a walkthrough handy. The game can be a bit tricky and buggy at times, and using a guide will definitely save you from some massive headaches.
The Bala Gi endgame missions unlock after you hit 5 million credits and some flight time. They are completely optional and have absolutely no relation to the main plot or lore of the X universe—except maybe for explaining how the M3+ class ships came into being :P There is no real story to it, just a series of semi-hard but short tasks (minus the brutal part where you suddenly need 40 to 60 million credits to buy a TL and a Trading Station to finish it).
Ultimately, unless you are a completionist who wants to experience the full narrative trilogy, feel the retro history of the franchise, and see how the X series evolved into what it is today... you can easily skip Reunion and just jump straight into X4.
