review:
It’s an X game... If you want the definitive sandbox experience of the classic X3 era, Terran Conflict is honestly the better choice. I am moving over to it the second I finish the Bala Gi missions (I just need to buy my TL and the trading station, otherwise I'm completely done).
The only real reason to play Reunion today is if you are deeply interested in the lore and want to see the conclusion of the original Brennan trilogy (X: Beyond the Frontier, X2: The Threat, and this one). Ironically, this campaign feels like the longest but easiest in the trilogy, and unfortunately, the least fun.
Personally, I still prefer X:BtF because it felt tighter, simpler, and more like a true space adventure. X2 didn't quite feel like an Alpha, but it did feel like a Beta. I liked X2's visual style more because it feels less empty, more colorful, and much more lived-in and atmospheric—especially with its cool cockpits. X3 feels a bit dull and colorless by comparison, and it completely lacks cockpits. X3 trades that unique charm for a more 2000s modern, Homeworld-like ship design. There is nothing wrong with that look, but I honestly prefer X2's 90s-style toy spaceships.
It makes me sad that Egosoft never put enough effort into their story campaigns to make them tight and genuinely fun. It always feels like they had a mountain of very cool ideas and features in mind that they simply never implemented. I bet there was originally a much bigger adventure game segment buried in the design—complete with dialogue choices, puzzles, mini-games, more varied missions, and better fleshed-out characters (I very much got that impression from playing X2). I genuinely liked the premise of the Brennan plotline, but it is sadly just a very unpolished, rushed story that was completely abandoned after this game. With that said, I do appreciate the banter between the characters in X3 (even if it's a bit buggy), and it was nice that Egosoft actually gave Julian a voice actor.
In Reunion's main story, you don't actually need to grind or trade much. If you capture or steal an upgraded M3 fighter, you are set, but you could honestly finish the entire narrative in your starting Buster with a bit of luck. The campaign has a very "alpha," unpolished feel and isn't particularly engaging, but at least it's relatively quick and doesn't force a massive grind on you. For both the main plot and Bala Gi, I highly recommend keeping a walkthrough handy. The game can be a bit tricky and buggy at times, and using a guide will definitely save you from some massive headaches.
The Bala Gi endgame missions unlock after you hit 5 million credits and some flight time. They are completely optional and have absolutely no relation to the main plot or lore of the X universe—except maybe for explaining how the M3+ class ships came into being :P There is no real story to it, just a series of semi-hard but short tasks (minus the brutal part where you suddenly need 40 to 60 million credits to buy a TL and a Trading Station to finish it).
Ultimately, unless you are a completionist who wants to experience the full narrative trilogy, feel the retro history of the franchise, and see how the X series evolved into what it is today... you can easily skip Reunion and just jump straight into X4.

review:
I had been searching for a game in which I could relax and chill out, preferably with my own set of music, and I was fed up with my usual go-to games for this purpose. I needed something else entirely. That was the moment when I remembered I had a game exactly for that. Flying in space. That's the stuff! The X3 game for relaxing purposes? Insane, isn't it? Well, I'm not swayed that easily. Yeah, I was in the past, but not this time.

It was... HELLA GRINDY! Absolutely confusing. I was pushed into infinite-universe dark waters without any understanding of what to do or how to do it. The learning curve is bonkers! Never in my life have I been so lost. Or was I? Yes, I suppose I was lost at the start of my gaming journey, when everything was so fresh and unknown. Just like in this game. Learn how to swim or drown, and failure wasn't an option.

Despite its age and a terrible learning curve that put my many previous games to shame, the game itself was absolutely brilliant! The sandbox aspect is phenomenal. It can blend into whatever game you want: a Space Truck Simulator, a space combat game, an economy simulator, a strategy game, a taxi game, and even an idle game! Basically, whatever space-something you prefer.

The X universe has vast lore! Sadly, the plot is not backing it up and is serviceable at best. Which is a shame. The premise for the first Terran campaign involving political intrigues and rogue artificial intelligence was mildly interesting. It took me 30 hours to finish, and there are at least 5 more? The world IS actually living, and being a part of it is so fun. Something is always happening in the universe!

Starting with one ship and building your own trading empire with a huge trading fleet. Getting ahead of your trading competitors by mere seconds gets your heart pumping so hard. Exploration, and I don't mean in the usual sense. I found out about JumpDrive only after 48 hours. That'll certainly put my competitors to shame! Building your factories and flying on patrol missions with your boys. There's so much more to explore even after 95 hours. It's a great time sink. And you know what? The more you break into the game's complexities, the more addictive it becomes. And it's only the vanilla game! I still haven't tried Albion Prelude, which improves the game drastically. There's a huge modding community! It's scary. I didn't expect it to turn out like this!

review:
After a long reflection, I can finally write a review on this game.
2000 hours on a single player game, how is that possible?

It wasn't until 20 hours into the game that I found the game inside this game, the realization that I can own every ship I see.
There was also a lot of research into the game while I was having lunch at work, first smartphone, browsing the x3tc wiki, while in line at a Chinese takeout (also realizing I will never have to wait again, I will always be able todo something while  in line).

Due to the mod like development, many feature where hidden behind strange menu choices, not obvious to discover. This added a lot of excitement. Any normal developer would have would have highlighted new features, would have shown their work. But that would have spoiled the discovery.

So, I boarded my first Hyperion maybe 200 hours into the game? Again, part of the excitement was the research to figure it out.

Building my first 22 station mega complex... then sitting there and wondering: "How do I turn this thing on?", did not roll over by itself, so awesome.

Someone said this game changes from a first person shooter to a spreadsheet game, they're not wrong. Macroing the traders, in your trade empire, is a whole new game in itself.

Collecting all the ships and.... Hunting for the Aran, I was hallucinating seeing a ship in a sea of asteroids, finally found it. It did not blow up, I was lucky. Later I shot it with a repair laser and had better marines. Even space walked it once from a Hyperion (or was that in X3AP?)

Then the Perma Death plan. Getting a UPC so the PC power would stay up, removed unneeded Windows services that could interrupt the game play, no windows update plz. Played a normal game in parallel with the Perma Death game, so I could practice the next steps, take notes. I do not count attempts that ended in under 24 hours. First run ended after 400 hours, with 6 main missions done, my Boreas appeared inside a Tyr after I went through a gate in Terran space. I took 6 months off. Second try, now with satellites at every gate in Terran space, I managed to grab the achievement.

The final act was reversing the WAD file, pulling all the sector data into a html/js file. I kinda knew I'm done playing, because now I'm peeking behind the curtain. Funny note, some asteroids have duplicates, that explained why I could not tow one of my mines.

I don't think the experience I got from this game could be replicated today. The was a multitude of website that supported this game (at the time, for me): X3TC wiki, x3tc.ru sector map (now .net), Roguey guides, Wolfsburgs complex calculator, Seizewell community and of course the developers boards.

TL;DR a game should hold features back, hide them from the player, allow for surprising discovery. Allow for research outside the game.

review:
Personally, I played this as a nostalgic time piece from my childhood. I never understood what the game really was as a very young kid. I was like 3 when it released probably 5 or 6 when I first played it. It captivated me and was a favorite for my brother and I growing up. 

That said, I don't think this game is for most people. Some things are very frustrating, like when you shoot your weapons your ship straight up has a seizure. It's so bad that by the end, when you've got good shields installed, it's almost better just to ram your ship into the enemy's ship just to destroy them. Not fun. The sim portion is very easily exploitable and you're basically just waiting for the credit numbers to go up by using SETA (a time warp device) to speed up the process. I had around 5 million credits by the end which is way more than anyone needs in a playthrough. Once you enough money to outfit your ship with the best weapons and shields, all there is left to do is complete the story, which is very short and not very engaging. To top it off, the last stretch of the story has you waiting on a painfully slow ship to return home. Again, you're basically just passing time using SETA until it reaches home.

This pretty much only exists as a piece of nostalgia for those of us who played it back in the day. You're better off watching a Let's Play on YouTube if you're legitimately interested in it for some reason. I love it and I'm glad I finally checked this game off the list of ones I never completed as a kid.

Please read (6/10)
A massive improvement over the first game, and surprisingly one of the most fun racing games I’ve played in a while.
I came into FlatOut 2 with absolutely no nostalgia for the series. I’d never played these games growing up, so I’m judging it entirely on how it feels to play today. After giving FlatOut 1 a 4/10, I honestly wasn’t expecting FlatOut 2 to win me over as much as it has.

The biggest improvement for me is the handling. The cars actually feel fun to drive now. There’s still plenty of chaos and unpredictability, but it feels intentional rather than frustrating. Crashing into other cars, smashing through objects and launching people through the windscreen never really gets old.

There’s also a much better sense of variety. Different cars actually feel different, the tracks are much more enjoyable, and there are loads of different events to keep things moving. The destruction is still a huge part of the game, but it doesn’t feel like the entire game is relying on one gimmick.

What I particularly like is how pick-up-and-play it is. There’s no huge amount of stuff getting in the way—you can basically load the game up, choose what you want to do and start causing absolute carnage. I’ve even found myself enjoying it more by increasing the number of races and just letting the chaos unfold.

It also has that perfect arcade-racing feeling where you can be having a completely normal race one second and then suddenly someone gets launched through the air, a pile-up happens in front of you and the whole race turns into absolute madness.

My only real criticism is that I’m still not completely convinced there’s enough variety in the cars and content to keep me interested indefinitely. I’m someone who likes a lot of variety, so that’s something I’ll have to see as I play further.

But compared with FlatOut 1, this is a completely different experience for me. FlatOut 1 felt like a game I was trying to appreciate because I could see what it was trying to do. FlatOut 2 feels like a game I’m actually having fun playing, I only had too play for a few hours to see the difference. I sadly downloaded another game and got hooked on that hence the current low play time HOWEVER I will be returning...

No nostalgia, no childhood memories influencing my opinion—just genuinely good arcade racing. FlatOut 2 has surprised me.

review:
[h2]Overall: 7.5/10[/h2]

[h3]Story:[/h3]

Just like the first game, this one doesn't have a narrative/story. However, rather than the campaign being divided into three quality rankings (that of course being Bronze, Silver, and Gold Leagues), the career mode here is instead sorted into car classes: Derby, Race, and Street.
I personally prefer this over the first game because not only does it give the gameplay more variety thanks to the different types of vehicles, but also progressing from beat-up junkyard scrap-buckets to sleek, street-tuned sports cars gives the whole career mode a much more satisfying "grind to glory" kind of vibe. Still though, the campaign provides no cutscenes, scripted events, or personal motivations explaining why you're racing.
However, instead of faceless drivers like in FO1, you're now competing against a recurring roster of AI opponents. They don't interact with you or push any sort of story forward, but they do serve as familiar rivals throughout the career for you to naturally build your own personal beef with/target for payback whenever you get the chance.
On an actual technical level though, the progression is still very straightforward. You buy and upgrade new cars, earn cash/championship points across various cups and tracks, and gradually unlock new events within whichever class you're currently competing in. It's still a purely gameplay-driven experience with no real narrative to speak of, but I do think the previously mentioned points give it just enough personality to feel more engaging than the original.

[h3]Gameplay:[/h3]

The gameplay isn't inherently different from the first game, but there are definitely a lot of changes, the most significant of which being the handling, for sure. Where the cars in FO1 are more grounded, have noticeable weight, and are harder to throw around corners, the gameplay here takes on a far more forgiving, arcade-style approach. It's a noticeable difference that 100% comes down to personal preference, but the driving in this game is straight up way more accessible, no matter how you paint it.
Additionally, this game is generally a lot more forgiving than in the first game. There's still aggressive AI rubberbanding to keep races intense throughout the whole track, but it's not nearly as ridiculous here, so other racers end up feeling like a fair but tough challenge rather than feeling like they're outright cheating. Furthermore, hitting objects doesn't flip you/slow you down nearly as much, it's a lot harder to get flung from your car after crashing, and using the reset button to place you back on the track actually places you proportionally to where you were in the race rather than putting you in dead last for having the audacity to use the mechanic.
Next, I love the swap from bronze, silver and gold leagues to instead be three different general car classes/groups because it provides a lot more variety and replay value since they all handle and behave differently rather than being variations of derby-style smashers. Each class feels distinct enough that moving between them can actually change how you want to approach the races, which gives you more of a reason to experiment with different cars instead of just picking whichever one has the best top speed or acceleration.
Lastly, this game vastly expands on the "Silly Bonus Game Modes" aspect by introducing new game modes and refining the ones from FO1, but I still simply don't enjoy this aspect of the series, regardless of how renowned FlatOut is for them. Launching your driver out of a car just isn't the kind of content I'm into, so I won't mindlessly rag on it, but I'd still say it's done way better here in general.

[h3]World:[/h3]

The world/track design has way more visual variety than the first game, and I personally think they're way more fluid and fun to drive on. The races do a great job of complementing the high-adrenaline gameplay, and there's not a lot of turns, shortcuts, etc. that consistently disrupt the flow unless you just completely crash out. The tracks generally feel much more open and naturally laid out, so you're able to carry your speed through most of the race without constantly having to slam on the brakes or deal with awkward sections that interrupt the flow.
Still though, the maps here follow the same clever trick that FO1 did by just re-routing the barriers, reversing the directions, or cutting off certain paths to create a "new" track out of the exact same few settings/backgrounds. So, while there's definitely more variety in the backdrops, you're still technically driving on a new set of the same roads even if it's not always the same route, and a lot of tracks are bound to repeat after a while. It's a smart way of getting more mileage out of the environments without making every race feel completely identical, but it does become noticeable once you've spent enough time playing and start recognizing the same stretches of road being reused in different configurations.

[h3]Visuals:[/h3]

I have mixed feelings about the visuals. While, yes, the graphics are technically "better" and more advanced than those of the previous game, the visuals also have this ugly, hardcoded post-processing bloom that gives the whole game a sorta, smeared, hazy look. Even worse, this game is a victim of the infamous mid-2000's piss filter, where a lot of the backgrounds have washed out, brown/amber-ish tones. FO1's simpler rendering doesn't necessarily give you more detail, but it's sharper and it provides a better color palette that's actually pleasing to look at because it lacks any major post-processing effects. You can actually see the geometry, textures, road surfaces, foliage, etc. without everything being surrounded by a layer of glowing light. In contrast, the graphics in this game attempted to have a cinematic flair that the hardware of the time couldn't really support, and like 9/10 games from that era that gambled with such aesthetics, it just hasn't aged too well. All that said, though, the graphics look BAD by any means, I'm just not really a fan of the art direction so it's unfortunate.
On a more positive note, this game has been technically well maintained throughout the years, runs well at high fps, and surprisingly has ultrawide support. I also [b]DO[/b] like how the developers chose to lean fully into the arcade-gameplay vibes and increase the visual destruction to your car, but toned down how fragile and easily disruptible the cars feel during a race, so you can continue the race with a hilariously mangled car without being constantly punished for taking damage due to driving aggressively.

[h3]Music/Sound Design:[/h3]

Although the overall quality of both is pretty compressed and dated by modern standards, the music and sound design is another clear improvement over the first game. The engines have more presence, more variation, and generally sound much meatier, which makes the cars feel a lot more powerful and fitting for the much more aggressive gameplay. There's also just a lot more going on sonically because FlatOut 2 is much more chaotic with its presentation. You're constantly hearing tires sliding, cars smashing into each other, debris flying everywhere, and all sorts of other sounds happening constantly, so there's a much greater sense of mayhem during races. It's not going to "wow" you from a technical standpoint, but it does makes all of the destruction feel much more immersive.
Additionally, I really like the OST. It has a much larger variety/more iconic selection of music that covers several rock-adjacent genres, and feels deliberately selected to reinforce the exaggerated, chaotic, arcade-racing presentation. Even though the audio quality itself is definitely dated, I think FlatOut 2's music and sound design hold up considerably better as an overall package because they do a much better job of complementing what the game is actually trying to be and the music rotation is simply better.

Please read (6/10)
A massive improvement over the first game, and surprisingly one of the most fun racing games I’ve played in a while.
I came into FlatOut 2 with absolutely no nostalgia for the series. I’d never played these games growing up, so I’m judging it entirely on how it feels to play today. After giving FlatOut 1 a 4/10, I honestly wasn’t expecting FlatOut 2 to win me over as much as it has.

The biggest improvement for me is the handling. The cars actually feel fun to drive now. There’s still plenty of chaos and unpredictability, but it feels intentional rather than frustrating. Crashing into other cars, smashing through objects and launching people through the windscreen never really gets old.

There’s also a much better sense of variety. Different cars actually feel different, the tracks are much more enjoyable, and there are loads of different events to keep things moving. The destruction is still a huge part of the game, but it doesn’t feel like the entire game is relying on one gimmick.

What I particularly like is how pick-up-and-play it is. There’s no huge amount of stuff getting in the way—you can basically load the game up, choose what you want to do and start causing absolute carnage. I’ve even found myself enjoying it more by increasing the number of races and just letting the chaos unfold.

It also has that perfect arcade-racing feeling where you can be having a completely normal race one second and then suddenly someone gets launched through the air, a pile-up happens in front of you and the whole race turns into absolute madness.

My only real criticism is that I’m still not completely convinced there’s enough variety in the cars and content to keep me interested indefinitely. I’m someone who likes a lot of variety, so that’s something I’ll have to see as I play further.

But compared with FlatOut 1, this is a completely different experience for me. FlatOut 1 felt like a game I was trying to appreciate because I could see what it was trying to do. FlatOut 2 feels like a game I’m actually having fun playing, I only had too play for a few hours to see the difference. I sadly downloaded another game and got hooked on that hence the current low play time HOWEVER I will be returning...

No nostalgia, no childhood memories influencing my opinion—just genuinely good arcade racing. FlatOut 2 has surprised me.

[h2]A 20-Year-Old Masterpiece That Still Shreds[/h2]
Firing up [b]FlatOut 2[/b] feels like stepping into a glorious time machine. It is mind-blowing how well this game holds up. For a title that came out two decades ago, the graphics are still stunning, and the visual direction has an undeniable, timeless charm. The opening rural tracks, with their dusty backroads and scenic country-sides, are absolutely mesmerizing.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3763443774
[h2]Absolute Carnage and Destructible Chaos[/h2]
The physics and environmental destruction in this game are legendary. Almost everything on the map can be smashed, splintered, and obliterated. This reaches its absolute peak in the Derby mode, which is flawlessly designed to deliver pure, unadulterated vehicular mayhem.

[h2]Brilliant, Rage-Inducing, and Beautiful[/h2]
The AI drivers in this game [b]are perfect.[/b]

They don’t just race; they hold grudges, they ram you, and they fight for their lives. Sofia and Jack Benton are, without a shadow of a doubt, the undisputed Gods of Driving. Watching them wreck you or each other is exactly the kind of chaotic energy this game thrives on.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3763443976
[h2]The Infamous Ragdoll Olympic Games[/h2]
It’s absurd, it’s frustrating, and honestly? [b]It’s iconic.[/b]

The mini-games are an absolute blast, but we need to talk about the stunt mode where you launch your driver out of the windshield. Trying to angle a human body through the air to score 160 points makes you truly wonder if the developers were completely hammered when they coded this.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3763456226
[h2]Progression Tuning & The Soundtrack[/h2]
If there is one slight bump in the road, it’s the car upgrade system. It’s not exactly perfect or even necessary, as saving up to buy a brand-new ride is almost always the smarter, more rewarding choice. Every single rock and alternative song is perfectly curated to pump your adrenaline and make you drive faster.

Review:
As someone who has played cowboy games—not to an extreme extent, but just enough to really love the genre—I have to say that, in my opinion, this game is absolute perfection.

Story and Characters:
The story is incredible, and the characters are brilliantly crafted. The game features two completely different protagonists, Ray and Billy, each with their own unique abilities, flaws, and playstyles. This contrast makes them exceptionally well-designed and memorable. Add to that top-tier voice acting, and the experience feels completely immersive.

Visuals and Mechanics:
Visually speaking, considering it came out in 2006, the graphics are more than decent, featuring beautiful environments that capture the true vibe of the Wild West.

The gameplay system also has some awesome details—for instance, the mechanic where you can pick up enemy weapons off the ground, only for them to occasionally break or explode in your hands, adding a great layer of tension and realism to the action. On top of that, the shooting mechanics are amazing; when things get intense, you get that awesome slow-motion effect where you draw your pistols and take everyone down like a true outlaw.

World and Freedom:
Although Call of Juarez isn't a true open-world game, it somehow manages to give you that exact feeling. It might not be fully open, but it delivers a specific atmosphere and a sense of freedom, giving you plenty of space to enjoy the surroundings depending on the mission and situation.

The Flaws and Rough Edges
As good as the game is, it also has its flaws, which are key to the overall experience.

1. Billy’s Stealth and Pacing:
First, let's talk about Billy. Even though he’s well-designed as a character, his gameplay sections can be a catastrophe when it comes to progression. When you have to play quietly and stealthily, the process is way too long, and if you mess up just a little bit, you have to restart from the very beginning. While playing as Ray—who just blasts everything in sight—is always fun, playing as Billy often feels more like a tedious delay and waiting for something interesting to happen. However, a huge plus is that if you get caught during these stealth sections, you aren't completely forced to replay it: you have the choice to fight your way out and defend yourself instead of strictly adhering to stealth (depending on the situation, of course).

2. Jumping and Lasso Physics:
The second major issue is the jumping and lasso physics. The way the characters jump is honestly funny and stupid—they jump like they weigh 300 tons, barely clearing 5 centimeters off the ground! And don't even get me started on the lasso. Because of this poor jumping physics, you can easily slip, fall, and die multiple times in the exact same spot. Things that look simple on paper turn into frustrating platforming hurdles when trying to get from point A to point B.

3. Clunky Duels:
The third thing is the duels. They are a bit imprecise; while I understand the developers wanted them to be challenging, the mechanic feels so clunky that a slight refinement would have made it much better.

4. Enemy Variety and AI:
Finally, the enemies are a bit repetitive. You mostly fight gang members and Native Americans, with no real variety beyond those two archetypes. On top of that, the AI isn't particularly smart—enemies often just stand in one place and wait until you shoot them, lacking the tactical awareness to properly take cover or adapt, though they do occasionally peek or react when you get close. Still, the AI could definitely use some improvement.

review:
A game which is at times clunky and misshapen, but also often gritty and admirable for its reach.

This was 2006, and we were still in the process of figuring out how to structure and design sweeping three dimensional narrative titles. Yes this is an FPS, but it is also at times an awkward 3D platformer, a sort-of-open world adventure, a stealth game, and a throwback to Sergio Leone's spaghetti westerns. 

The gunplay ranges from awful to quite good, depending on what you happen to be wielding. I understand the desire to create a sense of progression, but the early rusty poopoo-peepee guns you spend the first third of the game carrying around often leave you feeling at the mercy of luck rather than skill as bullet trajectory veers wildly from one shot to the next. Once you get rifles and bows in the mid-game it almost becomes too easy to mow down the millions of bandits that clog the west, although shots are always punchy and satisfying. 

Platforming is often dodgy, although the whip is the real culprit. Its momentum-based usage feels at odds with the otherwise stiff and deliberate nature of the vertical sections of the game. I suppose a solid 50% of my deaths in the first half of the game were due to missed whip-aided jumps rather than bullets, and it really doesn't feel good bouncing off the level geometry to your doom. The stealth segments are where we really suffer though, as the mechanics of hiding (crouch in a bush) are far too basic to facilitate anything other than tedious waiting games as racist ranchers and angry farmers amble slowly from one end of a field to another. They are mercifully brief if you can get them right, but good luck getting by without a half dozen retries.

Ultimately a half-shapen lump of clay that can be striking, but is often clumsy and narratively derivative. It is however an interesting look for those of you who are interested in exploring when game design in mainstream titles felt more like the wild west.

"I bring not peace but a sword"

In barren wasteland that is western based games a small polish studio set out to make an ambitious adventure.

One where you play as both the hunter Reberend Ray, a priest with a violent past on a quest of vengeance and revenge for his brother's death.
And the hunted Billy Candle, an ostracized coward who happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time.

The game alternates in between characters after ever chapter or so, with a first person monologue to set the stage.

The gameplay consists of mostly linear levels with grandiose vistas of canyons, valleys and creeks. With plenty a' cowboys and apaches to be shot by, and boy do these enemies have their sights zero'd properly as sometimes you peak out of cover just to get immediately remington'd back to your last save (on hard at least).

No setpiece, sequence nor engagement overstays its welcome as the pacing threads forward with the urgency the story requires. 

It does try to break the core gameplay with some basic stealth sections, some fistfights and even some sprawling sections on horseback.

Sadly for all its ambition, it falls short as the heavy focus on narrative, unskippable cutscenes/dialogues drags the game down specially on Billy's missions as when he is not crawling through bushes or platforming with his whip, he is whinning and moaning.

On the other hand Reverend Ray absolutely steals the show with well written dialogue, great character arc and a stellar performance by Marc Alaimo.

Overall Call of Juarez delivers a solid and fun albeit a little clunky western fps.

Review:
As someone who has played cowboy games—not to an extreme extent, but just enough to really love the genre—I have to say that, in my opinion, this game is absolute perfection.

Story and Characters:
The story is incredible, and the characters are brilliantly crafted. The game features two completely different protagonists, Ray and Billy, each with their own unique abilities, flaws, and playstyles. This contrast makes them exceptionally well-designed and memorable. Add to that top-tier voice acting, and the experience feels completely immersive.

Visuals and Mechanics:
Visually speaking, considering it came out in 2006, the graphics are more than decent, featuring beautiful environments that capture the true vibe of the Wild West.

The gameplay system also has some awesome details—for instance, the mechanic where you can pick up enemy weapons off the ground, only for them to occasionally break or explode in your hands, adding a great layer of tension and realism to the action. On top of that, the shooting mechanics are amazing; when things get intense, you get that awesome slow-motion effect where you draw your pistols and take everyone down like a true outlaw.

World and Freedom:
Although Call of Juarez isn't a true open-world game, it somehow manages to give you that exact feeling. It might not be fully open, but it delivers a specific atmosphere and a sense of freedom, giving you plenty of space to enjoy the surroundings depending on the mission and situation.

The Flaws and Rough Edges
As good as the game is, it also has its flaws, which are key to the overall experience.

1. Billy’s Stealth and Pacing:
First, let's talk about Billy. Even though he’s well-designed as a character, his gameplay sections can be a catastrophe when it comes to progression. When you have to play quietly and stealthily, the process is way too long, and if you mess up just a little bit, you have to restart from the very beginning. While playing as Ray—who just blasts everything in sight—is always fun, playing as Billy often feels more like a tedious delay and waiting for something interesting to happen. However, a huge plus is that if you get caught during these stealth sections, you aren't completely forced to replay it: you have the choice to fight your way out and defend yourself instead of strictly adhering to stealth (depending on the situation, of course).

2. Jumping and Lasso Physics:
The second major issue is the jumping and lasso physics. The way the characters jump is honestly funny and stupid—they jump like they weigh 300 tons, barely clearing 5 centimeters off the ground! And don't even get me started on the lasso. Because of this poor jumping physics, you can easily slip, fall, and die multiple times in the exact same spot. Things that look simple on paper turn into frustrating platforming hurdles when trying to get from point A to point B.

3. Clunky Duels:
The third thing is the duels. They are a bit imprecise; while I understand the developers wanted them to be challenging, the mechanic feels so clunky that a slight refinement would have made it much better.

4. Enemy Variety and AI:
Finally, the enemies are a bit repetitive. You mostly fight gang members and Native Americans, with no real variety beyond those two archetypes. On top of that, the AI isn't particularly smart—enemies often just stand in one place and wait until you shoot them, lacking the tactical awareness to properly take cover or adapt, though they do occasionally peek or react when you get close. Still, the AI could definitely use some improvement.

review:
A game which is at times clunky and misshapen, but also often gritty and admirable for its reach.

This was 2006, and we were still in the process of figuring out how to structure and design sweeping three dimensional narrative titles. Yes this is an FPS, but it is also at times an awkward 3D platformer, a sort-of-open world adventure, a stealth game, and a throwback to Sergio Leone's spaghetti westerns. 

The gunplay ranges from awful to quite good, depending on what you happen to be wielding. I understand the desire to create a sense of progression, but the early rusty poopoo-peepee guns you spend the first third of the game carrying around often leave you feeling at the mercy of luck rather than skill as bullet trajectory veers wildly from one shot to the next. Once you get rifles and bows in the mid-game it almost becomes too easy to mow down the millions of bandits that clog the west, although shots are always punchy and satisfying. 

Platforming is often dodgy, although the whip is the real culprit. Its momentum-based usage feels at odds with the otherwise stiff and deliberate nature of the vertical sections of the game. I suppose a solid 50% of my deaths in the first half of the game were due to missed whip-aided jumps rather than bullets, and it really doesn't feel good bouncing off the level geometry to your doom. The stealth segments are where we really suffer though, as the mechanics of hiding (crouch in a bush) are far too basic to facilitate anything other than tedious waiting games as racist ranchers and angry farmers amble slowly from one end of a field to another. They are mercifully brief if you can get them right, but good luck getting by without a half dozen retries.

Ultimately a half-shapen lump of clay that can be striking, but is often clumsy and narratively derivative. It is however an interesting look for those of you who are interested in exploring when game design in mainstream titles felt more like the wild west.

review:
It's a diamond in the rough, and the age is clearly showing in some places - but a fun experience nonetheless. The game looks very beautiful even now (play on DX10), and the scenery is very varied: towns, caves, mountains, even lakes. The story starts a bit slow but it's good and very interesting to follow as it unfolds. The protagonists have actual depth - they have a driving purpose and evolve throughout the game, but I think that Rey is more fleshed out than Billy.
  The gunplay is where the game shines, more so when you play as Reverend Rey. Headshots are always fatal, enemies ragdoll, you can dual wield pistols and use slow-mo to gun down everyone in front of you as you raise your pistols - very fun to use.
  There are custom maps on moddb and also a multiplayer fix, but the servers are empty, I guess no one plays this thing anymore...

There is bad, however:
[list]
[*]Some chapters are not as fleshed out as the others, mainly the first couple ones where you play as Billy, and you have to do parkour as you dodge enemy fire. You also need to jump across chasms by using a nearby tree branch and your rope - the most broken piece of ♥♥♥♥ I have ever had the misfortune of using in a videogame. Seriously, parkour in this game with the rope is AWFUL, and it almost made me quit. There are also moments when you are put in front of a bunch of enemies with very little cover - basically saying "♥♥♥♥ you, now deal with it".
[*]Shooting on horseback is a buggy nightmare - the bullets will never go where you think they would. Sometimes I think they just go into a parallel universe. The scenes that force you into doing this suck balls because of it.
[*]The game features a lot of time-sensitive scenes where you have to move quickly - sometimes you won't know what to do and fail - and that just become frustrating, they're used way too much.
[*]Hurting dead bodies ends the game...what ? Are you serious ? In a game all about cold-blooded outlaws, I can't shoot a dead body ? This also applies to friendly, living NPCs, and it ruins the immersion IMO.
[*]Saves/Quicksaves take more time than you would think, the game freezes for a couple of seconds and that becomes pretty annoying to deal with.
[/list]

If you like games with a western theme and don't mind the jank, this one is very good - and the whole franchise in general. There are guides on steam to show you how to remove the annoying black bars and customize the fov. [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2873267362]This one right here[/url] is the best one I feel.

[h1][b]Call of Jank[/b][/h1]
 
[h2][b]What I liked about the game[/b][/h2]
[list] 
[*]	The game has a nice selection of guns from that period. I like that the weapons you find vary in condition. 

[*]	The gameplay, despite being janky, is quiet enjoyable. You can duel-wield, ride a horse, and gun duel.  Each character has a special ability, like Ray being able to go into concentration mode and fast fire, while Billy can use the bow, which slows down time when aiming.  

[*]	I like that you can interact with things in the environment, like open drawers, pick up barrels, and smack a horse in the ass to move it out of the way. 

[*]	The stealth sections in the game were bearable. I do like that the game sometimes allows you to go in guns blazing when playing as Billy, instead forcing you to go stealth. 

[*]	Throughout the game you will be visiting the typical Wild West locations, like the mines, a Mexican fortress, Wild West town, and have a shootout on a train.  

[*]	I like that you get to play as two different characters. Billy is more stealth focused and ray is just a walking tank. 

[*]	The game has collectables to find (wanted posters). 

[*]	The voice acting was decent. 

[*]	The story is good. 

[h2][b]What I disliked or was disappointed with[/b][/h2]
 
[*]	The game is very janky, for example, Ray fell through the map dozens of times, enemies jumping up and down in cut scenes. Cut scenes are a bit rough around the edges in general, as well.   

[*]	Soundtrack wasn’t memorable.  

[*]	The game needed more blood and gore, like in the game Gun, to make the gamplay that bit more fun.

[*]	Shame you can’t aim down sight (properly). 

[*]	Characters aren’t particularly interesting.

[*]	Only one type of rifle.  

[*]	The game had some boring chapters that involved hunting rabbits and climbing a mountain. 

[*]	Collectables were a bit boring. The developer (Techland) definitely improved the collectables in Call of Juarez Gun Slingers with the nuggets of truth. 
[/list]
[h2][b]Conclusion[/b][/h2]
 
If you are interested in playing call of Juarez then I would highly recommend you play the prequel first (Bound in Blood). The game is a bit janky, but I enjoyed my time with it. It is probably the weakest Wild West game I’ve played.  

[h1][b]7/10[/b][/h1]

review:
A game which is at times clunky and misshapen, but also often gritty and admirable for its reach.

This was 2006, and we were still in the process of figuring out how to structure and design sweeping three dimensional narrative titles. Yes this is an FPS, but it is also at times an awkward 3D platformer, a sort-of-open world adventure, a stealth game, and a throwback to Sergio Leone's spaghetti westerns. 

The gunplay ranges from awful to quite good, depending on what you happen to be wielding. I understand the desire to create a sense of progression, but the early rusty poopoo-peepee guns you spend the first third of the game carrying around often leave you feeling at the mercy of luck rather than skill as bullet trajectory veers wildly from one shot to the next. Once you get rifles and bows in the mid-game it almost becomes too easy to mow down the millions of bandits that clog the west, although shots are always punchy and satisfying. 

Platforming is often dodgy, although the whip is the real culprit. Its momentum-based usage feels at odds with the otherwise stiff and deliberate nature of the vertical sections of the game. I suppose a solid 50% of my deaths in the first half of the game were due to missed whip-aided jumps rather than bullets, and it really doesn't feel good bouncing off the level geometry to your doom. The stealth segments are where we really suffer though, as the mechanics of hiding (crouch in a bush) are far too basic to facilitate anything other than tedious waiting games as racist ranchers and angry farmers amble slowly from one end of a field to another. They are mercifully brief if you can get them right, but good luck getting by without a half dozen retries.

Ultimately a half-shapen lump of clay that can be striking, but is often clumsy and narratively derivative. It is however an interesting look for those of you who are interested in exploring when game design in mainstream titles felt more like the wild west.

review:
It's a diamond in the rough, and the age is clearly showing in some places - but a fun experience nonetheless. The game looks very beautiful even now (play on DX10), and the scenery is very varied: towns, caves, mountains, even lakes. The story starts a bit slow but it's good and very interesting to follow as it unfolds. The protagonists have actual depth - they have a driving purpose and evolve throughout the game, but I think that Rey is more fleshed out than Billy.
  The gunplay is where the game shines, more so when you play as Reverend Rey. Headshots are always fatal, enemies ragdoll, you can dual wield pistols and use slow-mo to gun down everyone in front of you as you raise your pistols - very fun to use.
  There are custom maps on moddb and also a multiplayer fix, but the servers are empty, I guess no one plays this thing anymore...

There is bad, however:
[list]
[*]Some chapters are not as fleshed out as the others, mainly the first couple ones where you play as Billy, and you have to do parkour as you dodge enemy fire. You also need to jump across chasms by using a nearby tree branch and your rope - the most broken piece of ♥♥♥♥ I have ever had the misfortune of using in a videogame. Seriously, parkour in this game with the rope is AWFUL, and it almost made me quit. There are also moments when you are put in front of a bunch of enemies with very little cover - basically saying "♥♥♥♥ you, now deal with it".
[*]Shooting on horseback is a buggy nightmare - the bullets will never go where you think they would. Sometimes I think they just go into a parallel universe. The scenes that force you into doing this suck balls because of it.
[*]The game features a lot of time-sensitive scenes where you have to move quickly - sometimes you won't know what to do and fail - and that just become frustrating, they're used way too much.
[*]Hurting dead bodies ends the game...what ? Are you serious ? In a game all about cold-blooded outlaws, I can't shoot a dead body ? This also applies to friendly, living NPCs, and it ruins the immersion IMO.
[*]Saves/Quicksaves take more time than you would think, the game freezes for a couple of seconds and that becomes pretty annoying to deal with.
[/list]

If you like games with a western theme and don't mind the jank, this one is very good - and the whole franchise in general. There are guides on steam to show you how to remove the annoying black bars and customize the fov. review:
[h1][b]Call of Jank[/b][/h1]
 
[h2][b]What I liked about the game[/b][/h2]
[list] 
[*]	The game has a nice selection of guns from that period. I like that the weapons you find vary in condition. 

[*]	The gameplay, despite being janky, is quiet enjoyable. You can duel-wield, ride a horse, and gun duel.  Each character has a special ability, like Ray being able to go into concentration mode and fast fire, while Billy can use the bow, which slows down time when aiming.  

[*]	I like that you can interact with things in the environment, like open drawers, pick up barrels, and smack a horse in the ass to move it out of the way. 

[*]	The stealth sections in the game were bearable. I do like that the game sometimes allows you to go in guns blazing when playing as Billy, instead forcing you to go stealth. 

[*]	Throughout the game you will be visiting the typical Wild West locations, like the mines, a Mexican fortress, Wild West town, and have a shootout on a train.  

[*]	I like that you get to play as two different characters. Billy is more stealth focused and ray is just a walking tank. 

[*]	The game has collectables to find (wanted posters). 

[*]	The voice acting was decent. 

[*]	The story is good. 

[h2][b]What I disliked or was disappointed with[/b][/h2]
 
[*]	The game is very janky, for example, Ray fell through the map dozens of times, enemies jumping up and down in cut scenes. Cut scenes are a bit rough around the edges in general, as well.   

[*]	Soundtrack wasn’t memorable.  

[*]	The game needed more blood and gore, like in the game Gun, to make the gamplay that bit more fun.

[*]	Shame you can’t aim down sight (properly). 

[*]	Characters aren’t particularly interesting.

[*]	Only one type of rifle.  

[*]	The game had some boring chapters that involved hunting rabbits and climbing a mountain. 

[*]	Collectables were a bit boring. The developer (Techland) definitely improved the collectables in Call of Juarez Gun Slingers with the nuggets of truth. 
[/list]
[h2][b]Conclusion[/b][/h2]
 
If you are interested in playing call of Juarez then I would highly recommend you play the prequel first (Bound in Blood). The game is a bit janky, but I enjoyed my time with it. It is probably the weakest Wild West game I’ve played.  

[h1][b]7/10[/b][/h1]

review:
It's pretty fun, but I can't in good consciousness recommend this to anyone that is actually interested in completing games. The fundamental problem is that the game really is just the same thing over and over. You find a battle you can complete with acceptable losses, then you repeat. It drags on too long.

I had previously played "King's Bounty: The Legend" and I was hoping this one had better balance, and it does, but not enough to make the game worth playing. I think one of the fundamental problems is that obtaining higher troop counts requires more leadership, but troops have diminishing returns the more you get, so if you have 10 troops and get enough leadership to get 11 troops then you are only getting a 9% increase, if you have 100 troops and can finally get 101 you'd get less than 1% increase in power. Meanwhile leadership grows linearly so it's a long time before you can get enough troops for it to actually matter, so you never feel powerful. You always feel like you are just making it by.

While I don't like the progression, the game is balanced around it, so I can't say it's a flaw per se, but it just drags on too long. Apparently I've only played for 15 hours, but I don't want to go on. It's not even for lack of being able to find battles I can complete, it's because of boredom. I'm pretty sure I've had as much fun as I'm going to, and I've seen everything the game has to offer. Part of me wants to try to get to the end, but another part of me remembers that in "The Legend" after 40 hours I gave up and cheated to get to the end.

I actually started this game over a year ago, and just left it installed thinking I'd casually come back to it, but I always knew it wouldn't be good, and I was right.

EDIT: To follow up after completing the game, I should mention this is one of those games where boss battles are insanely difficult compare to the rest of the game. They require different strategies, and are inconsistent with the rest of the game. Ultimately I hate the game so much now that I've played it. It's really meant for people that want to punish themselves. Even easy difficulty is not for casual players, so yeah just pass this one unless you are super into strategy games (in which case I don't think this review applies to you).

- One of the most addictive casual management games ever made.
- Simple to learn but surprisingly strategic.
- Constant introduction of new fish and mechanics.
- Charming visuals, animations, and soundtrack.

- Timeless gameplay that still holds up today.

CONS
- Some grinding is required to unlock everything.
- The visuals naturally show their age compared to modern games.

VERDICT
Insaniquarium Deluxe is a timeless classic that remains just as fun today as it was years ago. It perfectly blends casual gameplay with resource management, creating an experience that's easy to pick up but difficult to put down. If you've never played it before, it's absolutely worth experiencing. Even today, it stands as one of the best casual management games ever made.

4/5

review:
[h1] Fun little game with potential. 4/5 [/h1]

This is not a hard or long game to beat. Under 6 hours to complete it and I think that is why people enjoy it. It plays like a quick romp through aquarium management and care taking with a fun twist to keep you engaged. 

The developers; PopCap games,  added aliens to make it an actual game vs a simple fish aquarium simulator. The aliens add a bit of craziness to the experience to make it fun. Check out the shared photos of this game in the community tab to see how crazy this game can get.  

My issue with the game is that I wanted more from it. I had a blast playing and completing this game, even with it being on the easier side. It's age does show but now that EA has acquired PopCap games, you would think a sequel or remaster is in the works to update this game. [spoiler] EA does not. They bought this game in the hype and then let it dry up. Lwk wasted IP purchase. [/spoiler]

If you are looking for quick fun with a relaxing time playing and love fish and aquariums, this game is it. It will scratch a certain itch...

[u] Side note [/u] - And as the comments do mention, this game was first released on a website to play videogames years ago, like more then 1 year ago. So for some this game is a nostalgia trip and playing it still satisfies. They just don't make games like this no more...

review:
Peggle, I would argue, is one of the highest-placing contenders for the greatest game of all time. Not because of its enriching story or whatever, but simply because it succeeds with flying colors on the one thing it sets out to do: be a fun, entertaining, casual video game.

It combines RNG and luck with strategy in a way that is easy for anyone in the world to pick up and play, but is insanely difficult to master outright. It has a boatload of content featuring 100+ levels and that's just for this game.

Despite the games 20-year-old age, what saves its low-quality graphics is Peggle's spectacular art design. It's weird, it's esoteric, but it's also calming. Combined with its infinitely satisfying sound effects and music, makes for an experience that gives you the perfect amount of dopamine when Ode to Joy plays after every level, or when you get a huge combo and the sound that plays when you hit a peg begins to increase on a chromatic scale.

The game is never too hand-holdy. It gives you powerups that are unique to every Peggle Master, but they are not required to complete every level. The gameplay is simple enough for the game to not have to explain every little bit to you, but the difficulty ramps up near the end of the game, and especially in the challenge levels.

The gameplay is perfect, there's not a note to be given. The physics are sometimes your friend, but sometimes your enemy. They're a slippery slope that requires you to think about trajectories, angles, and how to use the engine to your advantage.

Every person on Earth should at least have played one level of Peggle. Because at the end of the day, it's an exquisitely crafted masterpiece that deserves all the praise it gets.

Peggle is a casual puzzle video game developed by PopCap Games. Initially released for Microsoft and Mac OS X systems in 2007, it has since had versions released for Xbox Live Arcade, PlayStation Network, the Nintendo DS (with the help of Q Entertainment), Windows Mobile, iOS, Zeebo, and Android; the game has also been ported as a Java application, and an extended minigame incorporated into the massively multiplayer online game World of Warcraft. A sequel was released in September 2008, titled Peggle Nights. PopCap, a subsidiary of Electronic Arts, announced Peggle 2 at E3 2013.

Inspired by pachinko and bagatelle, each level of Peggle challenges the player to shoot a limited supply of balls at a field of colored pegs to clear out specifically marked pegs while attempting to achieve a high score through skilled shot planning. Special powers associated with a diverse cast of cartoon "Peggle Masters" can be activated to aid the player in this task. Peggle initially sold slowly but was boosted by the inclusion of a specially designed demonstration in Valve's The Orange Box, and has since been downloaded over 50 million times.

Hey kiddo, Handsome Jack here... and I just played Peggle Nights, and I have to say, this is either the greatest psychological experiment ever conducted or the most dangerously addictive game I've ever played. I'm supposed to be running a corporation, conquering planets, and generally being the most important man in the universe, and instead I'm sitting here shooting a tiny orange ball at pegs for six hours.

I have become the ball.

You line up the shot. You calculate the angle. You release it. And then you just sit there watching this tiny sphere bounce around the screen like it's personally determined to destroy every last peg. One hit becomes five. Five becomes twenty. Suddenly fireworks are going off, the screen is screaming, classical music is playing, and I'm experiencing a level of euphoria that should probably require a medical license.

And then you miss the bucket.

Oh.

THE BUCKET.

You spend ten minutes planning the perfect shot, and the ball lands one pixel away from that beautiful orange bucket.

That isn't failure.

That's sabotage.

The bucket moved.

I saw it.

Someone at PopCap is tampering with my trajectory.

And the Peggle Masters? Completely insane. Unicorns, pumpkins, robots, dragons, mystical creatures... apparently the entire Peggle universe is populated by adorable little freaks whose sole purpose is watching me destroy colored circles. And I respect them for it.

The dream levels are especially ridiculous. You'd think I'd be dreaming about Hyperion, money, power, my beautiful face...

Nope.

I'm dreaming about PEGGLE.

I've lost control, kiddo.

But when you get that perfect shot? Oh, it's glorious. Every peg explodes. The ball bounces exactly where you want it. The bucket catches it. The fireworks go off.

EXTREME FEVER.

That's not a bonus.

That's enlightenment.

10/10.

Absolute masterpiece.

I'd give it 11, but apparently there are only so many pegs you can destroy before the game decides you've had enough fun.

Cowards.

Now, if you'll excuse me, I have a corporation to run.

Right after this level.

And the next one.

And probably the one after that.

What's next: Peggle Deluxe chaos or a more unhinged 10/10 for Peggle 2?

review:
Peggle Nights really captures the dream logic driven narrative that the original Peggle was aiming for, in a much more well established and meaningful way. 

Opting in to use live action cutscenes instead of the animated stills of the original, the story is divided into several acts, where we get to see the fallout of the original Peggle. Jimmy Lightning is getting hammered every night, unable to accept the shame of what he did to Claude, Warren Rabbit now on a desperate mission to escape New Mexico after blowing up their Peggle Institution in the first one, and don't even get me started on the Lord Cinderbottom romance narrative.

Because of this, Popcap was able to create a sense of overwhelming terror that clutched the plot, leaving you the viewer unsure of what's true and what's a lie. I believe that by making Bjorn an unreliable narrator this time, it makes you question the ethics of what it is you're doing. Do the orange pegs really deserve my wrath, or is my anger just a product of the hatred Bjorn placed in my heart towards them?

I'm excited to see how they continue this story in Peggle 2, which I will soon be engaging with.

review:
After completing Plants vs. Zombies: Game of the Year Edition 100%, I can confidently say that this is still one of the most enjoyable tower-defense games I've played. What initially looks like a simple game about plants fighting zombies turns into a surprisingly deep, entertaining, and highly replayable experience.

The main Adventure Mode does an excellent job introducing the game's mechanics. You start with simple plants such as the Peashooter, Sunflower, and Wall-nut, but the game constantly introduces new plants and zombie types that force you to change your strategy. Each environment adds something different, from the nighttime stages and swimming pool to the fog-covered levels and challenging rooftop stages.

The biggest strength of the game is its strategic gameplay. Every plant has a purpose, and success depends on knowing when and where to use them. Sunflowers provide the resources needed to build your defenses, while offensive plants deal with incoming zombies and defensive plants buy valuable time. Special zombies such as Pole Vaulting, Digger, Balloon, and Football Zombies force you to prepare for different threats rather than relying on one strategy.

Reaching 100% completion makes you appreciate just how much content the game offers beyond Adventure Mode. The mini-games are particularly enjoyable because they completely change the normal gameplay. Wall-nut Bowling, Vasebreaker, Beghouled, and I, Zombie provide different challenges and demonstrate how flexible the game's mechanics are.

Survival Mode is where the game becomes significantly more challenging. Surviving multiple waves requires careful resource management, strong plant combinations, and a well-planned defensive layout. Some of the later challenges can be difficult, but successfully surviving them is extremely satisfying.

The Zen Garden is another nice addition. After spending hours fighting zombies, taking care of plants provides a relaxing change of pace. It also adds more personality to the game's world.

Speaking of personality, that's another reason the game remains memorable. The colorful art style, funny zombie designs, Crazy Dave's ridiculous behavior, catchy music, and amusing animations give the game a unique charm. Even after many hours, the presentation rarely feels boring.

There are a few weaknesses. Some mini-games can become repetitive after mastering them, and certain 100% completion challenges can feel more like endurance tests than strategic experiences. The visuals and interface also show their age compared with modern games. However, these issues are relatively minor.

After completing the entire game, my biggest takeaway is how well Plants vs. Zombies balances simplicity, strategy, humor, and replayability. It is easy enough for newcomers to understand but has enough depth to keep experienced players experimenting.

Plants vs. Zombies: Game of the Year Edition remains an excellent tower-defense game. Completing it 100% made me appreciate its variety and design even more. It's funny, challenging, relaxing, and addictive in equal measure.

Even after unlocking everything, I can still imagine coming back, planting a few Sunflowers, setting up my defenses, and thinking:

"Alright... let's defend the lawn one more time."

review:
The game that started a really good WW2 franchise! I got this game in primary school, because a colleague got it as a gift on a magazine, but was not playing games, so they gave it to me, and I loved it from the start.
The graphics do look now dated, but are still beautiful, walking through the ruins of Berlin in the dying breath of WW2 and the russian army getting closer and closer to finish the remnants of the german army.
The whole point of this game, the sniping, is done beautifully:
- The different types of rifles you come across the game
- The distances slowly increase every level
- Bullet drop, wind, heart-rate, everything influences every shot you take
- Set pieces of providing covering fire to your allies are action packed and fun
- Stealth also works nicely, being able to use a suppressed gun, and move the bodies away to not attract the attention of any other guard that may pass through
- The traps you can leave behind you as cover or to stop vehicles in their tracks(the trip wire grenades being so satisfying to use)
Also, as always, some cons:
- The level design feels at times repetitive: some are 100% unique, but some(probably due to the limitations of the time) use the same textures and structures, and feels like you never left the first stage, but the streets being so different and weather changing do manage to make up for it.
- The single most annoying: which is the ice skating walking. Clearly the movement system was not meant for this kind of purpose, with your character constantly sliding and it feels hard to control when you need to move faster
- Enemies sometimes have deadly accuracy even though they are far from you, and use automatic weapons, and can drain your HP in seconds
Overall, it is a game worth playing, and of course, the entry point in the franchise!

Not a good game. You can definetely play only from the V2 onwards and lose nothing. The game is unfair and unbalanced. There are bots that spawn out of nowhere in an area you just cleared for no reason, and they always know your location 100% of the time no matter if you remained stealthy the entire mission.

On top of that, the ballistics are unrealistic and linear, and the scope doesnt scales up the bullet drop markings with the zoom, so for every zoom level the markings are different, which completely turns off your aim. 

The damage is totally unrealistic, enemies tank bullets to the chest like its nothing, and they can accuratelly hit you with submachineguns while on the move from 100+ meter away, meanwhile your pistol and machinegun basically stop working from above 10 meter of distance. The gewehr and SVT, which carry 10 bullets irl, only have 5 bullets in the game, and the mosin nagant is missing the bolt action reload.

The level design is not good, the missions are choppy and its design and tasks are convoluted.

This game is unpolished, unbalanced and doesnt rewards stealth. It sucked finishing the campaign, the hardest difficulty felt too easy and too hard the entire time, and hard not in a fair or rewarding way, more like a guy spawning behind you in an area you just cleaned and coming to your position like an omniscient god.

One of the worst games Ive ever played in my entire life. And Im not saying this because its old, most of the games Ive played are pre-2010, and I always try to make an analysis based on the time it was released and the technology and techniques avaliable at the time, I would never analyse a game from a modern scope. That being said, this is not a good game I wouldnt recommend it. review:
The unfortunate reality is that even if it was nice reliving childhood for a bit, since I still remember the first levels of the marine and predator campaign even after all these years. It soon became clear why I do remember only the first levels.

The good:
[list]
[*] The game plays and looks good for the release date.
[*] Playing as marine and predator has some fun moments.
[*] The slowly flying head when using predator's speargun is funny.
[/list]

The bad:

Absolutely abysmal game design. The font is too small on higher resolution. Does not stay for long enough. Often times getting interrupted by aliens during dialogs. Which is problematic since it often times says what is your next goal. All of this is accompanied by often times highly questionable level design. Here are some examples:

[list]
[*] During the predator playthrough there are vents that had to be destroyed to progress. The "vents" do not look like vents at all, they do not even stick out, it is just a texture on a wall. 

[*] Marine campaign had mission where you had to turn on 5 valves. To get to the last two you had to shoot platform, which I am pretty sure that 99% players had to look up. The only thing that hints at it is yellow "warning" blinking light, which is not enough, since it simply looks like environmental detail. Together with this it is absolutely not clear which valves can be turned on and which not, since there is like 15 of them. 

[*] Playing as alien is awful experience (but to give the devs some slack, I really do not see how they could make it much better). The alien is weak and while I could stomach the wall movement some people may not. The other 2 campaigns do have some redeemable qualities, but the alien playthrough felt so bad that I had to stop during first level.
[/list]

The final result: 
[list]
[*] The alien campaign is probably not worth your time.
[*] The game really suffers from being way too confusing on first playthrough. The subsequent playthrough when you already know where to go would probably be more fun. But since I am "one and done" person I have to rate this negatively.
[/list]

review:
Its not a bad game at all but for someone who doesn't have a lot of time outside of my days off to play video games I just couldn't get into it. I'm into retro gaming and I've basically played video games from the 90s and 2000s for most of my life but I just couldn't get into this one.

I'm sure people with a lot of free time on their hands will enjoy this but with my limited time its a hard pass for me, If you're someone like me who just wants to sit down and have some fun after a long stressful day of work or to wind down on the weekends save yourself the trouble and consider another title this isn't for you this game has a high skill ceiling, outdated controls and a very unforgiving enemy AI plus the levels are so dark and those Alien bastards just blend in most of the time you dont even get to see where they come from lastly the game doesn't work well out of the box its a mess and you have to install a few patches to get it to work on modern computers.


If you're still someone who believes this is a skill issue then by all means go ahead and I hope you enjoy this. For others I've already explained why you shouldn't, Ultimately I wish anyone who plays this genuinely enjoys it. It's not a bad game so I'm not going to give it a thumbs down its just not for me
label: True

review:
You can tell it's an old one. The predator controls feel clunky, the graphics are half life 1 level, perhaps worse, and the biggest challenge you'll have doing the campaigns is not the enemies, but navigating them. The amount of time I lost being LOST takes up a good chunk of my playtime.

That said, it's still enjoyable for what it is. I 100% it today (Did all main campaigns on highest difficulty and finished the bonus missions). Honestly, the missions that are locked behind you beating the game on the highest difficulty, are worth it. I'd recommend (At least for Alien) beating the game on realistic first, then try director.


It's fun, what can I say? This specific version comes with bonus missions that let you interact with other species's campaign maps. It's interesting seeing maps from the perspective of a new person. 

6.5/10. Given how cheap it is usually, I'd recommend!
label: True

review:
The unfortunate reality is that even if it was nice reliving childhood for a bit, since I still remember the first levels of the marine and predator campaign even after all these years. It soon became clear why I do remember only the first levels.

The good:
[list]
[*] The game plays and looks good for the release date.
[*] Playing as marine and predator has some fun moments.
[*] The slowly flying head when using predator's speargun is funny.
[/list]

The bad:

Absolutely abysmal game design. The font is too small on higher resolution. Does not stay for long enough. Often times getting interrupted by aliens during dialogs. Which is problematic since it often times says what is your next goal. All of this is accompanied by often times highly questionable level design. Here are some examples:

[list]
[*] During the predator playthrough there are vents that had to be destroyed to progress. The "vents" do not look like vents at all, they do not even stick out, it is just a texture on a wall. 

[*] Marine campaign had mission where you had to turn on 5 valves. To get to the last two you had to shoot platform, which I am pretty sure that 99% players had to look up. The only thing that hints at it is yellow "warning" blinking light, which is not enough, since it simply looks like environmental detail. Together with this it is absolutely not clear which valves can be turned on and which not, since there is like 15 of them. 

[*] Playing as alien is awful experience (but to give the devs some slack, I really do not see how they could make it much better). The alien is weak and while I could stomach the wall movement some people may not. The other 2 campaigns do have some redeemable qualities, but the alien playthrough felt so bad that I had to stop during first level.
[/list]

The final result: 
[list]
[*] The alien campaign is probably not worth your time.
[*] The game really suffers from being way too confusing on first playthrough. The subsequent playthrough when you already know where to go would probably be more fun. But since I am "one and done" person I have to rate this negatively.
[/list]
